quarterly_data.signal: Vera Rubin preparation (CEO): Supermicro is 'also preparing for upcoming NVIDIA, Vera Rubin and AMD Helios solutions for the second half this year'. Asked whether orders had started for second-half delivery, he said 'we have a lot of highly interested customers, some already engaged' and that 'today, we already have some good commitment from customers'. Timing 'depends on our partner, depends on when their Vera Rubin or AMD solution will be ready'. On differentiation in the Vera Rubin cycle, he said Supermicro optimizes the whole DCBBS for customers based on NVIDIA's solution (energy consumption, energy backup and, 'maybe too early to say', grid power replacement). Speaking generally about time-to-market, he expects to keep bringing total solutions to market ahead of others, 'if not 6 months earlier, at least 3 months or 4 months earlier'.
quarterly_data.figure: Vera Rubin solutions targeted for the second half this year; time-to-market lead of 'if not 6 months earlier, at least 3 months or 4 months earlier'

quarterly_data.signal: Working with Intel and others on upcoming Xeon 6+ platforms plus new Arm-based and AMD EPYC 'Venus' additions to the portfolio; system building-block + data-center-scale architecture lets Supermicro support a wide variety of compute platforms optimized per vertical.
quarterly_data.figure: Xeon 6+, Arm, EPYC 'Venus' CPU platforms in portfolio

quarterly_data.signal: CPU / enterprise pivot is now the margin story. Enterprise and channel revenue was $5.6B in Q4 = 50% of total revenue (vs 28% in Q3), +172% YoY and +98% QoQ, driven by enterprise customers upgrading compute, storage and network infrastructure onto more efficient CPU platforms; OEM appliance + large-datacenter revenue was $5.5B, also 50% (-26% QoQ). Dedicated departments added since early 2026 for enterprise, plus expanded enterprise CPU-based server, storage and IoT product lines. Mix commentary: roughly 70-something % GPU / high-20s % CPU; of the ~80% AI revenue expected going forward, ~60-70pp is pure AI and 10-20pp is CPU-based AI / agentic AI / edge AI, with the remaining ~20% traditional server, storage and IoT. CPU-based AI is growing quickly across NVIDIA Vera, AMD, Arm and Intel.
quarterly_data.figure: Enterprise & channel $5.6B = 50% of Q4 rev (+172% YoY); ~high-20s% CPU mix

quarterly_data.signal: CPU platform roadmap: shipping the Intel GM6 Plus platform in volume and brought the Intel PUZZLE Edge AI system to market; developing product for strong demand on an Arm CPU platform (codename 'Phoenix' architecture) optimized for performance-per-watt inferencing; preparing NVIDIA Vera CPU and other high-density Vera systems; strong AMD EPYC CPU volume. Some AMD and Intel CPU platforms are moving to liquid cooling alongside Vera.
quarterly_data.figure: Intel GM6 Plus in volume + PUZZLE Edge AI; Arm 'Phoenix'; Vera CPU; EPYC

quarterly_data.signal: Enterprise diversification (CEO/CFO): the enterprise channel segment was $2 billion in Q2, about 16% of revenue versus 31% in the prior quarter (up 42% YoY and 29% QoQ). Supermicro is sharpening its focus on traditional enterprise, cloud and edge IoT customers to diversify revenue toward higher margins. It introduced X14 and H14 solutions: preconfigured systems that ship directly from the factory, are optimized for specific AI, cloud, storage and telco edge workloads, and are 'ready to power immediately' for enterprise customers, channel partners and SMB end users. The CEO said the company is 'very aggressively growing enterprise midsized' accounts while still pursuing large accounts.
quarterly_data.figure: enterprise channel revenue $2 billion (about 16% of revenue vs 31% prior quarter; up 42% YoY)

quarterly_data.signal: Component procurement scaled ahead of the FY2027 ramp: closing inventory $12.9B, up from $11.1B, built in anticipation of higher revenue; the $5.6B June equity raise is described as fully supporting component supply and business needs. Generation-transition risk on memory and other components is managed with non-cancellable POs, procurement matched to shipment schedules, and building-block subsystems that stay compatible across product lines and generations - with management noting that with prices rising so fast, older inventory has often been resold favorably.
quarterly_data.figure: Inventory $12.9B (from $11.1B); $5.6B raise funds component supply

quarterly_data.signal: Component shortage (CEO): near-term margin pressure includes 'key component shortage like memory and storage shortage', and Q2 gross margin was hit by the ongoing component shortage and volatile component pricing. The CEO said the key component shortage exists 'because the demand is getting so strong, not because of production capacity is reduced', and that the cost impact 'won't hurt us too much'. The full-year guide of at least $40 billion already assumes component prices keep rising and is conservative for that reason: 'If the cost -- if the shortage situation improve quickly, for sure, our [indiscernible] revenue will be more than that.'
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 guide of at least $40 billion already assumes rising component prices

quarterly_data.signal: Enterprise storage is now an explicit growth and margin vector: expanded enterprise CPU-based server, STORAGE and IoT product lines since early 2026, and Q4 enterprise/channel revenue of $5.6B (50% of total, +172% YoY) came from customers upgrading compute, STORAGE and network infrastructure. Enterprise storage is one of the pillars of the DCBBS total solution (GPU + CPU server, enterprise storage, DLC, switching, management software, lifecycle service), and storage/CPU/IoT carry higher gross margin than high-volume GPU platforms.
quarterly_data.figure: Enterprise & channel $5.6B (50% of Q4 rev, +172% YoY) incl. storage upgrades

quarterly_data.signal: Demand very strong in near-cloud, sovereign-AI and generative-AI segments, driving record backlog despite a Q3 sequential revenue decline from customer site-readiness delays (sites not yet equipped with power/networking) and industry-wide component shortages. Building traditional enterprise + storage business for ~1 year, now seeing strong growth (enterprise channel 28% of revenue, +46% YoY). One large data-center customer = 27% of revenue.
quarterly_data.figure: near-cloud/sovereign/genAI demand strong; record backlog; enterprise 28% of rev

quarterly_data.signal: Data-center management software (SuperCloud Composer suite — real-time control of tens of thousands of racks, CPU/GPU workload orchestration) grew from <$10M/qtr a few quarters ago to $34M last quarter and >$46M booked this quarter; DCBBS (incl. software/service, >20% margins) expected to reach >25% of total profit within a few years. Customer mix de-concentrating: largest data-center customer fell from 63% to 27% of revenue while enterprise channel hit 28% of revenue (+45% QoQ); more NeoCloud / mid- and small-cloud / enterprise customers driving structural margin improvement (Q3 non-GAAP GM 10.1% vs 6.4%).
quarterly_data.figure: Software $46M/qtr booked; top customer 63%->27%; enterprise 28% of rev

quarterly_data.signal: Record demand and de-concentrating customer base: over $60B of NEW ORDERS booked in Q4 FY2026 (~70% pure AI, ~30% CPU / CPU-based AI / edge AI), taking order book and backlog to record levels entering FY2027. NINE customers exceeded $1B of revenue in FY2026 versus four in FY2025, and the largest datacenter/CSP customer was 28% of FY2026 revenue. The $1B+ cohort is described as a lot of emerging Neoclouds and CSPs plus some enterprise customers. FY2027 revenue guided to $65-72B.
quarterly_data.figure: $60B+ new orders in Q4 (70% pure AI); 9 customers >$1B vs 4; top customer 28%

quarterly_data.signal: Deployment timing, not demand, is the constraint: Q4 revenue of $11.1B landed near the low end of guidance because large datacenter and Neocloud customers were not ready on power, cooling and networking - a timing story with the revenue expected in subsequent quarters, and OEM/large-DC revenue fell 26% QoQ to $5.5B while enterprise/channel doubled. September and December quarter order/shipment activity described as quite strong. On the ODM-disintermediation concern, management positions Supermicro as running BOTH an OEM and an ODM model and says it will keep growing in both. DCBBS is pitched as the answer to the readiness problem - a one-stop shop (power, DLC, CDU, chill door, water tower, 1.6T switching, management software, lifecycle service) that lets customers build AI datacenters in quarters rather than years and improves time-to-deployment (TTD) and time-to-online (TTO).
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 $11.1B (low end) on customer power/cooling/network readiness; OEM+ODM both

quarterly_data.signal: Supermicro disclosed approximately $39 billion of orders received in recent weeks for its advanced AI servers, including its Data Center Building Block Solutions, from more than 20 customers, which it plans to fulfill in future quarters; the company states these orders do not constitute firm commitments and are subject to cancellation and delays.
quarterly_data.figure: ~$39 billion of AI server orders from more than 20 customers

quarterly_data.signal: Customer concentration and mix (CFO): one large data center customer (not named) was approximately 63% of total Q2 revenue. OEM appliance and large data center revenue was $10.7 billion, approximately 84% of revenue versus 68% last quarter (up 151% YoY and 210% QoQ). By geography the U.S. was 86% of Q2 revenue (U.S. revenue up 184% YoY), Asia 9%, Europe 3% and the rest of the world 2%. Asked whether the 63% customer had been a 10% customer before, the CFO said only that Super Micro 'does most of its business with repeat customers' and has 'added a lot of new logos', and referred to the 10-K and 10-Qs. The CEO said the customer base now has 'many more large-scale customers' and is becoming more diversified, although customers sometimes pull in or push out their schedules.
quarterly_data.figure: one customer approximately 63% of total revenue; OEM appliance and large data center $10.7 billion (approximately 84% of revenue); U.S. 86% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Working capital funds the order ramp (CFO): Q2 closing inventory was $10.6 billion, up from $5.7 billion in Q1, 'as we prepared for continuing strength in Q3 shipments'. The cash conversion cycle improved from 123 days to 54 days. Operating cash use was $24 million, capex $21 million and free cash flow negative $45 million. Cash was $4.1 billion against $4.9 billion of bank and convertible note debt, for net debt of $787 million. New funding: a $2 billion secured revolving credit facility in the U.S., an approximately $1.8 billion secured Taiwan revolving debt facility closed in January, and an accounts receivable factoring facility (unused in the December quarter, used since), giving 'access to over $5 billion of additional capital'. The CFO tied the rise in receivables and inventory to having 'well in excess of $13 billion of orders' for delivery, as he had said the previous quarter.
quarterly_data.figure: inventory $10.6 billion (from $5.7 billion); well in excess of $13 billion of orders; access to over $5 billion of additional capital; net debt $787 million

quarterly_data.signal: Networking is now an explicit DCBBS pillar: the total solution spans CPU and GPU compute, storage, energy and a 1.6T HIGH-SPEED SWITCH plus 'upcoming optical networking', sold with the Supermicro management software suite (SCM, SuperCloud Composer, SVM, SOM). The new 32-acre Silicon Valley DCBBS campus features an ADVANCED OPTICAL PHOTONICS NETWORKING LAB alongside datacenter-scale manufacturing, and management calls out high-speed switch and optical technology as areas of very aggressive continued investment, with the 'high bandwidth switch and the whole networking design management tool' cited as a big room to grow toward the ~20%-of-gross-profit DCBBS target. Customer networking readiness (alongside power and cooling) was one of the causes of the Q4 revenue push-out.
quarterly_data.figure: 1.6T switch shipping in DCBBS; optical networking upcoming; SV photonics lab

quarterly_data.signal: Transforming from a US server maker into a total data-center solution provider via DCBPS (Data Center Building Block Solutions) — complete DLC facilities, cooling units, networking, power shelves, battery backup, management software and service; DCBPS expected to contribute >25% of total profit within a few years. Data-center/cloud management software (SuperCloud Composer, managing tens of thousands of systems/racks) revenue grew from <$10M/qtr to $34M last quarter to $46M+ this quarter. Expanding capacity (Taiwan, Malaysia ramping; new ~4M sq ft Silicon Valley DCBPS campus with clean room for DLC subsystems and optical-photonics networking) toward >6,000 of the most powerful racks per month. DLC leadership = industry's fastest time-to-online.
quarterly_data.figure: DCBPS >25% of profit target; software $46M+/qtr; >6,000 racks/month capacity

quarterly_data.signal: Backlog at another RECORD high despite industry-wide CPU/GPU/memory shortages. Capacity: on track to produce >6,000 state-of-the-art racks per MONTH; announced largest-ever US site — a new DCBBS campus in Silicon Valley (Bay Area footprint ~4M sqft, 8 new buildings) including clean-room facilities for next-gen DLC subsystems and ADVANCED OPTICAL PHOTONICS-BASED networking devices; Taiwan and Malaysia sites ramping aggressively.
quarterly_data.figure: >6,000 racks/month; new SV DCBBS campus w/ photonics clean room

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and footprint: total manufacturing capacity on track to exceed 6,000 racks per month, including MORE THAN 3,000 DIRECT-LIQUID-COOLING racks per month, with most DLC rack production lines supporting the densest 250kW rack platforms. Announced a new 32-ACRE DCBBS campus in Silicon Valley featuring an advanced optical-photonics networking lab and datacenter-scale manufacturing, bringing the U.S. footprint to nearly 4 million square feet; Taiwan, Malaysia and the NETHERLANDS facilities are also ramping strongly.
quarterly_data.figure: >6,000 racks/mo incl >3,000 DLC racks/mo at 250kW; 32-acre SV DCBBS campus

quarterly_data.signal: Power and cooling readiness at the CUSTOMER site was the direct cause of the Q4 revenue shortfall - short-term customer delays in power, cooling and networking pushed revenue out of Q4 into subsequent quarters. DCBBS is the response: a turnkey stack of DLC solutions, CDU, chill door, water tower, power shelves/battery backup, 1.6T high-speed switching and networking, Supermicro Data Center Management software (SCM, SuperCloud Composer, SVM, SOM Orchestration Manager) and full lifecycle services, plus a new PROACTIVE SERVICE model going online early next quarter where management software and field teams auto-alert and pre-stage repairs to stop compute capacity loss. DCBBS was previously guided to ~20% of gross profit and management says '20% should be not far away'. Liquid cooling penetration keeps rising - GPU and CPU platforms alike (Vera, Rubin) are liquid-cooling-ready and management expects liquid cooling to dominate the datacenter business soon.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 miss from customer power/cooling readiness; DCBBS ~20% of gross profit target

quarterly_data.signal: First full-year size for the software and services line: SVP of Corporate Development Michael Staiger said 'software and services, I think, in fiscal 2026, we just finished $538 million and growing, so it can be a substantial part of the business', and that it is higher margin. The management stack (SuperCloud Composer, Data Center Manager, Orchestration Manager) is not sold standalone - 'It's part of the solution... It'll go with our systems' - and is the control plane for racks, cooling and storage. New enterprise channel: 'We've integrated that with VCF, and so that's VMware AI Factory', which Staiger called another proof point for reaching more enterprise customers.
quarterly_data.figure: software and services finished fiscal 2026 at $538 million

quarterly_data.signal: Management's own market-size and share math, which it had not laid out before: 'the TAM itself has been segmented out as $2 trillion-$4 trillion... if we're thinking it's $2 trillion-$4 trillion, and we're 10% of that market, and we've said this before, we're 10% now of the market itself... that gives us a $200 billion look'. On ranking: 'if you look at the IDC numbers, our share gain, our position, I think we are number 2. We clearly have sights on number 1.' Staiger argued share gain follows from solutioning rather than being targeted directly, and that the industry is transitioning away from the traditional server / storage / networking compute stack toward application-optimized AI solutions.
quarterly_data.figure: $2 trillion-$4 trillion TAM; 10% now of the market; a $200 billion look; number 2 in IDC share

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity expansion beyond what has been disclosed on the earnings calls. Staiger: 'We have discussed our capacity at 6,000 racks per month, 3,000 liquid cooled, 3,000 air cooled. What we have not disclosed necessarily is the new square footage that we have been adding in Johor, and the new buildings that are coming on stream, and a couple of the clean room facilities, the manufacturing capabilities that we have... We are expanding pretty aggressively under the covers.' He said Supermicro will update the market when those are more solidified.
quarterly_data.figure: 6,000 racks per month, 3,000 liquid cooled, 3,000 air cooled; undisclosed added square footage in Johor plus new buildings and clean room facilities

quarterly_data.signal: Sovereign demand is moving from indirect to direct. Staiger: 'We have more than several sovereign deployments as we speak globally. They're clearly spending. I think the early motion was enterprise spending was into the neoclouds. Sovereign spending was into the neoclouds. We were capturing it early on, but we're seeing clear evidence of them moving forward and putting factories on the floor and expanding there.' Sizing: against the $2 trillion to $4 trillion TAM, sovereigns 'could be a pretty big 10%-25% of the total market', and 'They're fully funded, so they're wonderful in that respect.'
quarterly_data.figure: more than several sovereign deployments globally; sovereigns potentially 10%-25% of the total market

quarterly_data.signal: Structural explanation of the neocloud channel: 'If you think about what's happening at the neocloud level, and you see some of these major contracts where these neoclouds were, many of them and growing, that we're serving, they're getting hyperscaler contracts. In essence, our systems at the neoclouds are serving the hyperscalers. So they need to get those systems up and running immediately.' Deployment scale cited for these operators is '100 to 1,500 rack deployments', where slow stand-up destroys economics (Staiger cited a partner's figure that 8 racks taking 30 days to become operational costs about $3 million). That is the argument for L11/L12 integrated DCBBS racks - power, cooling, CDUs, rear door heat exchangers, storage, switching and software - over shipping bare racks, and for the higher margin content that comes with it.
quarterly_data.figure: 100 to 1,500 rack deployments; 8 racks taking 30 days to stand up costs about $3 million (partner figure cited by management)

quarterly_data.signal: Management restated the scale trajectory in its own terms and dismissed the recurring ODM-displacement concern: 'a couple of years ago we were $1.5 billion, and now we're on our way to doing $15 billion for a year, and now we're on our way to do $15 billion for one quarter and beyond'; 'The order book, obviously, at $60 billion, underpins the guidance for the year.' On the risk that mature neoclouds switch to Taiwanese ODMs: 'That concern was around at $7 billion, at $15 billion, at $22, at $39, and it is going to exist at $68.' He also said '75% growth at these numbers is pretty significant on a year-over-year basis', and that hyperscalers doing their own silicon expands rather than shrinks the number of rack platforms Supermicro must support - fragmentation 'would be difficult to theoretically mass produce'.
quarterly_data.figure: $7 billion, at $15 billion, at $22, at $39, and it is going to exist at $68; 75% growth year-over-year; order book at $60 billion

quarterly_data.signal: DCBBS (Data Center Building Block Solutions) economics and roadmap (CEO): DCBBS accounted for 4% of profit in the first half of fiscal 2026. Those were its first two quarters, since the line was officially introduced about 6 months ago. Revenue is still relatively small, but the margin is much better, 'for sure, more than 20%'. DCBBS profit should contribute meaningfully in 2H FY2026 and reach 'at least double-digit contribution by end of calendar 2026'. In about a year the line grew to more than 10 key subsystems: CDU, heat exchanger, chilled doors, power shelves, battery backup, water tower, dry-towers, high-speed switching, data center management software and service. Another 3 to 5 items are planned in the next few months or quarters, and the CEO said the line is expanding into new categories such as transformers, next-generation power generators, energy backup devices and grid power replacement. It is sold globally as a one-stop shop to large, mid-size and small data center builders to shorten time-to-deployment and time-to-online and to reduce power and water consumption.
quarterly_data.figure: DCBBS 4% of profit in 1H FY2026; at least double-digit profit contribution by end of calendar 2026; margin more than 20%; more than 10 key subsystems, another 3 to 5 items planned

quarterly_data.signal: Manufacturing footprint and cost structure (CEO): the Silicon Valley facility remains the cornerstone of U.S. operations. New production sites in Taiwan, Malaysia, the Netherlands and the Middle East are ramping to add capacity, serve regional AI requirements and optimize overall cost structure, and the CEO listed international facility expansion as a near-term margin headwind. Design-for-manufacturing work (more modularized subsystems, expanded automation across facilities) is raising yield and bringing new platforms to volume production faster.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

The largest share of the five-quarter pipeline is Grace Blackwell and Blackwell, with 'a rise in x86 Blackwell' driven primarily by enterprise deployments where 'air cooling' is the number one consideration, plus scientific computing and high-frequency traders using x86 air-cooled solutions.

AI server demand outstripping supply with a record $51.3B AI backlog; $60B AI server revenue guided for FY2027.

Dell frames that engineering, global supply chain and deployment complexity as its differentiator in moving customers from design to production.
quarterly_data.figure: upwards of 50 unique designs per engagement

quarterly_data.quarter: Dell Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Michael Dell on the supply set-up into 2027, a period the Q2 call did not guide: all of the improvements in the models, particularly from basic LLMs to reasoning to agents, has occurred well within the timeframe required to build a new semiconductor fab, so you just have a structural shortage, probably worse in 2027 than in 2026 from everything that we see. Costs are going up and Dell prices them through; customers move from objecting to price to asking whether Dell can supply them over the next year, two years. Dell says it watches closely for any signs of double ordering or things that are not being utilized, and we don't see that. Deferred demand keeps building behind the shortage: there are 400 million PCs that are over four years old and 1.3 million servers that are 13th generation or older, with customers sweating assets because memory cost has risen.
quarterly_data.figure: structural shortage, probably worse in 2027 than in 2026; 400 million PCs that are over four years old; 1.3 million servers that are 13th generation or older

quarterly_data.signal: Supply beyond this fiscal year, a step past what the Q2 call said: demand is still faster than supply for both traditional and AI servers and CFO David Kennedy says Dell sees the supply differential only getting worse, not getting better, into next year - there is a small bit of supply growth but it is pretty minimal on the basis of the demand signals, so that It is actually tighter next year than it is this year. Beyond DRAM and NAND (by far the big brother in that equation) and CPUs, he says any part associated with an AI box is short to some degree and names opticals, transceivers, T-glass as constrained; Dell's job is to assemble the available golden parts into fully configured units to maximise the P&L.
quarterly_data.figure: It is actually tighter next year than it is this year; constrained components now include opticals, transceivers, T-glass

quarterly_data.signal: A new commercial construct the call did not describe: customers are now negotiating multi-year supply ACCESS rather than price. Kennedy says enterprises are arriving wanting to buy four years' worth of equipment at once, which Dell will not fulfil for a single account; instead Dell is entering into conversations about what are your supply needs and your infrastructure needs going out into year 2, year 3, and year 4, and for customers who partner with it Dell will give them that supply access and provide some guarantees. His framing: Guarantee supply does not guarantee price - that is the specific differentiation, and supply access is what the market is looking for.
quarterly_data.figure: multi-year supply-access commitments out into year 2, year 3, and year 4; Guarantee supply does not guarantee price

quarterly_data.signal: AI customer growth rate: CFO David Kennedy said of the 6,500 AI customers, 'That’s up over 60% in the last 6 months'. He called this the infancy of the opportunity against the tens of thousands of customers Dell serves, estimating that 'pick a number between 10% and 15% of enterprises' have done meaningful AI agentic modernization, and said Dell expects a better conversion rate on enterprise.
quarterly_data.figure: 6,500 customers; up over 60% in the last 6 months

quarterly_data.signal: Vera Rubin status at the start of FY2027: 'There is no Vera Rubin in the backlog' (the $43,000,000,000 AI backlog is 'overwhelmingly' Grace Blackwell), but 'There is Vera Rubin in the five-quarter pipeline'. Dell has 'early engineering samples' and forward-deployed engineers are working with customers on designs; Jeff Clarke expects it 'to ship in the second half of the year because we know Vera Rubin is in production'. Management expects a smoother transition than Grace Blackwell thanks to manufacturing and test lessons, while keeping AI operating margin in the mid single digits through the transition.
quarterly_data.figure: no Vera Rubin in the $43,000,000,000 AI backlog; shipments expected in the second half of the year

quarterly_data.signal: Record Q1 FY2027: revenue $43.8B (+88% YoY), non-GAAP EPS $4.86 (+214%), GAAP EPS $5.24, operating income $4.2B (+154%), record cash flow from operations $4.1B; gross margin 18.1%. Booked $24.4B in AI orders and recognized $16.1B AI server revenue; exited with RECORD $51.3B AI backlog (pipeline multiples of backlog; AI revenue ~9x YoY). Customer count surpassed 5,000 (Neo Cloud, sovereigns, enterprise). RAISED full-year guidance by ~$27B revenue and ~$5 EPS: FY2027 revenue $165-169B, ISG +80% with ~$60B AI server revenue (~2.4x YoY), non-GAAP EPS ~$17.90.

quarterly_data.signal: ISG revenue record $29B (+181%, 9 consecutive double-digit quarters; record ISG operating income $3.1B); traditional server+networking $8.5B (+92%, demand outpaces supply); storage $4.3B (+8%, Dell-IP higher-margin mix). Top rack-scale infrastructure provider — launched Dell Power Rack (turnkey factory-integrated) and 18th-gen PowerEdge. Demand exceeds supply with DRAM/NAND MEMORY the primary constraint. Expanding the Dell AI factory ecosystem with partners including NVIDIA, Google Cloud, OpenAI, SpaceX AI, Mistral, ServiceNow, Palantir, CrowdStrike.
quarterly_data.figure: ISG record $29B (+181%); memory the primary supply constraint

quarterly_data.signal: Agentic AI is expanding the CPU TAM: 'the agent needs support of a CPU... the harness — the CPU runs it, makes the calls, manages memory, and is in the loop in every decision an agent makes' (all 3 microprocessor leaders cited CPU TAM expansion). Traditional server revenue +92% with absolute unit growth AND content growth. Architecture mix: large direct-liquid-cooled GPU deployments (GB200/B300, Vera) are biased to Arm, while enterprise B200/B300/RTX 6000 Pro systems are x86; traditional servers remain x86 today, with Vera CPU seen as future relief for the microprocessor shortage.

ISG delivered record revenue of $31.8B, up 89%, its 10th consecutive quarter of double-digit or better revenue growth, with record ISG operating income of $4.8B (up 225%) and an ISG operating margin of 15%, up 620 basis points.

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Hock Tan disclosed the multi-die XPU roadmap in explicit terms - the clearest statement yet of how Broadcom is 'substituting Moore's law with something else'. He said Moore's law has ended ('Moving down process node, you cannot achieve double transistor performance anymore. You barely eke out 5% improvement, but you get power'), that physics caps a single die at '800 square millimeters' ('That's the largest size die you can make'), and that Broadcom now puts '2 die together in one chip. So effectively, you now have 1,600 square millimeters, double.' Critically: 'The current generation we are working on has 4 dies. You can just imagine. The one after that probably will go to maybe no limit, 8 die. 8 die in one chip. So your chip size is equivalent of, say, 800 times 8, over 6,000 square millimeter running as one single chip.' He stressed this enabling technology 'is not just created at a wafer fab or with the memory guys. It is us designing it', and listed the moats as high-speed SerDes/IO IP, multiplier density per square millimeter, die-to-die communication at low power, and advanced packaging.
quarterly_data.figure: largest size die you can make 800 square millimeters; 2 die = 1,600 square millimeters; current generation has 4 dies; next probably 8 die in one chip = over 6,000 square millimeter; process node shrink now yields barely 5% improvement

quarterly_data.signal: Roadmap beyond the first OpenAI XPU (the Jalapeño itself was already disclosed on the Q3 FY2026 call): Tan said the relationship 'is very strong and continues to be very strong because we are working on the next and two generations to the Jalapeño' - i.e. two further generations already in development. He also explained why the first one took only a year ('within a year, we created an XPU called the Jalapeño'): co-design, where the customer's frontier-model team translates model specs into the architecture of what the compute hardware needs and Broadcom supplies the micro-architecture and physical design - 'When you have that very tight, almost seamless flow, it's not that much a challenge to be able to create chips of that caliber that quickly.'

quarterly_data.signal: Tan unpacked what 'supply constrained' means behind the 2027 and 2028 AI revenue forecast, and it is not silicon. On chips: 'We understand the need for wafers, leading-edge wafers, and memory, as well as even substrates. That is pretty well locked in. We can pretty well lock that in for sure in 2027, and the process of locking in 2028 gives us within some limits. That is more within our control.' The less deterministic constraint is a site that is power READY, not merely power available: 'If you want to make it power ready, say, in 2028, got to start construction on the sites now. That is not us, our customers, has to start construction on the site now to make it available and ready by 2028' - a year and a half to two years out, gated by transformers, gas turbines, local permitting and the rate of construction. 'It's a judged number based on not just supply of memory wafers, but availability and readiness of power sites.'
quarterly_data.figure: wafers, memory and substrates locked in for 2027, being locked for 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Customer concentration and the financing vehicle, in Tan's own words: 'we have only six customers today at this point. Very concentrated group, but I believe these six customers, all each of them are creating their own frontier models'. Of those six, 'two of them, two of the strongest guys do not have the cash flows to be able to generate the compute needed to train and create inference, productize their models' - he later referred to financing partners 'Anthropic and OpenAI'. Why Broadcom backs all six rather than picking: 'we cannot tell who is going to win' and 'they may coexist'. On the already-disclosed XPV platform he drew the line Broadcom had not drawn before: 'We do it by creating a platform, we call it XPV, where it would enable them to be financed. We do not finance directly.' Tan also rejected the circularity charge head-on: 'This is not circular financing... We are using financing to create demand. Demand is there' - when a customer sees the demand and could buy the compute from someone else, it is not circular.
quarterly_data.figure: only six customers today; two of the strongest do not have the cash flows

quarterly_data.signal: Tan gave the unit economics he uses to judge AI durability - useful as the demand test behind Broadcom's XPU forecast. On a single deployment: 'Take the case of a very good frontier model. 1 gigawatt could generate $30 billion ARR... The cost to run 1 gigawatt, as you all know, is about $10 billion a year. So you have $20 billion that accrue to the model guys and the application that goes with it, and $10 billion fought over by the power guys, the cloud provider guys, even the chip and memory guys.' On the industry today (inference only, sourced from OpenRouter and Vercel data): global token generation cost is 'around $200 billion a year now' against model-layer revenue of 'Around $150 billion'. Splitting it: more than half of tokens are generated on open weight models, but frontier closed models take 'at least' 75% of the revenue - 'That's $120 billion. They spend roughly $100 billion' - while open weight players spend 'the other $100 billion' for 'revenue $30 billion'. His conclusion: value accrues to the best frontier models, which is why Broadcom's XPU customers must be frontier-model developers.

Hybrid bonding / die-to-wafer bonding in logic (SOIC) brings 'a 10x change in specifications of defects that kill the die', pulling KLA's most advanced front-end systems into packaging, and the introduction of hybrid bonding in memory will tighten specs significantly as well. Economics: a logic wafer out of the front-end fab is worth '$30,000, $40,000, $50,000' and a memory wafer '$50,000, $60,000, $70,000', so a loss in packaging also loses that wafer's value and customers 'want to inspect every step'.

quarterly_data.signal: WHY MI450 RUNS UALINK OVER ETHERNET, AND WHAT IT MEANS FOR ASTERA CONTENT: asked about the first Helios server, CEO Jitendra Mohan declined to speak for AMD but reiterated AMD's public position - 'for the MI450 series, they are going to go with UALink running over Ethernet. That has really got everything to do with the fact that UALink switches are not yet available', so MI450 must tunnel UALink over Ethernet - while AMD has said it will keep offering both UALink over Ethernet and native UALink in future generations, which Mohan expects to coexist. The content consequence he spelled out generically: where Astera does not supply the scale-up switching, its content is limited to scale-out retimers, Scorpio P, Taurus Ethernet retimers and active electrical cables; where the scale-up protocol is one Astera supports (PCI Express, UALink or something in between) and a Scorpio X solution can be used, 'then our content really does explode a lot, because scale up is a very rich area for connectivity solutions'. He added that the in-network compute, Hypercast, diagnostics and telemetry built into today's Scorpio X, exposed through COSMOS software, carry forward to a UALink-based Scorpio X, making the migration easy for existing Scorpio X users.

quarterly_data.signal: Scale-up optics raised for a second time in two weeks: a quarter ago the next-fiscal-year outlook was zero to $300 million, on the Q2 call Murphy said it would be much higher, and at Citi he told investors to imagine that number is even greater, with NPO and scale-up optics a big part of the guide-up. Marvell already sells TIAs and drivers into third-party NPO modules built for hyperscalers, which he called a billion-dollar business for us already just on analog components, and said Marvell content is very high in the NPO module ecosystem with TIAs and drivers. NPO and CPO will coexist rather than replace each other, with a big NPO ramp in calendar 2028 and 2029 as CPO layers in.
quarterly_data.figure: next-year scale-up optics: prior guide zero to $300 million, now greater still; TIAs and drivers a billion-dollar business for us already just on analog components

quarterly_data.signal: DCI at 1.6T: Marvell was first to market announcing 2nm DSPs that go inside the module, bring-up has been excellent and the silicon photonics platform is tracking well, backed by 15 billion device hours of reliability data. Marvell builds the modules itself and is investing in its own module manufacturing capacity while also selling the DSPs to third-party module makers. Management cited market estimates that scale-across could 2, 3, 4, 5x the size of the DCI market on top of the ASP-per-generation growth DCI already delivers.
quarterly_data.figure: 2nm DSP first to market; 15 billion device hours of reliability data; scale-across could 2, 3, 4, 5x the size of the DCI market

quarterly_data.signal: Ordering of the optical transition changed inside Marvell in the last six months: Murphy said what has hit them is that NPO, or near package optics, probably will hit first in a bigger way, and then CPO's coming — it is all coming, but not at once, and certain customers are going to adopt CPO. The Celestial AI and Inphi photonics teams are now one organisation under Celestial AI's CEO, who also runs Marvell's silicon photonics, the DCI module business and the entire switching platform. The same silicon-germanium TIA and driver content Marvell has shipped for a decade is required for NPO and for linear-drive CPO, on top of 15 billion hours of silicon photonics reliability data.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Murphy sized the Teralynx switching franchise against its acquisition case: Innovium, bought five years ago, 'had no revenue, but was projected to do about $150 million of revenue. We now said that that business is on track to do $1 billion plus, and over the next years, we will probably grow even faster.' He said the Teralynx T100 part is already suitable for scale-up as is, with a suite of ESUN products coming and a parallel UALink investment because the market has not settled on a standard. Separately, he said connectivity 'this year is growing like 70% plus' and 'That growth rate’s going to roll over into next year as well.'
quarterly_data.figure: Innovium projected about $150 million at acquisition, now on track to do $1 billion plus; connectivity growing like 70% plus this year, rolling into next year

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 FY2026 results: record revenue of $2.219 billion, up 22% year-over-year and 7% sequentially, above the guidance midpoint on data center demand; data center revenue a record $1.65 billion (9% sequential, 21% year-over-year growth, 74% of total revenue) with sequential growth across optical interconnects, custom silicon, switching and storage; non-GAAP gross margin 59%, non-GAAP operating margin 35.7%, non-GAAP EPS $0.80. Fiscal 2026 revenue $8.195 billion, up 42%. Q4 inventory $1.39 billion (up $374 million QoQ to support growth), total debt $4.47 billion (gross debt-to-EBITDA 1.38x); $2.245 billion returned to stockholders in fiscal 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: $2.219 billion Q4 revenue (22% YoY, 7% sequential); data center $1.65 billion (21% YoY, 74% of revenue); FY2026 revenue $8.195 billion (42%); inventory $1.39 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Guidance and FY2027 outlook: Q1 FY2027 revenue $2.4 billion plus or minus 5% (8% sequential growth at the midpoint, 27% year-over-year), non-GAAP gross margin 58.25% to 59.25%, non-GAAP EPS $0.74 to $0.84; data center to grow approximately 10% sequentially in Q1. Management expects revenue to grow every quarter at a similar sequential rate, exiting FY2027 with Q4 revenue exceeding $3 billion, and FY2027 revenue to grow more than 30% to approaching $11 billion (up from approximately $9.5 billion given in September 2025 and approximately $10 billion in December 2025), entirely driven by data center, which is now seen growing 40%. Interconnect is now expected to grow more than 50% versus a prior expectation of 30%; communications and other to grow 10%. Celestial AI and XConn add approximately $75 million to FY2027 non-GAAP opex and are not expected to contribute meaningful revenue until fiscal 2028. Bookings are 'accelerating at a record pace'.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 FY2027 revenue $2.4 billion (plus or minus 5%); FY2027 approaching $11 billion (more than 30%); Q4 FY2027 exceeding $3 billion; data center 40%; interconnect more than 50% (prior 30%)

quarterly_data.signal: FY2028 outlook: total revenue to grow close to 40% to approximately $15 billion, roughly $2 billion higher than the December outlook, with non-GAAP EPS 'well over $5'; data center revenue to grow close to 50%, driven by interconnect significantly outpacing cloud CapEx growth, custom at least doubling and Ethernet switching ramping; Celestial AI and XConn to contribute approximately $250 million in aggregate revenue; communications to grow low single digits. Murphy said the outlook rests on 'extremely strong bookings and backlog' and detailed supply-planning conversations with customers, and that Marvell is on track to the calendar 2028 targets set in April 2024.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2028 revenue approximately $15 billion (close to 40%); data center close to 50%; Celestial AI + XConn approximately $250 million; non-GAAP EPS well over $5

quarterly_data.signal: Scale-out PAM: 800-gig demand remains robust and 800 will still be the majority of volume in FY2027, while very strong bookings from multiple Tier 1 customers for 1.6T (in production since the second half of fiscal 2026, with significant shipments at the end of last year) drive a very rapid 1.6T ramp in FY2027 and substantial additional growth in FY2028. Marvell was first to productize 200-gigabit per lane and has demonstrated 400-gig per lane technology for the later 3.2T transition. Murphy said the electro-optics business is now growing '50% plus' this year, tracking accelerator growth rather than CapEx, helped by a rising optics attach rate on new XPU/GPU generations and the higher ASP of 1.6T.
quarterly_data.figure: 1.6T in production since second half of fiscal 2026; electro-optics growing 50% plus in FY2027; 400-gig per lane demonstrated for 3.2T

quarterly_data.signal: Scale-across and campus: Marvell leads DCI with Coherent 400-gig and 800-gig modules and expects to supply DCI modules to all five major U.S. hyperscalers this year; industry forecasts see the DCI pluggable TAM growing by more than 5x by calendar 2030. Announced the industry's first Secure 1.6T ZR and ZR+ DCI modules on a new 2-nanometer Coherent DSP plus a 2-nanometer 800-gig DSP, sampling later this year. First-generation 1.6T Coherent light products (2 to 20-kilometer campus reach) are shipping, with a second generation adding integrated MACsec.
quarterly_data.figure: DCI modules to all five major U.S. hyperscalers this year; DCI pluggable TAM more than 5x by calendar 2030; 2-nanometer 1.6T ZR/ZR+ DSP sampling later this year

quarterly_data.signal: Scale-up CPO: the Celestial AI and XConn acquisitions have closed. Celestial AI's photonic fabric chiplets are to be co-packaged into custom XPUs and scale-up switches, enabling large-scale CPO deployment for scale-up starting next year; the first-generation chiplet is being brought into high-volume manufacturing. Celestial CPO revenue remains on track for a $500 million annualized run rate in Q4 fiscal 2028, doubling to a $1 billion annualized run rate by Q4 fiscal 2029; the scale-up interconnect market could exceed $10 billion by 2030. Murphy: 'we'll be shipping next year CPO for scale up at one large customer', with the rest of scale-up deployments still copper-based, and CPO in scale-out expected to stay relatively limited versus pluggables.
quarterly_data.figure: $500 million annualized run rate in Q4 fiscal 2028; $1 billion annualized run rate by Q4 fiscal 2029; scale-up interconnect market could exceed $10 billion by 2030

quarterly_data.signal: AEC and retimers: design wins with 3 Tier 1 U.S. hyperscalers plus model builders and hardware OEMs; combined AEC and retimer revenue expected to more than double year-over-year in FY2027; asked for the base, Murphy said 'it's doubling -- over doubling this year, but it's probably in the $200 million range', adding 'maybe that goes higher'. Marvell entered when retimers and AECs moved from NRZ to PAM and runs a Golden Cable program giving hyperscalers multiple cable OEMs on the same Marvell DSP reference design.
quarterly_data.figure: AEC + retimer revenue more than double in FY2027; 'probably in the $200 million range'; design wins with 3 Tier 1 U.S. hyperscalers

In scale-up, XConn adds PCIe/CXL switching (PCIe Gen 6 and CXL 3.1 monolithic switch supporting up to 256 lanes; engaged with more than 20 customers before the deal); UALink 115T solutions to sample in the second half of FY2027 with volume production in fiscal 2028, and Celestial CPO can be integrated directly with Marvell switches.
quarterly_data.figure: switch revenue exceeding $300 million FY2026; surpass $600 million FY2027 (prior $500 million); UALink 115T sampling second half, volume fiscal 2028

Marvell reaches production more than 90%-plus of the time on first-pass silicon on advanced nodes. TSMC remains the sole-source fab vendor, with long-term deals also struck on substrate and back-end capacity plus capex and prepays. Murphy spent a week in Asia with existing and new suppliers ahead of the October 6 Investor Day; conditions are very acute right now in some areas, and he warned that some substrate capacity cannot be obtained until the end of the decade by anyone who did not start five years ago.

He stressed that Marvell is running the same playbook across the whole spectrum of hyperscale customers for programs that have no warrant or 8-K attached, so their size is not public, and that XPU-attach products are largely Marvell's own IP built to spec with the customer's name on the chip.

quarterly_data.signal: Mix behind the raise: when next year's revenue outlook was still like $13.5 billion, custom was about the same size as it is today; the raise from $13.5 billion to $18 billion came mostly from interconnect and switching and storage, with only some from custom. Durn expects operating margin to walk from touching the low end of the 38%-40% range this Q4 to touching the high end next year at a similar range of gross margin, and Murphy expects gross margin flat-ish next year with operating margin expansion even though custom doubles, because custom NRE is booked as contra R&D.

quarterly_data.signal: Custom is penetrating faster than Marvell modelled: when the company sized this two years ago it assumed maybe 25% penetration of custom silicon versus merchant, and Murphy now says the prevailing view is that number is probably going to be higher in terms of units, while still rejecting the idea that custom takes the whole market. On XPU-attach he repeated the a-year-ago count of 15 or 18 different designs across all four big hyperscalers plus others, spanning the TPU, Trainium and MTIA ecosystems and also attaching to merchant GPUs, and put the content at up into the $500,000, $2,000 content level per accelerator — chips that are almost entirely Marvell IP, built to spec with little customer RTL.
quarterly_data.figure: custom-vs-merchant penetration assumed at 25% penetration now seen higher in units; 15 or 18 different designs across all four big hyperscalers; $500,000, $2,000 content level per accelerator

quarterly_data.signal: Memory expansion is accelerating on the memory shortage: Marvell's organically developed CXL line (expanders, pooling devices, CXL switches and CXL retimers, plus custom memory-expansion silicon) is on turbocharge, with customers that were already designing Marvell in now trying to go faster because expansion obviates the need to buy as much memory as they thought before, while inference KV caching drives disproportionate memory attached to the XPU. Murphy called it a billion, multi-billion dollar kind of business for us in the future with product and market leadership.
quarterly_data.figure: a billion, multi-billion dollar kind of business for us in the future

quarterly_data.signal: Custom design-win count updated while recounting the June 2025 custom AI silicon event: 'Look, we got 18, it is now 20-plus design wins across all the four U.S. hyperscalers of both XPU and what we called XPU-attach.' Murphy added that Marvell called XPU-attach 'about a $15 billion market in 2025' at that time. (The transcript frames the 20-plus count inside his account of that event, so its as-of date is not stated precisely.)
quarterly_data.figure: we got 18, it is now 20-plus design wins across all the four U.S. hyperscalers; XPU-attach about a $15 billion market in 2025

quarterly_data.signal: Custom business: grown from zero to $1.5 billion in fiscal 2026, doubling year-over-year in the first full production year. FY2027 custom revenue expected to grow more than 20% (Murphy: 'biased upwards'), with a stronger second half as the lead XPU program transitions to its next generation, for which Marvell holds purchase orders covering the entire fiscal year's forecast and is ramping production; Marvell is also engaged on the follow-on generation. FY2028 custom revenue expected to at least double, driven by existing programs, XPU-attach (custom NIC and CXL) reaching high volume, and a new Tier 1 XPU program with firm volume requirements for all of next year; Murphy said the plug for the new program is 'significantly lower than actually the wafers that we're planning on starting'. Marvell cites 20-plus design wins in or going into production an unprecedented level of activity across multiple new engagements, and a massive opportunity on 2-nanometer and below process technologies.
quarterly_data.figure: custom revenue $1.5 billion FY2026; more than 20% growth FY2027; at least double FY2028; 20-plus design wins

quarterly_data.signal: XPU attach: several programs ramp in FY2027, including initial CXL and NIC products; CXL demand is accelerating partly on tight memory supply, since custom CXL expanders let customers reuse prior-generation DRAM. Line of sight to revenue exceeding $2 billion by fiscal 2029 from custom NIC and CXL alone. Murphy sized XPU attach at roughly a couple of hundred million last year, doubling this year and perhaps more than doubling again, 'probably a $1 billion type business' by next year, against an XPU attach TAM of about $15 billion in calendar '28 where Marvell targets about 20% share (about $3 billion).
quarterly_data.figure: NIC + CXL revenue exceeding $2 billion by fiscal 2029; XPU attach a $1 billion type business by next year; XPU attach TAM about $15 billion in calendar '28

GM will trend DOWN through 2026 as production revenue surges. quarterly_data.signal: N3 AI accelerator for the #1 North American customer is READY FOR PRODUCTION - shipments begin JUNE 2026; Alchip secured the required capacity across ALL suppliers (wafer, CoWoS, substrate, COOLING, tester) for on-time delivery. Ramp: revenue jumps in June, another jump in Q3, monthly revenue PEAKS from mid-Q3; Q3 and Q4 each significantly above Q2; momentum extends into late 2027 followed by next-gen mass production. End-demand keeps rising (analysts cited the customer recently signing multi-gigawatt deals incl. a 5GW Anthropic deal), but 2026 upside is LIMITED - wafer+CoWoS turnaround is 6-7 months ("order today, chips in December"); upside levers = extra N3 wafers (the scarcest capacity in the industry, hard to get) and YIELD improvement; working closely with the customer to maximize 2027 upside. Wafers are the bottleneck, NOT CoWoS - TSMC commitment to this project is very high; open to non-TSMC 2.5D packaging only on capacity shortage (has done it before); HBM is consigned by the customer, Alchip handles everything else even at the chiplet stage.
quarterly_data.figure: N3 MP ships June 2026; monthly peak from mid-Q3; 2026 upside capped by 6-7mo turnaround

quarterly_data.signal: Next-gen N2 accelerator: Alchip is the ONLY physical-design vendor for BOTH the N3 and the future N2 projects (sole partner for compute die + whole-chip integration + part of the I/O-die physical design). N2 tape-out on track by END-2026; production revenue from late 2027; N2 NRE total contract value "much, much higher" than N3 and chip price much higher (chiplet set: compute die + I/O die + others); gross margin expected similar to current. N2 takes the project "to another scale" - the basis for the 4-year confidence (visibility through 2029). At the TSMC US symposium Alchip showcased 2nm ecosystem readiness, 3DIC integration, and a design with Ayar Labs OPTICAL I/O using TSMC COUPE technology (no comment on production use).
quarterly_data.figure: Sole PD vendor N3+N2; N2 tape-out by end-2026, NRE value >> N3; Ayar Labs optical I/O showcase

quarterly_data.signal: Pipeline & TAM: NRE pipeline "very, very strong", especially North America - accelerator, CPU and networking ASIC projects on hyperscaler capex; AI designs migrating N5/N3 -> N3/N2; multiple ASIC design opportunities from NA hyperscalers (in progress to win another hyperscaler; currently ONE major hyperscaler account). Networking: multiple NA data-center networking customers - ONE approaching production, another with N3 in design and N2 kicking off soon; each "meaningful" project = >$100M annual revenue in coming years. Accelerator startups: their N3 production revenue most likely H1 2027; their N2 ~2028. Automotive: volume production started, ramps Q2, #1 revenue contributor in H1 2026 / #2 for the full year; next-gen auto chip tape-out by Q3 2026; industry trend to 2-4 chips per vehicle; targeting 1-2 more China automakers (robotics applications too). TAM view: ~$100B AI-ASIC TAM next year called "pretty accurate"; TSMC raised its 2030 overall TAM to $1.5T at the US symposium; Google+Amazon still >90% of ASIC revenue. De-risking: majority of design resources now OUTSIDE China (Japan office up to 250 staff, Malaysia+Vietnam >120 engineers); new Chief Business Officer hired from NVIDIA (ex-Xilinx, data-center/hyperscaler background).
quarterly_data.figure: AI-ASIC TAM ~$100B 2027; networking projects >$100M/yr each; auto #1 in H1

quarterly_data.signal: LANDMARK AMAZON DATA-CENTER DEAL ANNOUNCED THE MORNING OF THE CONFERENCE (after the Q3 FY2026 call). CFO/COO Akash Palkhiwala: the strategic transaction with Amazon has two product components - a customized silicon business covering multiple generations, and optical connectivity solutions 'starting with 1.6T and follow-on generations'. It is structured with a warrant agreement (filed in an 8-K the same day): Qualcomm issues warrants against purchases of up to $60 billion from Amazon for data center products over the next 10 years, with an upfront vesting of about 15% of those warrants tied to the upfront commitments Amazon is making. Revenue with Amazon starts in the December quarter - 'we are already in production with them'. Palkhiwala says the deal makes the approximately $5 billion in revenue in fiscal 2027 target 'a very high confidence' number ('we have POs, we're building the chips'), positions fiscal 2028 for strong year-over-year growth, and is one of the core components of the $15 billion in fiscal 2029 data-center target. He calls it 'a first of many' and says Qualcomm is 'similarly proceeding with the other data center customer' (an undisclosed global hyperscaler).

quarterly_data.signal: Four-franchise data-center strategy laid out with named customers for the first time: (1) custom silicon - Amazon plus one other undisclosed global hyperscaler, working on 'their main AI accelerators', not ancillary custom chips; (2) AI accelerator built on High Bandwidth Compute (stacking compute and memory) aimed at memory-bandwidth-constrained inference decode, with Humane announced as an AI accelerator customer; (3) CPU, with Meta as the first data-center silicon customer, contributing 'late in 2028, going into 2029'; (4) connectivity - the acquired Alphawave SerDes is integrated into the custom-silicon engagements and Alphawave optical connectivity products are part of the Amazon agreement. quarterly_data.signal: HIGH BANDWIDTH COMPUTE (HBC) IS AN EXPLICIT ALTERNATIVE TO HBM, WITH SPECS AND A SHIP DATE. Durga Malladi (EVP Tech Planning, Edge & Data Center): HBC puts compute right next to memory and was 'a direct take on an alternative way of doing things as opposed to HBM'. Claimed '6x improvement compared to HBM in terms of tokens per second per watt'; where 'HBM today is about give or take 21, 22 terabytes per second. We are, like, in hundreds of terabytes per second'. Against SRAM the argument is TCO/area (more racks for the same work). Proof points: the silicon is taped out and 'back in the lab ... coming along very well', with silicon validation and engineering plus commercial samples on track. Generation 1 is 'slated to be commercial and shipping in 2027'; generation 2 lands in 2028 and is benchmarked against HBM4E, where Malladi says the relative gain looks even better because more arithmetic is moving into the logic die under the DRAM stack.
quarterly_data.figure: 6x improvement compared to HBM in terms of tokens per second per watt; HBM today about 21, 22 terabytes per second vs hundreds of terabytes per second; gen 1 commercial and shipping in 2027, gen 2 in 2028 vs HBM4E

quarterly_data.signal: HBC SUPPLY CHAIN AND DIVISION OF LABOUR: Qualcomm is not a memory vendor - 'We're not doing the DRAM stacking ourselves. What we prescribe is this is how things should be done. These are the TSVs that need to occur.' The compute die comes from Qualcomm, and 'We still have to work with the likes of TSMC to tape it all together'; Qualcomm positions itself as the overall system integrator and the single front end to the hyperscaler customer. On supply: right after Investor Day Malladi was 'in Korea with two memory vendors' and, instead of pushing back on the HBM comparison, they asked how to work more closely - 'we have been working with them because we need to make sure that we have the right supply as we do the commercialization', with additional inbound interest from the wider memory community. Hyperscaler engagement is modular across three independent tracks (standalone HBC, HBC plus Qualcomm CPU, or the full stack), and a hyperscaler taking HBC brings 'certain volume commitment, some sort of a demand signal'.

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY / QUALCOMM WARNS THAT HBM IS CROWDING OUT HANDSET DRAM. CEO Cristiano Amon: 'As memory suppliers redirect manufacturing capacity to HBM to meet AI data center demand, the resulting industry-wide memory shortage and price increases are likely to define the overall scale of the handset industry through the fiscal year.' In Q&A he called the March-quarter handset weakness '100% related to memory'. Handset demand and sell-through are strong, but 'DRAM availability for consumer electronics, especially handsets, is actually down bias on a year-over-year because of the prioritization of HBM for data centers', so customers are cutting builds to fit the memory they can get. Management added that 'memory vendors have prioritized the build out of HBM' and that memory supply for consumer electronics has been below demand, with similar commentary now coming from gaming consoles and other consumer devices. On duration: 'We can't really predict if this will continue for 2027 or 2028'. The answer depends on planned capacity build-outs and how fast the data-center trend accelerates. The issue 'is not just the price. The issue is just availability'. OEMs are expected to prioritize the premium and high tiers, and automotive is 'a little bit less sensitive to memory price increases'.
quarterly_data.figure: handset weakness '100% related to memory'; fiscal-year handset market size set by DRAM availability

quarterly_data.signal: Six-inch indium phosphide ramp running ahead of plan: Coherent significantly increased InP production in Q2 and is on track to double internal InP production by the fourth quarter of calendar 2026. Current-quarter wafer starts are already at 80% of the doubling target, after wafer starts more than quadrupled from the September quarter to the December quarter; a wafer start takes about six months to become a transceiver shipment, so the benefit starts this quarter and builds over coming quarters. Production is ramping in parallel at Sherman, Texas and Yarfala, Sweden, with EMLs, CW lasers and photodiodes all in production on six-inch and six-inch yields exceeding three-inch yields. A six-inch wafer produces more than four times as many chips at less than half the cost; almost all capacity being added is six-inch, about half of capacity will be six-inch by the end of calendar 2026, and plans go well beyond doubling in following years. Coherent has multiple six-inch InP substrate suppliers and has secured committed substrate supply supporting the doubling; management called Coherent the world's only producer of six-inch indium phosphide.

Moving into its own liquid-cooled data center with 'tons of power to the racks,' xAI asked Credo to extend its AEC family from 3 meters to 7 meters so that every connection in the row could be copper. Arista rejects the ~5 proprietary CPO implementations circulating and is committing to ONE OPEN CPO — socketed optical engines, pigtail fibers, fully pre-tested modules, a truly open multi-vendor interface (often called NPO) — with trials/examples NEXT YEAR; 'the MAJORITY of the world will still remain PLUGGABLE OPTICS AND COPPER; there will be SOME co-packaged optics in 2028 and 2029.' Scale-up positioning: 'we live in an NVIDIA world' — where NVIDIA supplies the full NVLink vertical stack there is little Arista participation (Arista wins scale-out/across), but for NON-NVIDIA accelerators (AMD MI series, Google TPUs — 'increasingly a FORMIDABLE training processor', in-house XPUs, inference chips) Arista works BOTH scale-up and scale-out, including CUSTOM RACKS tuned to customers' engines; 'feels like InfiniBand 2-3 years ago... it will take time to move from proprietary NVLink to alternatives, even if Ethernet's really good — I expect us to do much better there.' 1.6T cadence (history repeats 800G's trials-2023/24 -> ramp-2025/26): TRIALS H2 2026 with single-digit VERY LARGE customers; REAL PRODUCTION 2027 (liquid-cooling infrastructure required). EOS innovations for AI fabrics: SSU hitless upgrades, MRC packet-spray/reassembly (kills hash-collision slowdowns), SRv6 explicit-path load balancing with real-time congestion signals — one binary from scale-out to scale-across.

Lumentum remains confident in an ultra-high-power laser chip demand ramp in the second half of calendar 2027, ahead of customer scale-up deployments in calendar 2028. Because the first phase of scale-up optical connections spans across compute racks within a cluster, the ramp applies to any topology larger than one rack. Ultra-high-power laser revenue is expected to reach roughly the $50 million mark by the end of calendar 2026, with the first triple-digit ($100M+) quarter expected in fiscal Q3 FY2027.

quarterly_data.signal: First external light source (ELS) MODULE purchase order received, for delivery by the second half of calendar 2027 - Lumentum's first move up the stack from selling laser chips into selling the full ELS module. ASP is 'meaningfully higher than the set of lasers that we ship in'; module margins are above corporate average but below the laser chips, a deliberate trade of some margin for revenue acceleration. Wupen Yuen: the ELS module is positioned to enable 'customers who don't know how to deal with individual laser chips' to build CPO and NPO systems.
quarterly_data.figure: first ELS module purchase order (delivery H2 CY2027); ASP meaningfully higher than laser set

quarterly_data.signal: NPO (near-packaged optics) called 'completely additive' and 'significantly increasing the optical TAM.' The rest of the customer base beyond the lead CPO account is prioritizing NPO as an intermediate step to eventual CPO adoption; even the largest CPO customer is evaluating NPO for specific new use cases. Two laser types are being evaluated for NPO: a mid-power laser integrated directly into the optical engine, and a high-power laser in an external light source module. Lumentum's NPO/CPO laser family spans 120 mW, 150 mW, and 400 mW output levels off common design and process know-how. Wupen Yuen: each NPO set carries ~6.4T of bandwidth, roughly four times a local module, and NPO should hit the market in the late 2027 / 2028 timeframe to enable optical scale-up.
quarterly_data.figure: NPO additive to optical TAM; 120/150/400 mW laser family; ~6.4T per NPO set; market late 2027-2028

quarterly_data.signal: Supply-demand imbalance update: no change on EMLs (still shipping behind customer demand, previously cited at greater than 30%), but high-powered lasers have deteriorated sharply - 'we are way behind in our shipments... The demand signal has increased, and we are very much further behind relative to our ability to supply.' Management clarified the ramp execution itself is on track; the gap widened because demand accelerated. High-powered lasers were named as the one vector that materially changed since the prior quarter.
quarterly_data.figure: EML imbalance unchanged (>30%); high-power laser shortfall materially worse on accelerating demand

quarterly_data.signal: EMLs delivered another record-breaking quarter, primarily driven by 100G-per-lane devices. 200G EMLs are accelerating and now account for over 25% of total EML revenue; management expects 200G EMLs to be 50% or more of volume by mid-calendar-2027. Lumentum remains on track to deliver over 50% EML unit growth in the December 2026 quarter versus the year-ago quarter, but expects to remain significantly behind demand even at year end.
quarterly_data.figure: record EML quarter; 200G EML >25% of EML revenue; >50% EML unit growth by Dec-2026 quarter

quarterly_data.signal: CW laser strategy expanded materially. The new 200G-per-lane CW laser chip has a significantly reduced die size, is more efficient, and delivers margins accretive to long-term financial targets; Lumentum is commanding a significant price premium versus market price because tight spec width produces superior transceiver yields at customers. The margin gap between CW and EML 'has closed considerably' since the prior call (EML still better). Better-than-expected output in Japan is being allocated to CW, and Lumentum is now shipping CW lasers in a relatively meaningful way into the 200G-per-lane silicon photonics opportunity, on top of internal deployment in its own transceivers.
quarterly_data.figure: 200G CW laser: smaller die, price premium, margin gap to EML closed considerably

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity: expanding across the two indium phosphide wafer fabs in Japan to capture coming 200G and 300G lane-speed opportunities, qualifying both CW and EML process flows on the newest tools as they come online. Demand for both EML and CW lasers is expected to grow significantly through the second half of calendar 2026 and into 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: two Japan InP fabs expanding; CW and EML flows qualifying on new tools

quarterly_data.signal: Pump lasers: shipments surged more than 80% year-over-year and Lumentum will 'remain effectively sold out for the foreseeable future despite our rapid capacity expansion.' A fourfold increase in pump laser shipments is still expected over the next several quarters. Share is roughly 70%-80%. Capacity is ramping at Rose Orchard (US) with packaging and test in Thailand. Multiple long-term customer agreements have been secured to help offset planned capital expenditures - mostly three-year arrangements with built-in pricing levers and, in most instances, take-or-pay structures, formed largely with NEMs (network equipment manufacturers).
quarterly_data.figure: pump lasers +80% YoY; 4x shipment increase expected; ~70-80% share; 3-year take-or-pay LTAs

quarterly_data.signal: Narrow linewidth laser assembly shipments grew sequentially for the 10th consecutive quarter and were up over 130% year-over-year. Scale-across demand is being driven by inferencing and training applications requiring full-rate connectivity between data centers, plus political and regulatory constraints favoring smaller, more modular builds. Scale of the DCI opportunity: for one major hyperscaler, the network capacity connecting just two AI data center sites is double the total global backbone capacity that hyperscaler built over the entirety of the last decade.
quarterly_data.figure: narrow linewidth +130% YoY, 10th consecutive sequential growth quarter

quarterly_data.signal: Cloud transceivers: record 800G shipments in the quarter while initiating production of next-generation 1.6T modules. Transceiver profitability continues to improve on yield gains, capacity utilization, and the initial rollout of higher-ASP 1.6T units. 1.6T uptake is expected to intensify starting in fiscal Q1 FY2027 and sustain through calendar 2027, anchored by lead Tier 1 hyperscale customers rolling out custom AI clusters. Management believes Lumentum is first to market ahead of larger competitors in many instances and can hold that share advantage through the cycle, crediting its signal integrity team on difficult 1.6T designs.
quarterly_data.figure: record 800G shipments; 1.6T production initiated; 1.6T uptake intensifies from fiscal Q1 FY2027

quarterly_data.signal: OCS: shipments doubled from fiscal Q3 to fiscal Q4, and Q1 FY2027 guidance includes Lumentum's first triple-digit OCS revenue quarter - expected to be 'meaningfully above the three-digit mark' ($100M+). Tracking to (not ahead of) the previously stated $400 million of OCS shipments for the second half of calendar 2026, leaving room to run in the fourth calendar quarter. Demand signal for 2027 'continues to be incredibly strong'; initial work started to add capacity with contract manufacturers alongside increasing internal factory output. Lumentum describes itself as the only merchant OCS supplier with a shipping track record, and expects to cross over to become the number one OCS supplier sometime in early 2027 versus one customer's internal source of supply.
quarterly_data.figure: OCS shipments 2x QoQ; first $100M+ OCS quarter guided; $400M H2 CY2026 on track; #1 supplier expected early 2027

quarterly_data.signal: OCS roadmap broadened since the prior call: Lumentum is now planning higher and lower port count products, including specialized in-tray offerings. These are entirely additive to the TAM presented at OFC and are expected to hit in the 2028 timeframe, requiring significant engineering redesign.
quarterly_data.figure: OCS in-tray and higher/lower port-count products; additive TAM; 2028 timeframe

quarterly_data.signal: Greensboro, North Carolina fab (fifth InP fab, acquired March 2026): conversion from gallium arsenide to indium phosphide is 'well underway,' with long-pole items such as reactors already addressed. No change to schedule - first revenue in early 2028, ramping through calendar 2028 to full pitch by end of 2028 and into 2029. Capacity remains uncommitted and Lumentum is actively talking to customers about laser demand, expecting to announce new Greensboro arrangements (LTAs) over the next couple of quarters.
quarterly_data.figure: Greensboro GaAs-to-InP conversion underway; first revenue early 2028; ramp into 2029; LTAs in discussion

quarterly_data.signal: InP substrate supply: after a surge in ultra-high-power laser demand across a couple of customers, Lumentum spent the last three months securing additional substrate supply and signed a deal with AXT during the quarter. Hurlston: 'we went out and we found additional substrate help from AXT. They are a great partner.' Lumentum is comfortable near-term on the strength of its lead arrangement with a Japanese supplier plus the AXT deal, but flagged that given the rate of change in the demand vector 'that may not be true a quarter or two from now either' - more substrate help is likely needed if the vector continues.

quarterly_data.signal: Technology roadmap view: silicon photonics is a viable solution at 1.6T and CW lasers are taking a significant portion of transceiver output, but at 3.2T silicon photonics 'loses some of its advantages' and Lumentum expects EMLs to come back in a meaningful way. Wupen Yuen added that in a supply-constrained environment customers will use whichever laser source they can get, so the EML-versus-CW mix is a supply/demand dynamic as much as a technical one. CPO remains the natural end state - optics placed directly on the substrate or interposer for maximum power efficiency through foundry-level advanced packaging.
quarterly_data.figure: SiPho viable at 1.6T; EML expected to return at 3.2T; CPO the end state via foundry advanced packaging

I don't expect there to be any impact,' citing EML differentiation, high/mid-power laser differentiation for NPO and CPO, and an ability to price up even in CW because tight spec consistency drives superior customer transceiver yields. He cautioned that some Chinese laser suppliers are not yet delivering into the market.
quarterly_data.figure: no impact seen from new Chinese InP fabs; price premium sustained

quarterly_data.signal: Adjacent businesses: industrial lasers and cable access strengthened quarter-over-quarter. Within industrial lasers, increased adoption of ultrafast lasers targeting high-density PCB via drilling that supports advanced AI XPU boards and 1.6T optical modules. In 3D sensing, Lumentum has visibility to an expanding set of applications expected to drive growth in upcoming product cycles with its primary customer.

Sizing: CPO/ELSFP needs a 300mW laser (vs 70mW for 800G, 100mW for 1.6T) with ~6x larger die, so the industry laser market must grow 8-10x; DWDM ELSFP carries 40-50% worse yield loss than 1310nm, and laser equipment takes 21-24 months from order to high-volume output. AOI states only AOI, Lumentum and Coherent can hit acceptable DWDM CPO laser / CPO module yields.

quarterly_data.signal: New company guidance given at the conference, not on the Q4 FY2026 earnings call: 'in 2028, we figure that we can now deliver $40 of earnings power' (fiscal 2028). The driver is OCS - since the last earnings call Lumentum's largest OCS customer 'has taken up their orders very significantly', producing 'a huge uptick in our order book and the order rate'. Hurlston: 'The OCS numbers have come up a lot since our last earnings call, and that really gives us a lot of confidence, given the margin profile of that good, to substantially take up where we think our earnings power will be in 2028, in our fiscal 2028' - a take-up he described as running against where all the sell-side analysts had the company.

quarterly_data.signal: Hurlston pushed back on the assumption that Lumentum OCS equals Google: 'the breadth of customer engagement is very high on OCS. We started with customers other than Google... we actually have customers that were much more substantial than Google in our early rounds of shipments.' One of the more interesting emerging use cases is deploying an OCS inside the rack itself, one per rack, to route around GPUs or TPUs that have failed or are overloaded - a surprising number of GPUs in a data center fail, and a compute model can represent '$20, 30, $40 million of compute time'. At the lead customer the number of OCSs per torus is also going up. As a result the $8 billion OCS TAM Lumentum published at OFC 'now looks like it's significantly under called', and a new, significantly higher TAM number is expected at the next OFC in March of next year. OCS has power and optical-loss advantages over an electrical switch and Hurlston expects it to be 'one of the largest growth drivers in the company'.
