quarterly_data.signal: New EML economics and share math. Moving from 100G to 200G EML gives 'about a 2x uplift in price' - ASPs roughly double - and 200G lasers arrive at the 1.6T node. At 200G there is 'very little competition': Broadcom is a supplier of 200G EMLs, Lumentum is the other large supplier, and management sees no other entrants soon. On mix, EML-based transceivers are 'probably 70%-80%' of the 800G market but are expected to be only '40%-50% of the market at 1.6T' as silicon photonics takes share, so raw EML units go up while share comes down. At 3.2T Lumentum's transceiver engineers say 'silicon photonics again runs out of steam', producing 'a double whammy' where both EML unit numbers and EML share rise. Hurlston also framed the yield argument behind the price premium: the tolerance of the laser sets transceiver yield more than anything else, so a higher laser price 'more than makes up for itself in the high yields'.
quarterly_data.figure: 100G to 200G EML about a 2x uplift in price; EML share of transceivers 70%-80% at 800G falling to 40%-50% at 1.6T; share rises again at 3.2T

quarterly_data.signal: First run-rate history given for the Cloud Light transceiver business: acquired doing 'roughly $75 million a quarter', revenue then fell 'below $50 million, a quarterly run rate of 40 to 50' on quality problems that largest customer Google complained about; after retooling engineering it recovered to 'about a $100 million quarterly run rate' and is 'now running well over $200 million a quarter', expected to grow considerably throughout 2027. At the 1.6T transition Lumentum got to the head of the curve on signal integrity and is 'now shipping ahead of great competitors like InnoLight and Coherent' (Eoptolink also named), first to market on a lot of its SKUs. The unresolved problem is gross margin - still below the top competitors - which management plans to attack on the manufacturing side entering calendar 2027, while conceding it may never match InnoLight or Eoptolink.
quarterly_data.figure: Cloud Light about $75 million a quarter at acquisition, below $50 million trough (40 to 50 run rate), back to about $100 million, now well over $200 million a quarter

quarterly_data.signal: NPO timing moved materially since the earnings call: 'prior to our last earnings call, we probably thought that it was going to be a late 2028 into early 2029 event... It seems like now it's a late 2027 into early 2028 event', because customers competing with NVIDIA concluded they need to deploy a lot more optics and to do so sooner. Hurlston called the near-term NPO opportunity larger than the CPO opportunity, with a higher adoption rate of optical lanes than NVIDIA's, and said NPO customers are requiring Lumentum to ship the entire ELS rather than bare laser chips. The consequence is capacity: NPO 'is going to put a lot of pressure on that Greensboro fab', Lumentum needs a 'next leg of the stool' and is trying to lock up NPO business now to fill Greensboro and more, but would require an NVIDIA-style commitment before funding further capacity. NVIDIA underwrote Greensboro with a long-term agreement characterised as a multibillion-dollar deal plus an investment that helped Lumentum buy, equip and outfit the fab, acquired early calendar 2026 and not operational until early calendar 2028; the team running it was inherited from Qorvo, and qualification at NVIDIA itself took a year.
quarterly_data.figure: NPO pulled in from a late 2028 into early 2029 event to a late 2027 into early 2028 event; Greensboro acquired early calendar 2026, operational early calendar 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Geopolitical sizing not given on the call: Lumentum is 'probably correctly' viewed as a net beneficiary of a U.S. move to ban Chinese transceivers, but 'the Chinese transceiver suppliers make 70% of the transceivers in the U.S. market', so cutting that off entirely without a thoughtful, industry-coordinated phase-in 'would be a challenge' for the whole hyperscaler industry; Lumentum could mobilize relatively quickly, as could Coherent, but it would take time. The reverse risk is tit-for-tat curtailment of Chinese sub-component supply - substrates, isolators and other raw materials Lumentum currently relies on - against which its manufacturing footprint in Thailand, in China itself and in the United Kingdom (a safe harbour on substrates) is the hedge.
quarterly_data.figure: Chinese transceiver suppliers make 70% of the transceivers in the U.S. market

quarterly_data.signal: Kathy Ta sized the optical bandwidth step-up per interconnect tier for the first time: if Data Center Interconnect / telecom is a 1x multiple, scale-across and scale-out are each roughly 10x DCI; the first instance of CPO going to scale-up, starting in the second half of 2027, is 'probably 3x to 4x above the 10x that we are seeing for scale-out', and when all of scale-up goes optical it is 'a full 10x above the 10x of scale-out', with scale-in another 10x multiple beyond that. Wupen Yuen framed the same ladder as scale-across 1, scale-out 10, scale-up 100, scale-in 1,000, and positioned Lumentum as 'going all the way from scale across to scale out, to scale up, and later to scale in'.
quarterly_data.figure: scale-across and scale-out each about 10x DCI; scale-up CPO 3x to 4x above the 10x of scale-out from the second half of 2027; full optical scale-up a full 10x above scale-out; scale-in another 10x

quarterly_data.signal: Post-earnings supply update: the supply-demand gap is 'still extending' and Lumentum is 'still short everywhere' - DML short, CW laser short. Yuen does not see the shortage going away in 2027; the industry forecasts scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027 while laser supply does not catch up, and 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x increase of demand, so the laser supply-demand gap does not close within the next couple of years. Lumentum is still allocating capacity, in some cases on pricing and expedite fees, to serve the most profitable opportunities, and 'all the deals we are making today are equal or higher pricing than the escalated pricing that we already had before' - management's own read that the gap persists.
quarterly_data.figure: scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027; 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x demand increase; gap does not close within the next couple of years

quarterly_data.signal: Yuen reframed optical scale-up as an industry-wide story rather than the single-customer CPO story assumed at OFC: to serve 2028 optical scale-up volume the industry needs both CPO and NPO approaches, and by volume 'CPO will be half of the market. NPO is the other half of the market' - roughly 50/50. On the content Lumentum sells, CPO is 'an exclusive external light source market'; half of NPO also goes external light source (ELS) and the remaining roughly 25% of the overall market is still being debated between integrated light source (ILS) and ELS, with more and more movement toward ELS because the optical engine sits so close to the accelerator heat source that an integrated laser becomes the reliability-limiting factor. Even the ILS case will not use pluggable-class lasers: an NPO engine '1 inch by half an inch' packs 6.4T versus half an iPhone for a 1.6T module today, so fewer but higher-power lasers are required and the entire NPO/CPO application moves to '120, 150 milliwatt and above', not the traditional 70 milliwatt pluggable laser. Chinese CW laser supply chatter is aimed at that pluggable market, not this one.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO half and NPO half of the optical scale-up market; ILS about 25% of the overall market; NPO engine 1 inch by half an inch packing 6.4T vs a 1.6T module today; 120, 150 milliwatt and above vs traditional 70 milliwatt

quarterly_data.signal: Three-wave ultra-high-power (UHP) laser capacity ramp laid out for the first time: wave one is the San Jose fab, ramping today with line of sight through 2027; wave two is the U.K. fab, which 'will come in in second quarter 2027' and continues ramping through 2028; wave three is the Greensboro fab, starting to ramp in 'second quarter 2028 or mid 2028'. All three are on schedule and the biggest variable is customer qualification timing - Lumentum must submit a PCN for the customer to qualify the product, and accelerating that qualification can pull the ramp in. Capacity is additive rather than reallocated: a new clean room in the U.K. fitted with 'the latest and greatest state-of-the-art equipment', and the added capacity is '6-inch capable', so current telecom and scale-across products are not sacrificed - 'by and large, we do not sacrifice. We add.'

She expects a bigger ELS share opportunity in NPO because the majority of the NPO opportunity looks ELS rather than ILS, and many of those ELS customers want Lumentum to supply the complete ELS module rather than only laser chips. On sizing, the $8 billion OCS TAM Lumentum put on a slide six months ago now looks low: besides the largest customer's own success in the market, OCS is moving into serious R&D for tray-level / in-rack dynamic partitioning (a customer may not want a fixed 576 XPUs in a cluster) and for resiliency network applications that route around underperforming accelerators, which management says gives visibility to a lot more OCS being required by the late 2028 / early 2029 timeframe.

quarterly_data.signal: Competitive read on high-power CPO/NPO lasers: Yuen named Coherent as the single competitor - 'we see the one competitor, right, who is Coherent' - and said Lumentum is 'really not seeing anybody else in this high-power laser area'. He described why the part is hard (power, RIN noise, linewidth and mode hop all have to be achieved simultaneously at volume with good yield, and mode hop is the biggest problem with today's silicon photonics lasers), noted Lumentum is already ramping these lasers and seeing good real data, and then said the industry needs a second source: from a customer's point of view Coherent would need to be ramping 'sometime in 2027... Probably second half' to support the scale-up build in 2028.

In DRAM, D1C and D1D generation revenue is expected at roughly half of DRAM equipment revenue, with single wafer treatment PORs secured from the D1B generation onward and significant revenue growth expected; toward D0 and vertical channel transistor DRAM, more batch ALD adoption opportunities are expected. A U.S. demo center totaling JPY 20 billion opens in January 2027, and new land adjacent to the Tonami manufacturing center was acquired for production and R&D expansion.

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity utilization is expected at an average of 70%-80% in the first half and over 80% in the second half of March 2027, higher next fiscal year; production lead time is currently around eight months. Current capacity secures the JPY 340 billion revenue forecast, and capacity is being expanded for March 2028 and beyond: warehouse space at the Tonami plant is being converted to clean room, newly acquired land next to Tonami is being evaluated for rapid expansion, production engineer recruitment is ramping, and shifts (currently 1.5) can be increased. Monthly unit production capacity is targeted to reach 2.5 times the March 2025 level in 10 years. Investment timing has advanced about two years versus the WFE view at the start of the year; suppliers are also preparing capacity and are not currently a bottleneck.

quarterly_data.signal: Growth catalysts: GAA sales were about JPY 5 billion in Q1 and are expected at over JPY 20 billion for FY March 2027. Advanced packaging revenue, JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026, is now expected at JPY 15 billion in FY March 2027 (Q1 was JPY 4.5 billion) - a significant upward revision from the JPY 6 billion prior plan, driven by both rising customer CapEx and additional POR wins for its film deposition technology. In NAND, demand-supply is not fully adjusted - memory players are allocating clean room to DRAM while NAND wafer output needs to increase - so greenfield NAND investments are expected to resume, which converts all of Kokusai's PORs to sales and is broadly favorable. In DRAM, the D1C transition is complete and D1D is progressing. NAND sales could approach record highs, and DRAM plus NAND plus advanced packaging support growth above WFE (targeting more than a 20% sales increase).

quarterly_data.signal: Power: silicon carbide shipments eased slightly quarter over quarter as customers stay disciplined on capacity after the earlier build-out and put technology transitions first. A key Q4 CS&I driver was a large customer converting its silicon carbide tools from 150 millimeter to 200 millimeter and, in the same footprint, upgrading them to the recently introduced Purion Power Series+ platform. Only a very small part of the installed base has moved to 200-millimeter, with leaders outside China going first, which leaves ample upgrade opportunity. Select China customers are expanding SiC device capacity, while customers in other regions invest in trench and superjunction, which is driving growing interest in the company's newly developed high-energy channeling capability (essential for superjunction). Near-term SiC implant demand should stay muted while customers absorb capacity. Other power (silicon IGBTs) also eased, and power overall is expected slightly lower in 2026. Longer term, management expects power semiconductors (silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride) to benefit from the growing power needs of AI, from wider adoption of 800-volt EVs and from physical AI.

quarterly_data.signal: General mature: revenue rose quarter over quarter on select investments, mainly in high current tools. quarterly_data.signal: GPU PROBE-CARD MARKET SIZED AND A SHARE TARGET PUT ON IT FOR THE FIRST TIME. Slessor on qualifying for GPU applications at the world's largest foundry: 'we've now received qualification and are shipping pilot production volumes that are being used in production, for GPU test at the world-leading foundry'. On the size: 'We initially sized it maybe a little less than $100 million a year. That feels awfully conservative at this point.' On share against the entrenched incumbent, assuming the uptime/MTBF/test-cell-productivity advantages of FormFactor's advanced MEMS probes hold through the initial production ramp: 'we will be able to gain on the next generation, maybe somewhere in the 20%-25%-30% share range', which he called a useful goal — revenue from it becoming visible in 2027. Delivering it depends on capacity: 'We are pretty constrained on capacity right now.'

quarterly_data.signal: CUSTOM ASICs CROSS INTO ADVANCED MEMS IN 2027-2028 — THE NEXT TECHNOLOGY PIVOT. Slessor named the category directly: 'custom ASICs, things like Google's TPU, AWS's Trainium'. Their power envelope, both consumed and produced, is driving them out of legacy wire-based needle probe technology: 'We see custom ASICs really crossing this brink in 2027 and into 2028 of needing an advanced MEMS probe technology... much the same way GPUs did a few generations ago.' It will be mixed rather than wholesale — chiplet architectures mean some chiplets stay on legacy wire probes while the advanced compute chiplets require MEMS. FormFactor builds every probe with proprietary MEMS metallurgy and patterning, vertically integrated in Livermore, California and the ramping Farmers Branch, Texas site, enabling higher current, higher speed and higher/lower temperature test. Engagement is with 'all the names you'd expect us to be engaged with and their foundry and OSAT partners'; initial revenue has been booked on some projects, with designs and qualifications won in late 2026 and ramp in 2027. These may not appear as 10% customers because FormFactor is 'essentially operating at a billion-dollar annual run rate now', raising the 10%-customer bar.
quarterly_data.figure: custom ASICs crossing to advanced MEMS probe in 2027 and into 2028; FormFactor at a billion-dollar annual run rate

quarterly_data.signal: THREE NEW COMPUTE PROBE-CARD WINS DISCLOSED, ALL UNNAMED. (1) 'One of our historic long-term customers, one of the major CPU suppliers to the industry, their business obviously getting stronger associated with some of the turnaround they've done and the CPU strength.' (2) 'We recently qualified and won some designs at a fabless CPU and GPU manufacturer.' (3) 'There's a third customer building their own CPUs for their overall high-performance compute products, where we've won some designs and expect to have that as a 2027 contributor.' Slessor also explained why probe cards stay consumable even though high-performance-compute probes no longer wear out: each new mask set needs a new probe card — 'as a customer like NVIDIA goes from Blackwell to Rubin to Rubin Ultra, those are each new probe cards, even though they use the same capital equipment and test equipment' — so design-change velocity, not wear, now drives the recurring revenue.

quarterly_data.signal: CAPACITY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AND FARMERS BRANCH IS THE RELEASE VALVE. Slessor: 'right now, the simplest way to think about our situation is we are capacity constrained. What's limiting our growth, if you will, or what's constraining our growth, is our capacity.' Farmers Branch, Texas is 'close to a 300,000 square foot site' bought a little over a year ago with a ready-to-go clean room and expansion potential; a grand opening is set for 'late October'; the site is expected to deliver 'twice the current California probe card capacity in the current phase'. Timing: 'Start to ship the initial qualification units in the fourth quarter, and again, ramping through 2027 to deliver a substantial increase, essentially 2X the existing capacity as we get through the back part of 2027.' Capacity will be turned on in tranches matched to demand to avoid utilisation and gross-margin headwinds. On the target model — '55% gross margin, $5 of earnings per share on $1.6 billion of revenue' in 2030 — he said the external high-single-digit market growth assumption was arguably too conservative and that FormFactor could 'reach the target model faster than 2030' if demand holds.

quarterly_data.signal: Dragonfly G5 strategy clarified: management does NOT expect a G3-to-G5 transition. The G5 is instead about expanding into NEW markets - high resolution, 100 nm type inspection applications in the front end plus several specialty device applications - which is the focus for 2027. Onto had about 10 customers across 15 different applications a quarter ago and expects, based on evaluation feedback, that the majority of those will convert to orders throughout 2027. quarterly_data.quarter: Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: A new growth leg is forming in power semiconductors from data center power. Onto's earlier power-semi run was driven not by capacity expansion but by customers using Onto's inspection and metrology to drive yield improvement, with yields in the 60%-70% range rather than the 90s. The EV recovery has not really happened yet, but those same customers are now telling Onto they see demand from data centers driving adoption of power semiconductors and that Onto needs to prepare. Management is not seeing the actual orders yet and has no good clarity on timing, but said 2027 into 2028 is what the customers are thinking about; because the process control is already inserted in their process, Onto should benefit as they expand. Data center power is relatively small for Onto today and would be captured under specialty devices.

quarterly_data.quarter: Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: CFO Brian Roberts on the margin path and supply: 2026 margin gains have come from operational productivity and the move of manufacturing from the U.S. to the international extended factories - a year ago Onto was shipping its first tools from those factories and in Q2 it shipped about 70% of its tools from them. To date Onto has driven 250 basis points of gross margin and doubled that at the operating margin line. Into 2027, the accretive Dragonfly G5 and Atlas G6 add ASP lift which, alongside productivity, drives toward 'a margin that starts with a six'. The two major 2026 headwinds were memory cost and freight/fuel shortage, partly offset by being in region, and Onto is having pricing conversations with customers about the existing product portfolio for the 2027 pricing/budgeting season. On supply, the extended-factory move gave Onto partner capacity and new clean rooms without heavy CapEx; the supply chain is not perfect but Onto is using customer visibility to get ahead of bottlenecks, is carrying a higher inventory balance, is not missing customer dates and its lead times have not grown too much.

quarterly_data.signal: AI test intensity is compounding because design margins are shrinking: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' and must test in production too. A compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts - more insertion points - tested at signal level (VNAs, oscilloscopes), at bit level (new portfolio) and at protocol/packet level (AI workload emulators). The move from monolithic chips to CHIPLET architectures adds interoperability emulation, and customers now ask for emulation environments that stress a chip while it exercises a model (thermal shutdown, all cores active at higher power and speed). The ecosystem is shifting from a homogeneous integrated vertical stack to a HETEROGENEOUS one - GPU/CPU/DPU mixes and a growing number of protocols at every layer of the stack - which broadens Keysight's addressable tail. The four wireline pillars (AI infrastructure scaling, speed transitions, silicon photonics, system-level emulation) all drove growth. Hyperscaler engagement (rooted in the Ixia acquisition ~5 years ago) is deepening as they integrate Keysight pre-silicon emulation and workload solutions into their development pipelines; hyperscalers plus the model companies are ~10% OF REVENUE DIRECTLY but drive large downstream influence, and many are building their own in-house silicon. Switch designers use Keysight emulators to validate network performance across AI workloads and protocols; interconnect manufacturers use high-fidelity analyzers to characterize high-speed backplanes for signal integrity and manufacturing yield.

quarterly_data.signal: NAND/DRAM scarcity is the defining constraint. CEO Wallace Kou: the AI super cycle has driven substantial HBM, DRAM, NAND and HDD price increases and 'mounting substrate and supply pressure,' and he expects the scarcity to persist 'likely until 2028 when new fabs come online.' DRAM and NAND now account for almost 56% of total BOM cost on a low-end smartphone, forcing OEMs to trim specifications; smartphone units are still expected down 10-15% in 2026. NAND makers are redirecting focus and CapEx to DRAM and HBM, deemphasising eMMC/UFS and exiting automotive - which hands share to Silicon Motion's module-maker customers and gives it stronger pricing power. Long-standing relationships let Silicon Motion secure NAND from multiple suppliers through the shortage, which management calls a significant and enduring differentiator.
quarterly_data.figure: NAND scarcity expected to persist until 2028; DRAM+NAND ~56% of low-end smartphone BOM; smartphone units -10% to -15% in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: MonTitan enterprise SSD controllers entered commercial production in Q2 with TWO Tier 1 customers, with five additional Tier 1 customers expected to ramp in the second half. Management reaffirmed the target of 5-10% of total revenue coming from MonTitan exiting 2026. First customers are targeting the compute market with TLC NAND for AI platforms that use NAND for high-speed, low-latency storage dedicated to NEAR-GPU AND NEAR-CPU KV CACHE. TLC-based solutions are ramping ahead of QLC: early QLC shipments begin late 2026 but QLC only becomes meaningful late 2027 into 2028, gated by the availability and affordability of 2-terabit QLC dies. CFO Jason Tsai was explicit that the delay is a NAND-industry availability issue, not a controller issue.
quarterly_data.figure: 2 Tier 1 customers in production, 5 more ramping in H2; MonTitan targeted at 5-10% of revenue exiting 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Next-generation 4-nanometer PCIe Gen 6 MonTitan controller completes tape-out in August 2026, developed in close collaboration with customers and aimed at hyperscalers and cloud service providers. Multiple design wins are already secured with both flash makers and cloud service providers, and more than a dozen Tier 1 customers are waiting for samples. The architecture targets AI inference - management specifically cited NVIDIA's CMX architecture - plus multi-host operation under new AI workloads. Management expects the Gen 6 ramp to be 'much stronger and faster, bigger than our PCIe Gen 5 ramps' and set an initial target market share of at least 15-20%, with the controller becoming a significant growth driver in 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: 4nm PCIe Gen 6 tape-out August 2026; >12 Tier 1 customers awaiting samples; initial share target 15-20%; growth driver in 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Ferri for Automotive and Enterprise Boot Drive solutions MORE THAN DOUBLED sequentially and now represent nearly 30% of total revenue, up from 4% a year ago. These are controller-plus-NAND solutions, so ASPs are much higher than controller-only (and higher than MonTitan). The DRAM-less boot drive is the crown jewel: conventional DRAM-based boot drives for server CPUs stay with the NAND makers, but DPUs, TPUs, NPUs and switches favour DRAM-less designs for cost, security and performance - and NAND makers have no DRAM-less PCIe SSD controllers and little incentive to build them for a market where densities are only 256GB-512GB. A server rack can carry more than 30 or 40 boot drives, and per-drive capacity should rise. Management sees little competition from either NAND makers or module makers, and said Ferri plus Boot Drive reaching roughly one third of revenue in 2027 is 'certainly a possibility' given current backlog and pipeline.
quarterly_data.figure: Ferri + Boot Drive more than doubled QoQ to ~30% of revenue (from 4% a year ago); >30-40 boot drives per server rack

quarterly_data.signal: Edge SSD controllers grew 40-45% year over year in Q2 after a seasonally soft Q1, and SSD revenue is up about 50% versus the first half of last year on share gains despite declining PC units. The PCIe 4 to PCIe 5 transition is proceeding MORE SLOWLY than management expected six months ago: OEMs are pairing the latest, more cost-effective NAND with PCIe 4 SSDs in value and mainstream PCs to cut bill-of-materials cost. The 4-channel PCIe 5 controller introduced in Q4 of last year continues to ramp steadily in the mid- to high-end PC segment, and management still expects SSD average selling prices to rise through the year.
quarterly_data.figure: Edge SSD +40-45% YoY; SSD revenue ~+50% vs prior-year first half; PCIe 4-to-5 transition slower than expected

quarterly_data.signal: Embedded eMMC & UFS grew significantly ahead of the industry on share gains, as NAND makers increasingly outsource to third-party controllers while concentrating their own resources on DRAM and HBM. Silicon Motion already supports three of the NAND makers with its automotive controller and firmware after a decade of automotive certification work.

quarterly_data.signal: NAND/DRAM scarcity: CEO Wallace Kou said 'AI CSPs has attempt to lock up all the DRAM and NAND supply through 2026', making it hard for other buyers to get product and driving 'significant intra-quarter price increases'. NAND makers are shifting internal resources and capex to DRAM, HBM and customized AI memory, and new NAND capacity is limited by land, clean room and equipment lead times. The shortage is 'much more severe than anybody can imagine because CSP really demand much more than the current supply can support'; even leading smartphone makers struggle to procure NAND and LPDDR5, and many automotive Tier 1 suppliers (the lowest priority for NAND and DRAM makers) are asking Silicon Motion for help. Silicon Motion has no long-term supply agreement ('we did not have the LTA agreement') and relies on its NAND maker relationships; it takes NAND-bundled business case by case and may skip business whose margin misses the company target.

quarterly_data.signal: MonTitan enterprise SSD controllers: in the December quarter Silicon Motion began end-user qualification of TLC-based high-performance compute SSDs using MonTitan with multiple customers; qualification runs through the first half of 2026 with commercial ramp in the second half. High-capacity QLC storage SSDs, 'the largest addressable market for MonTitan', remain on track to begin qualification with multiple customers this year; QLC demand has accelerated given the current HDD supply shortage, and management expects QLC SSDs to become a compelling alternative to HDD. Management 'remain confident that MonTitan will ramp to represent at least 5% to 10% of revenue, exiting 2026' - a MonTitan-controller-only figure that excludes boot drive solutions (MonTitan is reported in the controller business). The CEO tied fast-growing AI inference (KV cache, latency, capacity) to storage demand that will 'all need MonTitan to fill the role'.
quarterly_data.figure: at least 5% to 10% of revenue, exiting 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Next-generation MonTitan: during 2026 Silicon Motion plans to tape out its first 4-nanometer chip, a PCIe 6 version of MonTitan targeting hyperscalers, NAND flash makers, storage system providers, CSPs and other Tier 1 customers, developed with multiple partner customers. Design wins are already secured with multiple Tier 1 customers; the controller should drive MonTitan success 'beginning in the 2027, '28 time frame' and is 'expected to ramp significantly in 2028'. CFO (point-in-time plan): the 'upcoming 4-nanometer tapeout in the second quarter' will drive higher operating expenses in the second and third quarters of 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: 4-nanometer PCIe 6 tapeout in the second quarter; ramp significantly in 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Enterprise boot drive storage (a complete SSD, so Silicon Motion must procure NAND) is 'rapidly evolving into a significant new era of growth'. CEO on the DPU boot-drive business: 'We see this year revenue relatively around $50 million but I think next year will be much higher', depending on NAND procurement and on passing incremental cost through with a meaningful margin; Silicon Motion is 'not the sole supplier for the DPU program' (leading CPU and GPU makers use 2 or 3 suppliers) and has multiple programs and customers beyond one GPU customer, with some new programs ramping from Q4. The largest AI platforms now process TENS OF BILLIONS OF TOKENS PER MINUTE and BILLIONS OF PROMPTS PER DAY with token volumes growing severalfold YoY. Roughly 80% OF DATA STORED IN A HYPERSCALE DATA CENTER SITS ON HARD DISK DRIVES, and management expects that to hold. On inference specifically: storing generated context is MORE ECONOMICAL THAN RE-RUNNING IT through compute and memory. Core cloud services (notably stored video/collaboration recordings) remain an underappreciated parallel driver, and cheaper open-source Asian models are viewed as demand-positive since more model access means more data

quarterly_data.signal: Execution, not demand, is the limiter: the CEO says the constraint is how much Applied Digital can build across multiple sites 'from a supply chain perspective, from a personnel perspective, on an annualized basis' (a limit it says it has not hit yet). It secured supply chain 18 months plus ago, locking in '600, 700 megawatts of MEP per year', and is now working to expand that because it 'needs to go larger'. Lessons from the first CoreWeave building (delivered on time and on budget) led to fewer SKUs and suppliers under its fourth generation design; modular buildings with prefabricated components shorten construction timelines and are designed for different GPU and ASIC chip architectures and networking, supporting training, inference and traditional cloud workloads.

quarterly_data.signal: Power: a traditional natural gas turbine ordered today would probably not be delivered 'until 2031, 2032', so Applied Digital is working with utilities (starting in the Dakotas) and strategic partners including Babcock & Wilcox Enterprises to explore ways to add power to the grid without increasing costs to customers. The 'BW solution' uses steam turbines (coal-plant-style boilers) fired with natural gas, which the CEO says can bring generation forward '3, 4-plus years'; more information on a site and a build schedule for that equipment is expected in the first quarter. Management cites the Dakotas' low-cost abundant energy and natural cooling as a durable advantage.

The CEO says the technology can use the same amount of liquid as chip power rises from 1 kilowatt to 3 kilowatts or 5 kilowatts (up to a point, after which more liquid is needed), helping Applied Digital future-proof its data-center infrastructure for chips with 3x the power density.
quarterly_data.figure: $15 million in a $25 million funding round for Corintis

The cloud business generates over $60 million in trailing 12-month revenue with $313 million in assets; the CEO says ChronoScale's key advantage will be access to Applied Digital's large-scale data-center facilities to deploy accelerated compute (GPUs, TPUs or LPUs).

quarterly_data.signal: Christopher Ferraro: subsequent to quarter end, Galaxy completed a large load interconnect study and received approval from ERCOT for an additional 830 megawatts of power capacity at the Helios campus, which "more than doubles Helios' footprint of approved power capacity". The 830 megawatts was part of a larger request; ERCOT concluded the grid could accept an additional 830 megawatts today, and the approval came before ERCOT's new batch process is in place. The timeline to energize it depends on completion of approved transmission infrastructure, including a private substation; based on current procurement and construction schedules, Galaxy expects to begin energizing this capacity in late 2028 through early 2029 (the power "still cannot come online until late 2028. On the earliest"). With more than 1.6 gigawatts of approved power, Helios "is projected to be the largest known 100% front of the meter data center campus." Novogratz: "There is not a lot of 830 megawatt new sites of power being granted in The United States."

quarterly_data.signal: Beyond the approved capacity, Galaxy has two applications totaling approximately 1.8 gigawatts of incremental requests progressing through various stages of ERCOT's load study process. Ferraro: between the prior interconnect request for the Helios campus (purchased from Argo back in 2022) and requests accumulated through land acquisitions adjacent to Helios, Galaxy has had "north of 3.5 gigawatts in total". The incremental 1.8 gigawatts will be part of ERCOT's new batch-processing framework (groups of requests studied together, with approvals parceled out pro rata step by step), so timing of the next incremental load approvals "is still a little unknown"; getting the 830 in one large chunk before the batch process was "worth its weight" for Galaxy.

quarterly_data.signal: Tenant search for the next 830 megawatts: Ferraro said the major tenant category is hyperscalers, a term broadening to larger neoclouds, direct model builders and "perhaps even some equipment manufacturers", all looking for large chunks of power capacity; "the ambitions have not shrunk at all", with "reiterated and elevated CapEx expectations" from a lot of companies. "all potential tenants are on the table", but availability of capital and credit on economically attractive terms is "paramount", and "already having such a large exposure to CoreWeave, means a natural focus on higher credit quality tenants" (investment-grade counterparties), with CoreWeave potentially acting as agent and GPU cluster management partner. Tools such as NVIDIA MaxLPS, which smooths GPU power draw, and the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture, which runs chips at higher temperatures without giving up performance, let IREN direct more of each megawatt to IT load. Headline PUE has been deliberately conservative at 200 megawatts of IT load for 300 megawatts of gross capacity, and IREN uses a highly efficient CLOSED-LOOP liquid cooling system with minimal ongoing water usage.

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — THE FIBER-CONTENT-PER-GPU FRAMEWORK (the definitive supply-side math for optical in AI factories). Base case: enterprise grows at the rate GPUs grow; THREE drivers add on top. (1) CLUSTER SIZE: clusters ABOVE ~130,000 GPUs exceed a 512-radix switch's two-layer span and need a THIRD OPTICAL LAYER -> ~50% MORE CONTENT PER GPU for very large clusters. (2) BANDWIDTH (doubles ~every 2 years): Hopper -> Blackwell kept 100G SerDes so fibers went 8 -> 16 per GPU (content DOUBLED); the RUBIN era jumps SerDes to 200G with lane count flat -> NEUTRAL; Feynman (~2029-30): fibers double again IF SerDes stays 200G, neutral if 400G arrives (BiDi/WDM could offset) — Springboard conservatively assumes NEUTRAL. (3) SCALE-UP, today 100% COPPER: Vera Rubin Ultra NVL576 is a HYBRID step — copper inside each 72-GPU rack, DIRECT OPTICAL rack-to-rack. Bracketing a full-optical scale-up: 14.4 Tbps scale-up / 200G = 72 lanes x 2 fibers = 144, plus scale-out 1.6 Tbps / 200G = 16 fibers -> 160 FIBERS PER GPU = 10x today's 16-fiber scale-out-only content (reality lands between; % of optical ports is confidential). COMBINED: optical content per GPU +1.3-1.5x BY 2028 and 'much, much higher' toward 2030. Status: Q2 enterprise strength is 'ALL JUST SCALE-OUT — we are not yet seeing scale-up or photonics in our results'; orders accelerating; 'if we could make more, we could sell more.'
quarterly_data.figure: Content/GPU drivers: 3rd optical layer >130k GPUs (+50%); Blackwell 16 fibers; full-optical scale-up = 160 fibers/GPU (10x); +1.3-1.5x by 2028

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — PHOTONICS: A $10B MAP BY 2030, AND THE LTA MODEL: Corning's new PHOTONICS Market-Access Platform targets $10 BILLION of revenue by 2030 — passive photonics INSIDE THE BOX (FAU harnesses and everything that moves/manages light between the faceplate and the silicon-photonics optical engine) for CPO/NPO, where Corning historically had ZERO content; likely starts with scale-out, and optical SCALE-UP supercharges it; the plan is built on 'assumptions and discussions AND AGREEMENTS with customers.' Despite industry chatter on scale-up timing, 'NO CHANGES to our fundamental belief... inside the real ecosystem there is much less drama than what it looks like from outside.' Business model: long-term agreements (Amazon multi-billion, NVIDIA, Meta up-to-$6B, Apple) will be 'the LION'S SHARE of our optical business' — every major capacity expansion is underpinned by risk/reward-sharing LTAs; profitability comes from innovation value-share, not bare-fiber pricing (optical NI +77% to a record 21% margin). Springboard math: run rate $20B by end-2026 (Q3 guide may hit it a QUARTER EARLY) -> $30B (2028) -> $40B (2030), 19% CAGR; high-confidence variant $27B/$35B; biggest risk-adjustment between the two = SCALE-UP TIMING. New applications: solar-cell substrates for drones and low-earth-orbit satellites (including radiation-resistant flexible solar panels, with an LEO satellite project this year), and VCSELs used as the heating source in HAMR HDDs - in development for two years, with a meaningful contribution expected next year and the year after.
quarterly_data.figure: receiver-side 100G and 200G in mass production; 800G the mainstay this year with a 1.6T breakout expected next year; transmit-side 400G in mass production from Q2; CW lasers in production since Q4 2024

quarterly_data.signal: China substrate export licence still pending: VPEC has not yet received the export permit for substrates affected by China's export controls, but two weeks ago it was notified to file supplementary documents (routine paperwork) and completed the filing last week - management likens the situation to finally seeing the light at the end of the tunnel.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

products.product: GaN epiwafers (GaN-on-Si / GaN-on-SiC) for power and RF devices

quarterly_data.signal: FY2025 (calendar year) group revenue GBP 97.3 million. Photonics revenue rose 15% to GBP 57.1 million, "driven by continued growth in AI and data center related markets... as well as the funding releases for certain U.S. military and defense programs." Wireless revenue fell 40% to GBP 40.1 million on macro/tariff uncertainty and mobile handset softness, "with some end customer requirements met from existing inventory." Adjusted EBITDA of GBP 3.2 million was "a direct reflection of the low utilization of our manufacturing footprint." The first half was weak (tariff uncertainty, handset inventory build, delayed military and defense funding); conditions improved through H2 as wireless customer inventory depleted and U.S. defense budget was released.
quarterly_data.figure: Group revenue GBP 97.3M; Photonics GBP 57.1M (+15%); Wireless GBP 40.1M (-40%); adjusted EBITDA GBP 3.2M

quarterly_data.signal: FY2026 outlook: "Trading in Q1 2026 was in line with management expectations, reflecting strong demand across all of our core segments... we expect full-year revenue growth for 2026 exceeding 20% year-on-year. This is expected to result in high single digit to low double digit adjusted EBITDA position." Named growth drivers: indium phosphide photonic products for AI compute and data center deployments, VCSEL and wireless products for consumer smartphones, and ongoing aerospace and defense strength.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue growth >20% YoY; adjusted EBITDA "high single digit to low double digit" (unit not specified on the call)

quarterly_data.signal: InP demand for AI optics is accelerating: "In the last year, we have seen market demand from these indium phosphide solutions significantly increase due to the exponential growth in AI... The nature of the supply they're demanding is very much in the here and now. This is a live market opportunity." On the order book: "We have strong order book visibility going into the second half." Management frames InP as the crucial enabler of the ultra-fast optical and wireless data communications that data centers rely on, with IQE positioned by decades of InP epitaxy experience, and says hyperscale AI and data centers are "a massive opportunity for us across our materials portfolio, but especially in relation to indium phosphide."
quarterly_data.figure: strong order book visibility into H2 2026 (no backlog figure disclosed)

quarterly_data.signal: Indium phosphide substrate shortage, asked directly on the call: "Indium phosphide is a very sought-after commodity these days. We are working closely with our suppliers to mitigate any kind of indium phosphide shortages that we are seeing. Ultimately, the main component here will be to dual source or to increase really our sourcing capabilities and ensuring that we are just not reliant on one supplier alone." IQE is monitoring it jointly with suppliers and customers. On its own epi capacity, by contrast: "Right now, we are not seeing any capacity constraints as mentioned in our revenue outlook" - the existing asset base can support the 2026, 2027 and 2028 demand increase "without significantly increasing our fixed cost base."
quarterly_data.figure: InP substrate shortage across the market; IQE dual-sourcing to de-risk. IQE's own epi capacity unconstrained - can absorb 2026-2028 demand without material fixed-cost increase

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity conversion is the swing factor for InP epiwafer supply, and it is gated on customer commitment: "We also have the ability to flex assets and convert existing tooling to support indium phosphide growth, but this would need to be tied to concrete customer commitments." On converting GaAs lines to InP: "Our tool set is flexible to some degree. We can certainly transfer or convert capacity from our technology to the next. That kind of conversion would again need to be tied to discrete customer demand and visibility to that, because obviously it does come with downtime of the tools and also CapEx commitments." On Taiwan 6-inch InP epitaxy: "We are monitoring demand very closely, and as mentioned, we are converting capacities if and when that demand materializes." Additional MOCVD tools would come via LTA, customer co-funding, or tool consignment - "any kind of capacity expansion or addition of tools will need to come with customer commitments." Wafer-diameter transitions (4->6 inch, 6->8 inch) are customer-driven, with no company-wide push.
quarterly_data.figure: GaAs->InP tool conversion and Taiwan 6-inch InP epitaxy, both gated on concrete customer commitments (LTA / co-funding / tool consignment)

quarterly_data.signal: Balance sheet transformed after year end. FY2025 closed with cash and cash equivalents of GBP 15.7 million, adjusted net debt of GBP 31.5 million, and a working capital inflow of GBP 11.2 million. The GBP 81 million fundraise - GBP 45 million from MACOM (GBP 30 million cash plus GBP 15 million of convertible loan notes), with the remainder from existing shareholders - closed the morning of this results call. Proceeds fully repay the HSBC revolving credit facility and redeem existing loan notes, "leaving us without bank debt," with net cash inflow to IQE of around GBP 27.9 million. Management does "not foresee any additional fundraisers in the future" absent a large customer-backed capacity expansion. The 18-month strategic review - which assessed options from a sale of Taiwan up to a full sale of the company - concluded that staying independent creates the best shareholder value.
quarterly_data.figure: GBP 81M raised (GBP 45M from MACOM); net cash inflow ~GBP 27.9M; FY25 cash GBP 15.7M; FY25 adjusted net debt GBP 31.5M

quarterly_data.signal: Capex discipline: FY2025 capex fell from GBP 11 million to GBP 6 million. "2026 and beyond CapEx spend is limited right now to just purely maintaining our asset base. This is maintenance CapEx... any kind of capacity increase or significantly other CapEx requirements will have to come with customer engagements, customer commitments, and potentially even customer funding." IQE is a heavily fixed-cost business, so incremental volume falls through hard to EBITDA; a mix weighted toward InP and GaN carries better margin than commodity VCSEL/wireless.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2025 capex GBP 6M (prior year GBP 11M); FY2026 maintenance-only

quarterly_data.signal: Footprint and positioning: IQE describes itself as "the world's only pure-play epitaxy foundry" and "the only pure-play epitaxy provider with manufacturing facilities on three continents," retaining U.K., U.S. and Taiwan sites after the strategic review - each with its own technology focus and headroom to scale without significant further investment. The materials portfolio spans indium phosphide, gallium nitride, gallium arsenide and gallium antimonide. Site optimization completed the exit from the silicon site in South Wales in H2 2025. IQE positions itself upstream of the packaging ecosystem, "particularly in advanced photonics, heterogeneous integration, and AI optical interconnects," and remains engaged with governments - including on U.S. CHIPS funding - across all three geographies.
quarterly_data.figure: 3 manufacturing geographies (UK, US, Taiwan); South Wales silicon site exited H2 2025

quarterly_data.signal: GaN is one of IQE's four core markets and is being pulled by the datacenter build-out: "In power, we see rising demand for our GaN solutions driven by data centers, aerospace and defense, and space applications." Management expects the 2026+ trend to create opportunities "across indium phosphide and GaN in particular," and notes a mix weighted to InP/GaN carries better margin than commodity VCSEL/wireless. IQE is the world's only pure-play epitaxy foundry, growing the epitaxial compound-semiconductor layers on purchased base substrates (InP, GaN, GaAs, GaSb) at sites in the U.K., U.S. and Taiwan; existing MOCVD capacity can absorb the 2026-2028 demand increase without a material fixed-cost increase, and any tool additions for GaN or InP "will need to come with customer commitments" via LTA, customer co-funding, or tool consignment.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure (GaN not separately disclosed; FY2025 group revenue GBP 97.3M)

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 revenue $1.634B (+3.1% YoY, -11% QoQ), in the high end of guidance, with non-IFRS gross margin and operating margin well above the high end of the ranges: gross profit $474M (~29% gross margin, +510bps YoY - the largest YoY gross-margin expansion in over 3 years), operating profit $271M (16.6% operating margin, +320bps YoY), net income ~$227M (+~$38M YoY), diluted EPS $0.40; cash flow from operations $542M, capex net of grants $309M (~19% of revenue), adjusted free cash flow $233M. Communications infrastructure & data center (~14% of revenue) +32% YoY - sixth consecutive double-digit quarter; automotive (~23%) +24% YoY. Design wins +50% YoY (building on record 2025).
quarterly_data.figure: $1.634B rev (+3.1% YoY); non-IFRS GM ~29% (+510bps), op margin 16.6%, EPS $0.40; design wins +50%

quarterly_data.signal: Industry leadership in optical networking via silicon photonics + silicon-germanium (SiGe). Launched SCALE (Silicon Photonics Co-packaged Advanced Light Engine) — the industry's first OCI-MSA-capable NPO/CPO optical-module platform, with specs exceeding the MSA (OCI MSA founders include AMD, Broadcom, NVIDIA, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI); executed tape-outs for two CPO design wins on the OCI scale-up standard. SiGe (TIAs/drivers for electrical<->optical conversion) demand strong — Vermont fab oversubscribed into 2027, margin-accretive, expanding capacity. On track to roughly DOUBLE silicon-photonics revenue in 2026 and reach a >$1B silicon-photonics run-rate exiting 2028; now designed in at 3 of the top 4 pluggable optical-transceiver companies (1.6T solutions, roadmap to 3.2T+). Partnerships at OFC: Senko (detachable fiber), Corning + EXFO (CPO ecosystem), Siltech (200G/lane receiver PICs for pluggables).
quarterly_data.figure: SCALE = first OCI-MSA CPO platform; SiPho rev ~2x in 2026, >$1B run-rate by 2028-exit

quarterly_data.signal: The OCI (Optical Compute Interconnect) MSA — the CPO industry standard for scale-up networks established at OFC in March — was founded by AMD, Broadcom, NVIDIA, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, and aligns directly with GF capabilities (DWDM heritage). One month later GF announced SCALE (Silicon Photonics Co-packaged Advanced Light Engine), the industry's FIRST OCI-MSA-capable complete optical module platform for NPO/CPO, with specs exceeding MSA requirements (natively broadband fiber coupling minimizing insertion loss). Q1 saw tape-outs at Malta, NY for a PAIR of CPO design wins supporting the OCI standard.
quarterly_data.figure: OCI MSA founders: AMD/Broadcom/NVIDIA/Meta/Microsoft/OpenAI; SCALE = first OCI-capable platform

quarterly_data.signal: Designed in at 3 OF THE TOP 4 pluggable optical transceiver companies (enabling 1.6T today, roadmap to 3.2T+); strategic partnership with SilTech to mass-produce 200G/lane receiver photonic ICs for pluggables; CPO ecosystem demos with Senko (wafer-level detachable fiber interface) and Corning+EXFO (attachable fiber + automated die-level test). SiGe TIAs/drivers are 'required on virtually every data center connection' with Vermont fab oversubscribed well into 2027. Company-wide design wins +50% YoY. Onshoring: founding partner in Apple's American manufacturing program — first US availability of silicon for upcoming Apple devices (next-gen Face ID components) at the Malta NY fab.
quarterly_data.figure: 3 of top-4 pluggable cos; design wins +50%; Apple US-manufacturing founding partner

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 revenue was $1.786 billion, up 9% sequentially and 6% year over year, with revenue and non-IFRS profitability at or above the high end of guidance. GF shipped approximately 625,000 300-millimeter equivalent wafers, up 8% sequentially and 8% year over year. Gross profit was $534 million for a 29.9% gross margin, above the high end of guidance and up 470 basis points year over year - a second-quarter record that reached the ~30% target well before the end of 2026. Operating profit was $298 million (16.7% margin, +140bps), net income $256 million and diluted EPS $0.46 on ~556 million shares. Manufacturing services were ~89% of revenue and technology services ~11%.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 revenue $1.786B (+9% QoQ, +6% YoY); gross margin 29.9% (+470bps YoY); operating margin 16.7%; EPS $0.46; ~625k 300mm-equivalent wafers

quarterly_data.signal: Q3 2026 guidance: revenue of $1.885 billion plus or minus $25 million; gross margin approximately 30.5% plus or minus 100 basis points (about 450 basis points of year-over-year expansion at the midpoint); operating expenses excluding share-based compensation of $260 million plus or minus $10 million; operating margin 16.7% plus or minus 170 basis points; diluted EPS $0.51 plus or minus $0.05. Full-year 2026 gross margin is now expected at about 30 points for the whole year rather than only as an exit rate, and management reaffirmed the path to a 40% exit run rate in the 2028 timeframe. Full-year adjusted free cash flow margin is still expected at approximately 10%, with capex at the higher end of the 15-20% of revenue range.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 guide $1.885B ±$25M; GM ~30.5% ±100bps; EPS $0.51 ±$0.05; FY2026 GM ~30%; 40% GM exit run rate targeted in 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Communications infrastructure and data center was approximately 16% of Q2 revenue and grew 20% sequentially and 62% year over year - the seventh consecutive quarter of double-digit year-over-year growth and the fastest quarterly year-on-year growth since 2022. Full-year 2026 growth for the end market was RAISED to 50-60% from a prior expectation of high-30s percent. The implied exit rate is roughly $350 million per quarter, and management reaffirmed the long-term model of 30-plus percent year-over-year growth for this end market into 2027 and beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: CID ~16% of Q2 revenue, +20% QoQ, +62% YoY; FY2026 growth raised to 50-60% (from high-30s); ~$350M/quarter exit rate

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon photonics revenue reported within comms infrastructure and data center is now expected to MORE THAN DOUBLE in 2026 versus the prior year. GF secured 7 new optical networking design wins in Q2 across both pluggable transceiver suppliers and major hyperscaler and networking players, and is actively engaged with 4 OF THE TOP 5 optical transceiver players. Pluggables contribute the vast majority of silicon photonics revenue today. High-volume manufacturing of 200-gig-per-lane technology is underway, 400-gig capability has already been demonstrated, and the multiyear roadmap advances module enablement to 1.6T, 3.2T and beyond. GF has more than 40 silicon photonics customers, and CEO Tim Breen said GF is on track and potentially ahead of the growth targets set for end-2028 through 2030. He also cited an expectation that 70% of data center links will be optical by 2030, calling that 'perhaps even conservative' given scale-up as well as scale-out penetration.
quarterly_data.figure: Silicon photonics revenue to more than double in 2026; 7 new design wins in Q2; engaged with 4 of top 5 transceiver players; >40 SiPho customers; 200G/lane in HVM, 400G/lane demonstrated

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE, described as the industry's first OCI MSA compatible solution for near and co-packaged optics, has 7 ACTIVE ENGAGEMENTS with leading companies. GF taped out a SCALE-related design win in Q2 and expects to tape out another in Q3. Management reiterated a consistent timeline: the NPO ramp BEGINS IN 2027 and the CPO ramp BEGINS IN 2028. Because near and co-packaged optics are built on a common photonic IC - an EIC bonded to a PIC with a micro-optic and a fiber-attached unit - and differ mainly in that NPO is bonded to the board while CPO sits within the package (plus SerDes architecture differences), GF expects to benefit regardless of which form factor customers adopt. Many customers are pursuing both, with NPO ramping sooner. Breen attributed the sudden industry interest in NPO to SerDes synergies that make the system transition smaller than a jump straight to full CPO, and expects pluggables, NPO and CPO all to coexist in the data center.
quarterly_data.figure: 7 active SCALE engagements; 1 SCALE tape-out in Q2 and another expected in Q3; NPO ramp begins 2027, CPO ramp begins 2028

quarterly_data.signal: GF entered a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for a $300 MILLION award to accelerate next-generation silicon photonics technologies in the U.S. The funding supports three components: continued PIC-level innovation and improved modulator technology to reach 400-gig per lane and beyond; NEW MATERIALS to be introduced into the system - management named barium titanate, thin-film lithium niobate and indium phosphide; and packaging capability and capacity for the integrated optical engines needed for near and co-packaged optics, building directly on the SCALE platform. Management said the endorsement came from the world's top XPU providers, hyperscalers, AI connectivity leaders and ecosystem partners.
quarterly_data.figure: $300M U.S. Department of Commerce letter of intent for next-generation silicon photonics

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon germanium is OVERSUBSCRIBED THROUGHOUT 2027 and, notably, GF's SiGe business is LARGER THAN ITS SILICON PHOTONICS BUSINESS TODAY. GF secured multiple new SiGe TIA and driver design wins across networking customers in the quarter. The growth has two compounding drivers: the shift to optical networking itself, and the fact that what could previously be done in CMOS at 50-gig and 100-gig per lane cannot be done at 200-gig and definitely not at 400-gig per lane, forcing transimpedance amplifiers and increasingly the drivers out into high-performance analog processes like SiGe. High-performance analog also appears in near and co-packaged optics depending on architecture. GF is expanding SiGe capacity at Burlington, Vermont and qualifying 300-millimeter SiGe in Singapore for additional capacity, better economics and higher fT/fMAX performance. The SiGe lineage traces to IBM Microelectronics, which invented SiGe and is part of GF today.
quarterly_data.figure: SiGe oversubscribed throughout 2027; SiGe business larger than silicon photonics today; Vermont capacity expanding, 300mm SiGe qualifying in Singapore

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity strategy is a structural advantage: GF is adding capacity WITHIN ITS EXISTING FAB FOOTPRINT rather than building new fabs, which management contrasted with competitors on longer lead times. Breen said GF 'could 10x our photonics capacity within our current 4 walls' globally on its long-term plan. Q2 utilization was in the high 80s, leaving about 10 points of headroom to grow into with installed capacity. Confidence in bringing capacity online plus factory productivity improvements was cited as a direct contributor to raising the full-year CID outlook. On competition in silicon photonics, Breen said customers are coming to GF saying they do not have enough capacity secured and want more, partly to mitigate geopolitical risk, and he sees no customer-concentration concern given 40-plus customers.
quarterly_data.figure: Photonics capacity expandable ~10x within existing fabs; Q2 utilization high-80s with ~10 points of headroom

quarterly_data.signal: GF implemented PRICING INCREASES in partnership with customers across several technology corridors during Q2, following what management called constructive conversations. The adjustments will be reflected in revenue COMMENCING IN 2027, with magnitude varying by end market and technology based on differentiated value, supply/demand dynamics and inflationary absorption. GF will continue assessing 2027 pricing through the second half of 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: Price increases agreed across several technology corridors, revenue impact commencing 2027

quarterly_data.signal: GF launched Quantum Technology Solutions in May 2026, a dedicated team aimed at taking the quantum industry from prototypes to high-volume production. The strategy is qubit-agnostic across superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, topological and spin modalities, using the FDX platform as a cryogenic CMOS foundation and extending advanced packaging into the cryogenic regime for 3D heterogeneous integration. GF is working with 8 of the world's leading quantum computing players including PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Quantum Motion plus endorsements from the quantum arms of large hyperscalers, and has already begun 4 new customer-specific engagements in the three months since launch. The effort is anchored by an expected $375 MILLION grant from the U.S. Department of Commerce. Over the next 1 to 3 years quantum revenue comes largely through engineering engagements booked in technology services, with manufacturing-services revenue ramping toward the end of the decade. Several quantum players are working on the photonics side of their solutions, which maps directly onto GF's silicon photonics roadmap.
quarterly_data.figure: $375M expected U.S. Department of Commerce quantum grant; 8 leading quantum players engaged; 4 new customer engagements in 3 months

quarterly_data.signal: IP, software and custom silicon: GF completed the acquisition of the Synopsys ARC processor IP Solutions business in June, adding CPU, DSP, NPU and RISC-V technologies, a software development toolkit and application-specific processor design capability - over 150 patents, 300 existing customers and 400 R&D engineers. Combined with MIPS, this lets GF engage customers earlier in the design cycle for edge AI and on-device inference in automotive, industrial and robotics. Full-year 2026 technology services contribution from MIPS plus ARC was RAISED to $100-120 million from a prior $60-100 million, skewed roughly one third Q3 and two thirds Q4, and technology services revenue is now expected toward the high end of the 10-12% of total revenue range with gross margin significantly above corporate targets. Design wins in the quarter included 3 strategic chiplet wins with Lockheed Martin on FinFET and FDX, an expanded FinFET win with Microchip, a first-ever PMIC design win with MediaTek on the BCD platform, an ADAS radar tape-out for Bosch on FDX, and a new microLED display backplane win for augmented reality wearables at a leading hyperscaler.
quarterly_data.figure: Technology services contribution raised to $100M-$120M for 2026 (from $60M-$100M); ARC adds 150 patents, 300 customers, 400 R&D engineers

quarterly_data.signal: End-market split and the memory-shortage read-across: smart mobile devices were ~36% of Q2 revenue, up 15% sequentially but down 6% year over year, and are now expected to DECLINE BY A LOW-TEENS PERCENTAGE in 2026 because 2026 handset forecasts have been cut meaningfully on continued memory pricing and associated shortages. Automotive was ~19% of revenue, down 13% sequentially and 10% year over year on customer-led shipment timing, but full-year low-double-digit growth is still expected weighted to Q4. Home and industrial IoT was ~19% of revenue, up 30% sequentially and 10% year over year - its fastest year-over-year growth since 2022 - and the full-year outlook was raised to 10-15% growth from mid-single digits, partly because mobile customers reallocated demand into IoT connectivity applications. GF credited a deliberately flexible manufacturing footprint for reusing capacity to capture data-center upside as mobile weakened.
quarterly_data.figure: Smart mobile ~36% of revenue, FY2026 down low teens on memory shortage; automotive ~19%; IoT ~19%, FY2026 raised to 10-15% growth

quarterly_data.signal: Cash and capital returns: Q2 cash flow from operations was $405 million and capex net of government grant proceeds was $408 million (roughly 23% of revenue), leaving adjusted free cash flow at negative $3 million as previously guided. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities were approximately $3.3 billion against $1.1 billion of total debt, with a $1 billion revolving credit facility undrawn. GF paid its first-ever quarterly cash dividend of $0.12 per share on July 14 and declared another $0.12 per share payable October 9, 2026. Approximately $100 million remains under the share repurchase authorization; the stated objective is to return up to 50% of trailing-twelve-month non-IFRS adjusted free cash flow after investments over time.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 OCF $405M; capex $408M (~23% of revenue); adjusted FCF -$3M; $3.3B cash and securities; first-ever dividend $0.12/share

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Tim Breen on the silicon photonics growth targets: 'the industry adoption needed to reach those targets has already happened. So I think we now have very limited adoption risk baked into that.' The constraint is now supply, not demand - 'All indicators right now from a demand point of view are flashing kind of bright green relative to those targets... we see much more demand than we can supply out of our current install base, so we will definitely be accelerating that.' Pluggables alone get GF 'pretty much all the way' to the first milestone, with NPO rollout already picking up steam on top. The upside case is co-packaged optics: if CPO sees really broad adoption in the latter part of the period GF 'could blow past those targets materially', because CPO is the technology for the scale-up transition and 'you are replacing 10x the links of scale-out with those solutions, so you are not going to see a linear growth story'.
quarterly_data.figure: co-packaged optics replaces 10x the links of scale-out

quarterly_data.signal: First photonics customer count disclosed: 'We have more than 40 customers in photonics today, and that number keeps growing as players really invest in their optical roadmap.' Breen added that 'everyone who was touting copper two years ago has either launched an organic or inorganic effort to get into optical'. On the form-factor transition, near-package optics and co-packaged optic designs are 'even taping out in our fabs today' and are 'going into production in 2027 and 2028', while pluggable optical transceivers ramp strongly now; the NPO rollout is being led by 'many of the same players who are in pluggables today'. The core photonics platform roadmap runs from 100 gig per lane to 200 gig per lane to 400 gig per lane and beyond with new materials and modulators, paired with advanced packaging (hybrid bonding, fiber-to-chip attach) as the optical link moves closer to the XPU and switch ASIC.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 40 customers in photonics; NPO and CPO designs taping out today and going into production in 2027 and 2028; 100 gig per lane to 200 to 400 gig per lane roadmap

quarterly_data.signal: Breen put GF squarely in a supply-constrained posture for the next couple of years: 'We are clearly in a chasing supply moment today'; 'for the next couple of years, we will be more in a supply-constrained than a demand-constrained environment'. Job number one is ramping technologies GF already produces to higher volumes, and capex is going up again - 'We already are increasing our CapEx this year from last year. We'll be increasing further again next year' - with tool install and qualification speed, not demand, the thing that 'will gate or accelerate our growth going into next year'. Two new-cycle features: customers are co-investing financially alongside GF in the ramps ('customer skin in the game... they are willing to put capital to work'), and government partnerships provide tools that let GF 'accelerate CapEx at significant recovery rates that were not there in the past'.
quarterly_data.figure: capex increasing this year versus last year and increasing further again next year; supply-constrained, not demand-constrained, for the next couple of years

quarterly_data.signal: Progress against the long-term model GF 'laid out early this year': GF set targets for communication infrastructure and data center of '30% or in the 30s' and, per Breen, 'We are doing 60 in Q2' - well ahead of plan in that segment. Automotive is tracking in line with the long-term plan and IoT slightly ahead year to date. Breen said he does 'not see a demand constraint to meeting and exceeding that plan' and that the diversification across platforms 'may even make those numbers look a bit conservative'.
quarterly_data.figure: communication infrastructure and data center target of 30% or in the 30s versus doing 60 in Q2

quarterly_data.signal: Mobile mix and a new read-across on foundry tightness: GF was 'more than 50% mobile going back a couple of years', is 'down to the mid-30s today' and the long-term model takes it to 'the mid-20s', with absolute mobile revenue assumed relatively flat rather than growing. 2026 is a tough year in mobile but 'not as tough at the higher end', where GF has more of its exposure. The new behaviour is that handset customers are now booking forward supply: 'mobile companies were the first to the queue in COVID... Now they are worried about being late when the data center is the one pushing all the demand. You are seeing actually more visibility where they are actually still saying, I need my supply for 2027. I need my supply for 2028.'
quarterly_data.figure: mobile more than 50% of revenue a couple of years ago, mid-30s today, mid-20s in the long-term model; handset customers booking supply for 2027 and 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Quantum status update since the Q2 call: 'today we announced that we completed the deal that we announced earlier in the year with the government', a partnership that accelerates GF's investment in infrastructure, tooling and PDK enablement for the more exotic processes - compressing a plan Breen framed as 'What would it take to do those in 2 years instead of over 5, 6 years?'. He stressed the roadmap is not orthogonal to the rest of GF: the exotic materials being proven for quantum - thin-film lithium niobate and barium titanate - 'will be needed for the next generation of photonics', i.e. the next generation of photonic modulators. The platform rests on cryo-CMOS (conventional FDSOI CMOS characterised at 4 degrees Kelvin) for qubit readout, plus novel-material integration, advanced packaging and high-speed photonic interconnect.
quarterly_data.figure: government partnership compressing a 5, 6 year plan into 2 years; cryo-CMOS characterised at 4 degrees Kelvin

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 headline results, with revenue, gross margin and EPS at or above the high end of guidance: revenue $1.83 billion, up 8% sequentially and flat year-over-year; gross profit $530 million (approximately 29% gross margin, up 300 basis points sequentially and 360 basis points year-over-year); operating profit $335 million at an 18.3% operating margin; net income approximately $310 million; diluted EPS $0.55. Non-wafer revenue (reticles, NRE, expedite fees) was approximately 12% of Q4 revenue. Full-year 2025: revenue approximately $6.791 billion (up 1%), approximately 2.3 million 300-millimeter equivalent wafers shipped (up 10%) at utilization of approximately 85%, gross margin 26.1%, operating margin 15.7%, diluted EPS $1.72 (up 10%), adjusted free cash flow $1.2 billion (a record). 2025 was the first full year in which more than 60% of revenue came from markets other than smart mobile devices. The Board authorized a share repurchase of up to $500 million.

quarterly_data.signal: GF delivered on its objective to roughly double silicon photonics revenue within the CID end market, to over $200 million in 2025. Even on this higher base it expects to NEARLY DOUBLE the silicon photonics contribution again in 2026, driven by strong customer demand, a robust ramp in supply capacity and the integration of Advanced Micro Foundry (AMF, Singapore), whose acquisition closed in November last year and is expected to be accretive to corporate gross margin targets in 2026. As pluggable applications ramp and co-packaged optics begins to scale, management now believes GF is on a path to a $1 billion run rate revenue level for silicon photonics by the end of 2028 - 'a substantial acceleration from our prior objective.' The majority of photonics revenue today is in the pluggable space, and silicon photonics comes through at a highly accretive gross margin.

Breen said the CPO transition was always 'a '27 scale ramp more than a '26 scale ramp', and design wins and tape-out planning indicate it is on track because 'CPO is the only way to address certain performance workloads, especially on scale up networks'; the form-factor changes will drive significant increases of content. Technology roadmap: an offering for 200 gig per lane technologies today and a road map to 400 gig per lane and beyond; the InfiniLink design team in Cairo, Egypt helps customers building co-packaged optics solutions onboard faster; the collaboration with Corning brings detachable fiber attach, which management called critical for the transition to co-packaged optics; silicon photonics is being scaled in Singapore and the U.S., including on a 300-millimeter platform.

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and capex: FY2026 non-IFRS net capex is expected at 15% to 20% of full year revenue (versus 2025 net capex of approximately $574 million, or 8% of revenue), driven primarily by strong customer demand in capacity corridors where GF is OVERSUBSCRIBED - silicon photonics, FDX and SiGe - plus establishing new capabilities such as advanced packaging. Breen: 'those corridors are running hot'; GF is meeting customer demand today, but the ramp profiles of designs already won and now taping out require investment, done within the existing 4-wall footprint (New York, Burlington and a legacy facility being converted in Germany) with quick ramps, good capital efficiency and eligibility for government support. High-performance SiGe (TIAs and driver ICs) is pulled through by pluggable optical transceivers, and that capacity is being 'very, very well utilized' today. 2025 gross capex was up about 15% but net capex down about 7% as government support in the U.S., Germany and Singapore began to flow, expected to grow again in 2026. 2026 free cash flow margin is guided to approximately 10% of revenue as GF receives customer prepayments. Footprint: a $16 billion U.S. investment commitment (June 2025) to expand manufacturing and advanced packaging in New York and Vermont, and a EUR 1.1 billion Dresden expansion to over 1 million wafers per year by the end of 2028.

quarterly_data.signal: Data center power is GF's third named growth pillar alongside silicon photonics and SiGe. In July GF closed a strategic acquihire of the custom power team from Photon Technologies in Europe, bringing an experienced design team focused on INTEGRATED VOLTAGE REGULATORS (IVRs). Combined with GF's BCD, GaN and integrated-inductor capabilities, the goal is a new power architecture that brings power conversion closer to the processor to meet the efficiency, power density, bandwidth, high-current and transient-response requirements of next-generation XPUs. CEO Tim Breen framed it directly: 'IVR is to power what CPO is to photonics' - moving from traditional industrial/automotive-style power modules to a much more wafer-level integrated solution delivering power closer to the chip. The Photon team is already engaged with a number of existing GF customers, and early feedback from fabless companies, IDMs and hyperscalers has been very positive.

The newest shift is from lateral to vertical power delivery, behind which GF has put process technology, integrated passives and the recent acqui-hire of a small voltage-regulator design team so it can co-design with power semiconductor players and hyperscalers alike.

Scale-up requires roughly 10x more density than scale-out pluggables — the industry conversation spans XPO, CPX, NPO and ultimately CPO — and Credo is approaching it agnostically: leading with the silicon photonics PIC in all NPO solutions including CPX, pursuing component sales where customers prefer them and complete optical engines / system-level solutions long term, bringing pluggable-ecosystem advantages (telemetry, interoperability, serviceability) to the consortium.

(2) OmniConnect — a licensed low-power short-reach SerDes (reach up to 10in) plus Weaver gearboxes (LPDDR5 first, then LPDDR6, no XPU re-tape-out needed for the memory transition) attacking the memory fan-out limits of inference; potentially THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS of Credo content per GPU; first customer Positron's first announced product scales memory capacity up to 2TB (fitting frontier models fully in memory), and the roadmap targets bandwidth comparable to HBM5.
