quarterly_data.signal: MACOM raised its fiscal 2026 Data Center year-over-year revenue growth base case from 20% to 35 to 40%, with upside that is 'a bit unquantifiable right now'. CEO Stephen Daly said 'the key underlying driver is 1.6T', where MACOM sees the most design wins transitioning into production runs; the Data Center backlog is very healthy and the second half should be stronger than the first half in absolute revenue dollars. Growth is primarily in pluggable optical modules and optical cables using its 800G and 1.6T PAM4 products (supporting DSP, LPO and LRO module architectures, plus coherent DCI including ZR and ZR Lite), and hyperscaler capital investments are robust. A significant portion of Data Center revenue is 400 gig and above with 1.6T the fastest-growing portion; 'The real action is at 200 gig per lane PAM4' and next-generation coherent, while 25 gig per lane NRZ is holding up, 50 gig per lane PAM4 is flat and 100 gig per lane PAM4 is solid. MACOM supports all of the US hyperscalers as well as international hyperscalers, selling to builders of modules, AOCs and cables. Management does not frame the growth as share gain: 'I think the market's growing. We're winning designs.' The product roadmap extends to 3.2T.
quarterly_data.figure: Data Center FY2026 growth base case raised from 20% to 35 to 40%

quarterly_data.signal: LPO, LRO and copper: MACOM now has three hyperscalers embracing LPO and is 'in various phases of production' with them - in all cases 100 gig per lane for generally 800 gig modules; management expects LPO to remain a small part of the market for the next one to two years and to evolve into NPO/CPO/XPO. Customers are also investigating LRO at 1.6T using 200 gig per lane chips, and management sees LRO as more likely to happen first than 1.6T LPO. LPO interest is also appearing in PCIe, NPO and telecom front haul. On copper, there is renewed interest in MACOM's linear equalizers to extend active copper cable (ACC) reach at 800G and 1.6T and for backplanes (eliminating retimers, and important at 400 gig per lane), but Q1 contained no ACC revenue; management sees the ACC opportunity as bigger than backplane equalizers, and some customers are evaluating converting AECs to ACCs. MACOM launched a PCIe 6 optical chipset supporting sideband data streams over fiber and a new PCIe 7 equalizer, giving it new exposure to the compute side of the data center network.
quarterly_data.figure: three hyperscalers in LPO production phases (100 gig per lane, 800 gig modules); no ACC revenue in Q1

quarterly_data.signal: Photonics and CPO/NPO: demand for MACOM's 200 gig per lane photodetectors (for 800G and 1.6T) continues to grow, with indications that demand will remain strong into calendar 2027; the indium phosphide photodetector business is growing rapidly, higher-speed photodetectors are in development, and EML lasers are in test. CW lasers: two customers - module makers, the first line of entry before a hyperscaler PCN process adds MACOM to the approved vendor list - have confirmed MACOM's 75-milliwatt CW lasers meet their requirements electrically for their silicon photonics solutions, followed by a qualification phase lasting 'some number of months' and a fab production-readiness review. CEO Stephen Daly called it 'a watershed moment because six months ago, we were not in a position where we had a compliant laser'; MACOM does not make 400-milliwatt class lasers and does not sell lasers into 1.6 applications today, so this would be share gain. The product set sold into CPO or NPO platforms is very similar to pluggables (drivers, TIAs, photodetectors and possibly lasers); these platforms are moving quickly to silicon photonics, putting heavy demand on CW laser and photodetector chips, with far more channels per chip, and some systems are moving to coherent light. MACOM's future products are increasingly optimized for CPO and NPO.
quarterly_data.figure: 75-milliwatt CW lasers: two customers confirmed requirements met electrically; 200 gig per lane photodetector demand strong into calendar 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and supply: MACOM is adding indium phosphide photodetector manufacturing capacity to keep up with customers' forecasted demand (amount not disclosed for competitive reasons). The North Carolina (RTP) fab has 'a very aggressive plan to increase output by 30%', with some equipment bought and cycle-time reduction as the site's number one priority. Gross margin gains this year and next come mainly from higher utilization of the Massachusetts fab and to some degree the French fab, whose three-inch to six-inch wafer transition is targeted to be fully qualified and released to production by June 2026; one high-mix fab runs GaAs, GaN, silicon and indium phosphide. Benefits from insourcing IPDs and capacitors now bought from a third-party vendor will most likely come in 2027 and beyond. On supply, 'we are absolutely in ramp mode in various programs', and availability of indium phosphide and other exotic materials is a key focus; pricing is rational, and 'we're in an environment where there is scarcity in some areas'. Fiscal 2026 capex is still estimated at $50 million to $55 million (Q1 capex $12.9 million).
quarterly_data.figure: RTP fab plan to increase output by 30%; FY2026 capex $50 million to $55 million; Q1 capex $12.9 million

quarterly_data.signal: Telecom: MACOM's previously announced $55 million satellite contract (with the potential of an additional $25 million add-on) is planned to start production in 2026, delayed mainly by satellite system changes flowed down from the customer, which management views as positive because added functionality should bring new customers to the constellation. MACOM says it is engaged at some level with all of the major LEO constellations (microwave, optics, satellite-to-satellite, direct-to-device and ground stations), has multiple SATCOM LEO programs in design, and expects SATCOM to grow nicely into 2027. In 5G, one competitor is exiting the RF power GaN market; MACOM hired a team of experienced engineers and is sampling next-generation GaN4 products, but expects share gains to take one or two years with a flat RAN market in 2026. Cable TV is expected to be a modest contributor to fiscal 2026 telecom growth.

quarterly_data.signal: Industrial and Defense revenue was a record $133.4 million, up 11% sequentially. The Defense business grew 19% last year and is expected to grow approximately 25% this year across radar, missile and missile defense, drone and drone-defense, communications and wideband electronic warfare systems. At the International Microwave Symposium in June MACOM showcased an X-band front-end module built from its GaN ICs in a highly integrated multichip module, delivering 16 WATTS of transmit power and OVER 40% power added efficiency in a footprint suited to compact high-volume radar. MACOM also received INCREMENTAL FUNDING FROM THE AIR FORCE RESEARCH LABS to support MILLIMETER WAVE GaN-ON-SILICON CARBIDE production maturation. Industrial submarkets - test and measurement, medical, automotive and general multi-market - are also improving, with test and measurement demand driven partly by AI-related engineering and production facilitation, and the small automotive business expected to double its revenue this year.

quarterly_data.signal: Compound semiconductor manufacturing build-out. In Q3 MACOM began installing a new G10 EPITAXIAL REACTOR at the MACOM European Semiconductor Center (MESC) in France to support future growth and technology development for European commercial and defense markets. MESC completed conversion of one production line FROM 3-INCH TO 6-INCH this year with two more process sets to convert in the next four to six months - a conversion that improves quality, reduces cost and DOUBLES CAPACITY, and which many defense contractors have been waiting for. MACOM expects to receive one of the largest orders in MESC's history from a U.K. defense company working on airborne defense systems within a month or two, and expects European defense revenue to start growing materially around 2028. The France site was acquired as a 'fixer-upper' for about EUR 38 million against roughly EUR 25 million of land value and approximately $100 million of capital equipment.

LPO has generated meaningful revenue since Q1 FY2027 and is growing moderately, but its bigger effect is PROVING THE LINEAR ARCHITECTURE, which now carries into MPO, XPO and 'some form of CPO'. Stated R&D priority: lasers, photodiodes, drivers and TIAs for 3.2T coherent light, XPO, MPO and CPO applications. Analyst day 10-15-2026 (San Jose) will publish TAM, share and the multi-year model.

quarterly_data.signal: LASER ACQUISITION: Semtech acquired HIFU Corporation (name as printed in this transcript), a California-based maker of indium phosphide optoelectronic devices (gain chips and CW laser chips for optical transceivers), with a comprehensive investment plan for the Alhambra, California facility. Combining its InP lasers with Semtech's TIAs and laser drivers raises Semtech's content opportunity 'from high single-digit dollars in an 800G module to about $80 in a 3.2T module'. The fab is vertically integrated (epi growth, multi-step regrowth, wafer processing, internal test; backend packaging via the ecosystem). The gain chip for tunable lasers is in volume production, capacity limited, and should contribute 'roughly about a high-teen level of revenue' in fiscal 2027. The CW laser for transceivers has 42% wall-plug efficiency at room temperature vs a typical about 25%; there is not enough capacity for industry demand, multiple customers asked for samples, and Semtech plans to intercept at 3.2T transceivers (1.6T also supported). Go-to-market: co-optimized chipsets (TIA, laser driver, modulator driver + lasers) with a reference design; 'the major inflection point is 3.2T transceiver modules. It could be earlier than that.' Deal expected to be accretive to non-GAAP EPS within the first year.
quarterly_data.figure: content from high single-digit dollars (800G) to about $80 in a 3.2T module; CW laser wall-plug efficiency 42% vs about 25% typical

quarterly_data.signal: CAPACITY: FY2027 priority is supporting customer ramps 'as we compete in a capacity-constrained environment'. For the Alhambra InP fab, CapEx intensity is moderate — it can be supported with about one quarter of free cash flow — but the whole industry is ramping and epi/fab equipment is in high demand, so Semtech will combine new and used equipment; the ramp runs over multiple quarters. CFO: the CapEx should qualify for the Section 48 investment tax credit of 35%, plus other government grant programs. Revenue guidance for CW lasers will come once equipment lead times and capacity are clearer.
quarterly_data.figure: Section 48 investment tax credit of 35%; CapEx about one quarter of free cash flow

quarterly_data.signal: COPPEREDGE / ACC: Semtech expects to start shipping CopperEdge for the 1.6T ACC hyperscaler deployment this quarter — toward the end of the fiscal quarter, in the April time frame, to the cable manufacturers (its direct customers) — to support a rack-level volume ramp in the middle of the year, with demand accelerating through the year; DAC vs ACC mix still being set in rack-level validation. Semtech co-authored the ACC MSA (12 founding members spanning IC, XPU and cable suppliers with major hyperscalers) and says other hyperscalers are 'lining up to get their racks designed by using ACC'. Copper linear equalizers onboard have multiple customer engagements, with customers defining five or six use cases (switch, merchant GPU board, hyperscaler ASIC board, active backplane); qualification expected within the coming quarters. OFC demos: 1.6T ACCs running live traffic to NVIDIA's 224G SerDes and next-generation 448G per-channel CopperEdge chips.
quarterly_data.figure: ACC MSA with 12 founding members; 1.6T ACC shipments start in the April time frame; next-gen 448G per-channel CopperEdge

quarterly_data.signal: LPO / 1.6T FIBEREDGE / NPO: design wins with several leading U.S. hyperscalers validated Semtech TIA and driver solutions in 800G LPO transceivers; 1.6T LPO drivers and TIAs expected to come to market this year; FiberEdge design wins for 1.6T transceivers expected, with a significant ramp in the second half of the year as hyperscalers roll out new XPU and switch platforms using reduced-power 1.6T transceivers. Some hyperscalers are 'increasingly bullish on 1.6T LPO' for the first layer of scale-up fabrics. Semtech is a member of the new XPO MSA (released by Arista) and is developing the NPO (Near Package Optics) MSA with other industry leaders. OFC demos: NVIDIA's 1.6T DR4 transceivers powered by Semtech TIAs and laser drivers running live in NVIDIA's switch platform; a switch on the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 platform running FR4, LR4 and LPO configurations on Semtech silicon; next-generation 448G per-channel modulator drivers and TIAs.

CFO Csaba Sverha: the thumb rule is 'whatever the product's getting deployed, if it's a data center or hyperscale, then it goes in the data center, everything else goes into the communication infrastructure.' quarterly_data.signal: CEO Seamus Grady walked the capacity ladder to a single consolidated number: capacity right now is about $5.8 billion (the $5.3 billion Q4 exit run rate plus the Pinehurst office-to-manufacturing conversion); Building 10 when fully available adds about $3.5 billion at the high end; Nava, the new factory in Nava Nakorn, adds about $250 million; and the newly acquired Santa Clara operation adds about another $250 million - which gets to $9.8 billion of capacity in calendar Q1, early in the March quarter, an 85% increase versus where the year ended. Beyond that, Building 11 - not yet announced - would take probably 18 months to build and add capacity for another $2.1 billion approximately, and the same for Building 12, so over the next three years Fabrinet could add another $4.2 billion on top of the $9.8 billion, taking it to approximately $14 billion of capacity. Even with all of that, Fabrinet is still looking for more land in Bangkok, in Thailand.
quarterly_data.figure: $5.8 billion now -> $9.8 billion capacity in calendar Q1 (an 85% increase); buildings 11 and 12 at about $2.1 billion each, 18 months each, to approximately $14 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Grady quantified the build-ahead economics of Building 10: it is about a 2 million sq ft factory costing about $132 million, $133 million for the building, and even if it were to sit idle the gross margin headwind is about 15 basis points, while just over five months' worth of operating profit at full run rate would pay for the whole factory. It will not sit idle - Fabrinet is already installing equipment and getting going on Floor 1 and will start to occupy Floor 3 in October. 'The downside risk is tiny and the upside opportunity is immense', with the real downside being that if the capacity is not put in place customers have to go somewhere else. Fit-out follows the customer: generic or standard equipment is paid for by Fabrinet, product-specific or unique equipment is paid for by the customer.
quarterly_data.figure: idle Building 10 gross margin headwind about 15 basis points; just over five months' worth of operating profit pays for the factory; building cost about $132 million, $133 million

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Csaba Sverha on funding the expansion: total CapEx for the last year was about $250 million and the company anticipates these elevated levels continue in fiscal 2027 in this $250 million range, covering the finishing of Building 10 and the fit-outs plus the Santa Clara facility that was just acquired for $76 million. Fabrinet took a small $75 million term loan signed with a Thai bank in August to finance growth in Thailand and is expanding credit lines, but is very comfortable with the balance sheet and comfortable financing growth from its own free cash flow rather than equity, because return on invested capital is close to the 40% mark. On the Q1 guide, the usual first-quarter merit salary increases add about 20, 30 basis point headwinds sequentially, which management expects to make up with efficiencies through the year.
quarterly_data.figure: CapEx about $250 million last year and in the $250 million range in fiscal 2027; Santa Clara acquired for $76 million; $75 million term loan; ROIC close to the 40% mark; Q1 seasonality 20, 30 basis point headwind

quarterly_data.signal: Datacom diversification status: Fabrinet is actually shipping to both hyperscale-direct and merchant transceiver manufacturers right now, and it is early days. The non-NVIDIA datacom customers are mostly initially 800 gig short reach transceivers and then moving to 1.6 in the future, with the initial foray at 800 gig. Grady reiterated Fabrinet will never become an ODM or own the IP - companies like Ciena, Cisco and Nokia would be deeply upset if it became a product company - and said Fabrinet has been picking up and winning business with some customers precisely because some competitors chose the ODM route. Management said it does not overly analyse share (customers do not always disclose it) and focuses instead on growing each opportunity to the multi-$100 million level where it can properly resource the customer. Beyond hyperscale, Fabrinet is also working with quantum compute customers that would fall into the new data center category, because moving those workloads around will need optics and not just electronics.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: First margin math on NPO/CPO: on a typical product, if COGS is 100%, roughly 70%-80% is material and 20% is value add. For NPO the material content is much lower - in many cases the wafer is consigned by the customer and Fabrinet singulates it, does the packaging and the testing at die and device level - so it is much higher value add, probably a lower ASP but a higher margin, and Grady said NPO 'would be much better gross margin than our traditional business'. He cautioned the business needs a mix of both higher-volume lower-margin work and this higher-margin lower-ASP work, and described NPO as probably a little bit more straightforward than CPO, with the opportunity in NPO extending well beyond ELSFPs to the packaging of the devices themselves.
quarterly_data.figure: typical COGS about 70%-80% material, 20% value add

quarterly_data.signal: OCS ramp timing put on the clock for the first time: Fabrinet has shipped some OCS product but it is quite small today, and is working with a number of companies, one of whom it is actually shipping product to, while the others are early days and more startup-type companies. Management is looking forward to really beginning to ramp that over the next 12 to 18 months. On Coherent specifically, Grady said Coherent has a lot of its own in-house capacity at both the system level and the wafer level and does a lot of the in-house silicon itself, so he believes Coherent will continue to manufacture in-house. Fabrinet is happy to do sub-assemblies or the finished product, whatever the customer wants.
quarterly_data.figure: ramp over the next 12 to 18 months

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q2 2026 (quarter ended December 26, 2025) revenue was a record $1.13 billion, up 36% year over year - the fastest year-over-year growth since the IPO over fifteen years ago - and up 16% from Q1, above the guidance range. Non-GAAP EPS was a record $3.36, above guidance despite a $3 million (9¢ per share) FX revaluation loss. Non-GAAP gross margin was 12.4% (up 10 basis points from Q1, flat year over year despite FX headwinds) and operating margin reached 10.9% (up 30 basis points from both Q1 and a year ago); net income was $122 million. Cash and short-term investments ended at $961 million; operating cash flow was $46 million and free cash flow an outflow of $5 million (CEO Seamus Grady and CFO Csaba Sverha).

quarterly_data.signal: ADI's optical franchise targets the CONTROL PATH, not the electro-optic data path: 'there are two critical pathways, the data path of electro optics and the control path, which guides, optimizes, and ensures the integrity of the data path. Our focus is on the control path.' Customers increasingly rely on ADI for the timing, power management, data conversion, monitoring and control that let LASERS AND TRANSCEIVERS operate with precision, reliably and efficiently at AI scale. Data center optical revenue grew MORE THAN 100% year-over-year in fiscal Q3 2026 (data center is now 80% of ADI communications revenue, which itself was +84% YoY).
quarterly_data.figure: Data center optical revenue +100%+ YoY; control-path timing/power/conversion for lasers & transceivers

quarterly_data.signal: 800G -> 3.2T TRANSITION: as customers increase the number of optical lanes, signal bandwidth, or both, to accelerate network speeds from 800 Gb to 3.2 Tbps, ADI expects to benefit THREEFOLD - unit growth in pluggables and coherent light modules, INCREASING BOM CONTENT per module, and GREATER SHARE as these transitions unfold.
quarterly_data.figure: 800Gb -> 3.2Tbps: threefold benefit (units + BOM content + share)

quarterly_data.signal: OPTICAL CIRCUIT SWITCHING: based on current DESIGN WINS AND CUSTOMER COMMITMENTS, ADI's OCS revenue is poised to approximately DOUBLE this year, and ADI is targeting a SIMILAR LEVEL OF GROWTH IN 2027. OCS is called out alongside CPO as a new architecture gaining traction in next-generation large-scale AI clusters, expanding control-path complexity and ADI's long-term opportunity.
quarterly_data.figure: OCS revenue ~2x in 2026, targeting similar growth in 2027 (design wins + customer commitments)

quarterly_data.signal: CO-PACKAGED OPTICS: ADI views the nascent CPO space as a SAM EXPANDER - the criticality of its precision control technology increases further as THERMAL AND SERVICEABILITY challenges rise in co-packaged architectures. Combined with market growth, expanding content and increasing share, management says data center optics will remain a strong growth vector for ADI over the coming years.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO framed as SAM expander; no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Optical connectivity: as AI data movement grows exponentially, 'industry leaders are re-architecting their networks, increasingly replacing traditional electrical switching with Optical Circuit Switches or OCS.' Performance 'increasingly depends on the precision control monitoring and power solutions, the nervous system, if you will, around the laser, DSP and photodiode signal chain' - ADI integrates precision control, temperature regulation, real-time monitoring and compact power management so optical systems run at higher speeds with lower power in smaller form factors, raising front-panel bandwidth density and cutting cost per bit. The optical 'nervous system' mixes digital functionality with ADI's mixed-signal conversion and power. Data center revenue is 'pretty balanced between power and optical', and Q1 communications growth was led by data center demand for ADI's optical and power portfolios.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure (data center revenue pretty balanced between power and optical)

quarterly_data.signal: POWER franchise detail: customers are pushing for greater than 98% conversion efficiency, multi-kilowatt delivery with peak power up to 2x rated load, plus protection, telemetry and fault recording. Significant design uptick for ADI protection and 800V-to-intermediate conversion technology delivering 20 kW at industry-leading power density exceeding 2.5 kW per cubic inch, as the industry transitions to 800V DC power distribution. At the intermediate-to-core conversion layer - called ONE OF THE FASTEST AND LARGEST GROWING ANALOG OPPORTUNITIES IN THE AI ERA - ADI combines advanced power conversion, intelligent system control and real-time telemetry for next-generation processors operating at 6,000 A and sub-1V. Framing on efficiency: a 97% converter loses roughly 50% more energy as heat than a 98% one, compounding into cooling infrastructure and opex.
quarterly_data.figure: 800V->intermediate: 20 kW at >2.5 kW/cubic inch; core rails 6,000 A at sub-1V; >98% efficiency

quarterly_data.signal: Empower Semiconductor acquisition CLOSED July 7, 2026 for $1.5 BILLION in an all-cash transaction, extending ADI's vertical power story by taking power INTO THE PROCESSOR PACKAGE itself. In large-scale AI deployments the architecture reduces compute power consumption and temperature by approximately 10%-15%, equating to roughly $30 MILLION IN ANNUAL SAVINGS IN A 1 GW DATA CENTER. Cash and short-term investments fell to $2.3B on the close; net leverage ratio now 0.9.
quarterly_data.figure: Empower closed 07-07-2026 for $1.5B cash; -10-15% compute power/temp; ~$30M/yr saved per 1GW DC

quarterly_data.signal: GRID-TO-CHIP strategy: data center capacity is now measured in GIGAWATTS rather than FLOPS/TOPS and POWER AVAILABILITY HAS BECOME THE PRIMARY CONSTRAINT TO FURTHER AI PROGRESS. ADI supplies grid monitoring (real-time voltage, current, power quality, system health) to utilities, energy operators and infrastructure providers, plus battery management for energy storage - one of the grid's fastest-growing sectors. To accelerate time-to-power, hyperscalers are increasingly exploring DEDICATED MICROGRIDS, opening additional growth avenues that augment ADI's $500M+ energy business (inflected in 2025, accelerating in 2026). ADI now spans the entire electricity value chain: generation, transmission, storage, distribution, rack power and ultimately processor power delivery - 'essentially the vascular system of the data center.'
quarterly_data.figure: Energy business $500M+, inflected 2025 and accelerating in 2026; microgrid opportunity

quarterly_data.signal: 2030 SAM RESET: ADI's current assessment is that its 2030 data center AND energy SAM has MORE THAN DOUBLED versus what it envisioned just one year ago - driven not simply by higher AI infrastructure CapEx but by new markets and architectures requiring ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE MORE ANALOG CONTENT delivered via higher-value solutions. Supporting math from the call: ~100 GW equivalent of data center infrastructure is expected to be built between now and 2031, with EACH GIGAWATT generating a $1B-$1.5B analog SAM. Runway seen extending to at least 2030 for strong double-digit data center growth; the ~$0.5B energy business is expected to DOUBLE by the end of the decade. ADI is contemplating long-term company growth above the 5%-7% model set at its 2021 investor day.
quarterly_data.figure: 2030 DC+energy SAM >2x prior view; ~100GW to 2031 at $1-1.5B analog SAM per GW; energy to 2x by 2030

quarterly_data.signal: Data center power franchise breakdown: 'ADI's hot swap and high-performance protection solutions which represent roughly 1/3 of our data center power revenue today' enable fault isolation, fast recovery and live maintenance as customers migrate to higher-voltage architectures; 'Roughly 1/3 of our data center power revenue comes from DC power control, including our power system management ICs and multiphase controllers.' Strong growth continues in point-of-load converters, micro modules and high-performance regulators, and 'new approaches such as vertical power and higher voltage distribution, are now opening incremental SAM for ADI.' ADI 'shipped our smart power stage to our first vertical power customer last quarter, and adoption of our intermediate bus converter modules is accelerating for 48- and 54-volt architectures.' CEO: power systems are becoming more digitally controlled (multiphase, very high-speed conversion managing more rails), and 'computing performance equals availability of power'.

quarterly_data.signal: Announced the acquisition of Renesas' timing business (the Timing Products Division, ICS then IDT heritage; 500 clock products and 160 engineers) for $1.5 billion in cash plus approximately 4.13 million newly issued SiTime shares (15% symmetrical collar). The cash portion is funded from cash on hand and approximately $900 million of committed debt financing from Wells Fargo; leverage is targeted under two times within twenty-four months of closing, closing is expected by the end of 2026, and China SAMR approval is not expected to be needed. The business is expected to add $300 million of revenue in the twelve months after close at approximately 70% gross margins, 75% from CED, and SiTime's pro forma 2025 CED revenue almost doubles with Renesas' AI data center comms revenue. Management said the deal is accretive to non-GAAP EPS in the first full year, keeps the 25% to 30% long-term growth target intact (clocking grows more slowly than oscillators), moves SiTime faster to the upper end of its 60% to 65% gross-margin target with operating margins above 30%, and accelerates the path to $1 billion in revenue.

quarterly_data.signal: Cross-sell from the Renesas timing deal: Renesas clocks are typically designed in alongside quartz crystal, opening those sockets to SiTime's MEMS oscillators, while SiTime already has design wins in AI GPUs, accelerator cards and switches where the clock is Renesas' or another competitor's, allowing an oscillator-plus-clock offer that is 'notionally integrated' with one source of supply. The deal brings faster access to 10 hyperscalers, seven AI server leaders, 10 networking and communication vendors, plus leading automotive OEMs and tier ones; customer overlap is reasonably solid but product overlap minimal. A separate MOU explores integrating SiTime's Titan resonators into Renesas microcontrollers (a several-billion-dollar MCU revenue base), and the Renesas CEO joins SiTime's board at closing.
quarterly_data.figure: 10 hyperscalers, seven AI server leaders, 10 networking and communication vendors

quarterly_data.signal: Supply, not demand, is the binding constraint: the industry needs to add significant capacity and management does not see supply and demand getting back into balance BEFORE 2028 — a similarly constrained dynamic is expected going into 2027 and likely into 2028. In recent weeks Ciena FINALIZED LONG-TERM AGREEMENTS that secure supply of certain key components THROUGH 2029, including incremental capacity for those key components; the June five-year zero-coupon convertible (economic conversion premium of 114%, proceeds retiring the 5.5% interest term loan) partly provided the capital to help secure supply over the next three years, and cash from operations will step down in Q4 as those investments are dispersed. Ciena is also qualifying additional suppliers — expanding both the number of suppliers and alternative technologies for the same functionality. Capital investments this year increased capacity sufficient to support RLS, plug and Waveserver revenue growth all over 60% year to date; capex expected at the high end of the $250 million-$275 million range; $2.8 billion in cash and equivalents. Value exchange with customers: price increases from high single digits up to high teens/low 20s depending on customer and product line, some of it selectively hitting backlog, alongside payment-terms and fill-rate discussions; possible new Canadian tariff impact of ~$10 million a quarter being mitigated.
quarterly_data.figure: Key-component supply secured through 2029; supply/demand balance not before 2028; price increases high single digits to high teens/low 20s; capex high end of $250M-$275M

quarterly_data.signal: AI portfolio catalysts: WaveLogic 6 Extreme — after 18 months still the ONLY 1.6 Tb high-performance modem on the market — with a ramp already exceeding WaveLogic 5 Extreme and output doubled. RLS holds roughly 70% market share in disaggregated optical line systems; next-generation RLS HYPER-RAIL (co-created with the hyperscalers for scale-across / distributed AI training over greater distances) is on track for initial customer standardization by the end of calendar 2026 and will ramp to SEVERAL HUNDRED MILLION DOLLARS of revenue in 2027 (could be faster with more components), with economics a step function above RLS and accretive to corporate average margins. Interconnects: Q3 800 ZR pluggable shipments MORE THAN TWICE the previous quarter's volume; strong market receptivity to Nitro, the linear redriver for active copper cable solutions; VESTA, the open co-packaged optics (CPX) solution, received SAMPLE ORDERS FROM SEVERAL ANCHOR CUSTOMERS in the ecosystem — CPX revenue expected to begin in 2027 and ramp into 2028. Coherent moving inside the data center is viewed as inevitable with the right general-market intercept at 3.2 Tb; OCS is welcomed as driving coherent adoption inside the data center faster (no comment on Ciena entering the OCS market itself). The major-hyperscaler WaveLogic 6 Extreme win announced last quarter — DSP, drivers, TIAs and coherent expertise in a complete module deployed across the customer's own global optical platform, a significant takeaway from a component competitor — is one of two bespoke performance-optics consumption-model relationships. TAM expected to effectively double from approximately $25 billion today to approximately $50 billion by 2029; scale-across is a major demand driver, almost entirely North American/US-based and just beginning, with asynchronous training and inference traffic still ahead.

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: PCF (Private Connectivity Fabric) NUMBERS AND THE BUILD-ECONOMICS DOCTRINE BEHIND THEM. Q2 PCF revenue was ~$91M (from $78M in Q1) against the ~$13B of PCF deals announced to date; ~$36M of it was another STATE OF CALIFORNIA delivery milestone ACCELERATED into Q2 from the back half and 'now largely complete'. PCF CASH RECEIVED was ~$476M in the quarter and ~$300M of the ~$780M Q2 capex was PCF-related - and PCF capex is 'paid for up front by the customer', 'pretty much on schedule' with no significant efficiencies or risk found. The strategic doctrine is the important part: every PCF deal signed so far monetized CONDUIT 'paid for a quarter of a century ago' - underutilized assets - and created 'proximity with those hyperscalers'. On NEW builds, CFO Stansbury was blunt: 'if you look at the cost to build new trenches, deploy new conduit, you're looking at returns that are AT OR BELOW COST OF CAPITAL levels... there's great headline generating news in those, but the RETURNS ARE TERRIBLE'. Lumen's answer is to ride others' fiber: 'we're quite happy for others to build at or below their cost of capital so that we can provision higher margin, higher growth services on top of them.' A pipeline of 'fairly material' further PCF deals is in conversation, unannounced until signed.

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: NEOCLOUDS ARE 'GOING LONG' IN 100G/400G WAVES - THE CLEAREST CARRIER-SIDE AI SIGNAL IN THE QUARTER. Strategic WAVES revenue (100G and 400G) grew nearly 11% YoY in North American enterprise, and strategic WAVES SALES were up nearly 35% YoY - management called the sales number 'a nice precursor to future revenue'. CEO Johnson attributed it to share gain, not market growth: 'the neo clouds go long in 100 and 400 gig'... 'Yes, we're taking share', enabled by RAPIDROUTES turning up circuits 'in days, versus what used to take months' and by the density of '58 million fiber miles'. Neocloud PCF deals are 'relatively small' - neoclouds are buying WAVES, not conduit ('That is a part of the Waves growth... that's how they're choosing to buy their net connectivity'). Framing of the cycle: the uptick in 100G/400G 'is indicative of the SECOND PHASE OF THE AI ADOPTION CURVE, where more customers are starting to realize that they've got to upgrade their capacity', while legacy low-bandwidth wave circuits decline. Separately, satellite backhaul is a growing fiber-demand source - 'data needs to find fiber as fast as possible. We do the backhaul for the satellite companies and it's growing pretty significantly'.
quarterly_data.figure: 100G/400G waves revenue +11% YoY, SALES +35% YoY; 58M fiber miles; neoclouds buying waves not PCF

quarterly_data.signal: SPEED-NODE, CPO AND OCS ROADMAP FROM THE TEST SEAT. SPEED MIX: '800 Gbps is still the biggest driver, but 1.6 Tbps is ramping very quickly, and that's mainly a lot of the production' - management expects 'probably in 2027 it may get to PARITY between 800 Gbps and 1.6 Tbps, and then 1.6 Tbps will continue to get bigger while 800 Gbps may pull back'; 400G 'is going to be around for quite a while as well. They just don't go away' - multiple nodes running in parallel. CPO: asked about yield-driven slippage, Khaykin was emphatic - 'there's been a lot of industry talk, like, oh, because the yield is going to be slower. That's all NONSENSE. CPO and all that thing is MOVING FORWARD... I have POs to show for that.' Viavi is already recognizing some CPO revenue in the September quarter with December 'starting to accelerate'. Crucially, yield management INCREASES test intensity: 'to manage yields, you just do more tests - more of a KNOWN GOOD DIE, KNOWN GOOD OPTICAL ENGINE, KNOWN GOOD SUBSTRATE... which means a lot of testing, which ultimately pretty good for us.' And the cleanest statement yet of why CPO happens at all: 'if you have co-packaged optics, your THREE NANOMETER SILICON PERFORMS AS A TWO NANOMETER SILICON. You are getting almost a WHOLE NODE OF ADVANTAGE by co-packaging the optics' - taken either as performance or as cost, at the price of complexity and yield. OCS: some revenue already in the numbers with 'the majority... coming in the next several quarters'; Viavi has been selling equipment to 'a big OCS vendor, hyperscaler, who makes their own stuff', and it is now broadening as 'many other companies are looking to do more optical switching in their core' - 'I see this demand as being very healthy.'

quarterly_data.signal: 1.6T TEST ECONOMICS THE CALL DID NOT SIZE: CEO Oleg Khaykin said a 1.6T tester carries 'about 50% price increase' over an 800G box, 'because the components are much more expensive', comparing it to TSMC raising price per wafer 'about 1.5x' each node. The box is backward compatible - one 1.6T tester can test four 400G modules, two 800G or a 1.6T - so cost per bit falls even though cost per box rises, and one high-performance tester can service multiple production lines at once. Content per test is also rising: 400G was laser/dispersion/power in-out, 800G adds precise laser and insertion-loss measurement, and 'as you go to 1.6T, it is a whole new ballgame... a lot more functional test on the line'. quarterly_data.signal: CPO TEST - TIMING AND WHERE VIAVI SITS: Khaykin said Viavi has been working on a CPO test 'now for well over 12 to close to 2 years. We are now started shipping, I would say even this quarter is early shipments.' Test capacity is facilitized ahead of demand and the next increment is added at about '60%, 70% utilization'. CPO pulls Viavi into semiconductor test next to Advantest, Teradyne and FormFactor - the configuration is an IC tester plus a prober plus an optical rack, all interconnected - and he expects a HIGHER share for Viavi there than in pluggables because Viavi sells an automatable integrated platform with '2,500 SKUs' of measurement modules rather than a point solution. Content per port rises sharply: pluggable is power, dispersion and insertion loss, CPO is multiple insertions plus extensive functional test, with known-good-die, optical-engine and interconnect-platform insertions all before the ASIC and memory go on a module worth 'thousands of dollars' - skip them and 'you will be throwing away tens of millions of dollars'.

He noted OCS demand is not only from module vendors: 'there's also some hyperscalers who do it directly'. The driver is power - 'there's not enough power in the world to power all these data centers' - pushing architectures from electrical to optical. Because the cost of one bad port pair is a bad switch, customers 'test everything to the nth degree', and for a '100 terabit switch, I don't think anybody's going to skip any tests'.

Northern Virginia: 'We are running out of available capacity in a place like Northern Virginia. We have 50 megawatts available today for lease, and probably another 96-megawatt building behind it. But after that, it could be some time.' Digital Realty is siting new capacity in markets like Kansas City instead. On moratoria: no new development exposure in places like New York or Pennsylvania; a temporary moratorium in Charlotte covers three projects that are all vested (two underway, the third buildable and approved). Customers are pulling delivery forward - asking for extra crews and paying for early handover ('May cost a little extra and they're paying for it') - because time to power is paramount.
quarterly_data.figure: Northern Virginia: 50 megawatts available for lease plus a 96-megawatt building behind it; three vested projects in Charlotte under a temporary moratorium

Digital Realty is happy to hold them on balance sheet, they could later feed its strategic private capital business, and more recapitalizations like this are likely.

quarterly_data.signal: Power and supply constraints (CEO/CFO/CIO): in 2025 power became 'the industry's primary constraint', and power availability and ability to execute are now 'the defining constraints' across digital infrastructure; in most core markets new supply will arrive gradually as generation and transmission upgrades continue, and hyperscalers increasingly lease from operators that can secure and deliver power capacity on a predictable schedule. Digital Realty leans on its five-gigawatt power bank. 'Data center supply remains tight, especially within our footprint'; availability across the 800 megawatts in-place Northern Virginia portfolio 'remains very limited, with strong demand queuing for the 300 megawatts of capacity we are readying for delivery in the 2027 to 2029 time frame.' The CEO said 2027 deliveries are 'pretty exceptional and sought after' with multiple customers per capacity block, 2028 should be as attractive, and the company is 'not seeing a tremendous amount of competitive unleashed capacity'; labor is 'getting challenging more challenging by the day', though every project in the 10 plus billion under construction has workforce and supply chain security. The CIO expects demand to increase two and a half to three times over the next five years against severely constrained supply (power, nimbyism, zoning). On an IT load basis, occupancy was approximately 91% (same capital) and 89% (total portfolio) at year-end, with reporting moving to power-based metrics.
quarterly_data.figure: Northern Virginia 800 megawatts in place with very limited availability; 300 megawatts for 2027 to 2029 delivery; five-gigawatt power bank; IT-load occupancy approximately 91% (same capital) / 89% (total)

quarterly_data.signal: Hyperscale demand and design (CEO/CRO): hyperscale activity was strong in Q4, especially in the Americas (Northern Virginia, Charlotte, Atlanta, Dallas), and demand is globalizing into Europe, South America and Asia. Wherever Digital Realty has large capacity blocks (Northern Virginia, Paris, Osaka, Tokyo, Atlanta, Charlotte) hyperscalers want to deploy, with conversations running over 2026 through 2028, and customers are looking further out on the horizon than six or twelve months earlier. The latest hyperscale designs mix cloud and AI inside the same building, with cooling that's 'a mixture of air and liquid', which the CEO said leads towards inference; the AI roadmap includes preinstalled liquid cooling capacity and higher density deployments. On power sourcing the CEO said the company has 'not given up on the grid' and treats behind-the-meter as a form of bridging while utilities reinforce transmission and distribution; land sites in cloud zonal markets of 200 megawatt and 100 megawatt are 'gonna continue to get bigger.'
quarterly_data.figure: hyperscale conversations over 2026 through 2028; 200 megawatt and 100 megawatt land sites

quarterly_data.signal: Funding strategy (IR/CFO): by year-end Digital Realty had closed $3.225 billion of LP equity into its inaugural closed-end hyperscale data center fund, with a final $25 million closing expected before the next call; in late December it contributed another 40% stake in the five stabilized seed assets, taking the fund stake to 80% and generating $427 million of net proceeds. About $15 billion of dry powder supports hyperscale data center development through private capital initiatives, and fee income more than doubled in 2025. Q4 financing: a EUR1.4 billion dual-tranche green Eurobond (€600 million at 3.755% due 2033 and €800 million at 4.25% due 2037), partly used to redeem $1.075 billion of 2.5% Eurobonds, a modest interest expense headwind starting in 2026.

He added that pre-sales are 'higher than they've ever been' - capacity is sold before it is completed - which leaves 'less latitude for slippage', and that if demand keeps increasing Equinix will look at further acceleration within its committed capital envelope.

quarterly_data.signal: Build-cost economics disclosed for the first time at this level of detail. Abdel gave an 'indicative range' of build cost of '$10,000-$20,000' depending on geography and project type, and said power connection has gone from free to a major line item: 'Costs us tens of millions of USD to deliver power to a site now. It used to cost us nothing.' He is seeing cost inflation in heavily built markets - electricians 'are making $150 an hour these days' - while cost 'definitely moderated on the manufacturing side of the equation'. The response is to shift work offsite: more prefabrication to minimise onsite labour.

quarterly_data.signal: The two binding bottlenecks are energy and trades labour, not demand. Abdel: 'Electricians in many locations are very constrained. There's not enough of them' - electricians and plumbers are 'probably being the most acute' trades. Example given: the greater Chicago metro area has '15 gigawatt' of planned data-center expansions on the docket 'with another 15 that's at least marketed to be planned', and 'there is just not enough electricians'. On power he said generation is 'the tertiary issue' - distribution and transmission are the bottlenecks - and that a site requested the old way 'could be 8 years before you get that power'; Equinix therefore now secures the utility conversation and line of sight to power BEFORE taking down land.

quarterly_data.signal: Fleet density and liquid-cooling retrofit detail. Abdel: Equinix has '280 data centers today' before the announced capacity; asked whether 60 megawatts is now the standard block size he answered 'That's our template'; and cooling is now sized one-for-one with power ('If you are delivering 5 megawatts to a pod, well, you have 5 megawatts of cooling'). Existing sites are not drawn down to 100%, so churn events are backfilled at higher density - 10, 15 kW a cab in a 20-year-old site, not 40, 50 kW - and 'We've also retrofit a bunch of our older data centers with liquid cooling', either direct-to-chip or liquid-to-air. All new builds are liquid-cool ready. He cautioned that headline rack numbers are peaks, not averages: 'one of our latest builds is 18 kW average', which supports 50, 60, 70 kW cabinets alongside 4 and 5 kW ones. Modern designs removed raised flooring, so heat can be placed anywhere inside the pod envelope.

quarterly_data.quarter: Advanced Energy Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-10-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: 800V TIMELINE PINNED: 2027 IS THE DESIGN-WIN YEAR, REVENUE IN 2028-2029. Kelley: 'we do not expect 800V to be significant from a revenue standpoint until 2028 at the earliest. So we think 2027 is a design win year for us, and 2028 and 2029 start to see revenue on 800V product.' AE is attacking it with a modular architecture - 'we have what we call a PDU, a power distribution unit. Think of it as a motherboard, essentially, where we could plug in these different 800V modules... 800V to six volts or to some other intermediate voltage' - explicitly because 'I do not think anybody knows exactly how the architecture is going to look a year or two from now.' He confirmed AE has solutions and active customer engagements for the AC/DC move out of the rack into a sidecar or power rack, and expects content per rack to rise as it has every generation. On cadence: 'every year a new solution is required. That is loosely tied to new introductions from Nvidia and other suppliers. The power requirements go up every year. But the space that we have to operate in does not change.'
quarterly_data.figure: 800V: 2027 design-win year, revenue 2028 and 2029, not significant until 2028 at the earliest

Expects approximately 100 gigawatts under contract by end-2026 (split shifting toward 60% orders / 40% SRAs), shipping high teens in gigawatts in 2026 with new contracts north of 30 gigawatts; CEO Scott Strazik: at 100 gigawatts, '29 and '30 will be 'largely sold out', though 'there are still slots available for 2029' as of January 28; framework discussions for '31 to '35 slots are active. Pricing: 'another 10 to 20 points of pricing strength in the SRAs today' versus existing backlog. Q4 booked 41 heavy-duty gas turbines (the largest orders quarter of the year, an increase of more than 70% YoY, including 15 HA units) and 18 aeroderivative units; about 63 aeroderivative orders in 2025. Management does not view smaller turbine makers as competition — they enable earlier power ahead of heavy-duty units and later serve as reliability backup.

quarterly_data.signal: RECORD BACKLOG OF $53 BILLION - and the big work is not in it yet. Duke Austin: 'The record backlog we reported reflects the demand in front of us, but we're still in the early stages. The larger programs across the utility generation and technology load center markets are ahead of us, and we expect them to stack in the years to come.' The 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV transmission are still in engineering ('We're not in backlog on any of the bigger work yet'), and about 95% of the generation work is not in backlog either. He expects record backlog again in the third quarter and probably the fourth. Book-to-burn will be lumpy: 1:1 to 1:2 in ordinary quarters, 1:5 to 1:6 in quarters when big chunks of projects land (the 765 kV work brought in last quarter was that kind of boost) - 'lower lows and higher highs all the way through'. A large share of the technology work never touches backlog at all: MEP crews can 'book and bill $300 million on a site in a quarter' against an MSA and 'you never see it show up in backlog'. CFO Jayshree Desai on data-center backlog discipline: only items with limited notices to proceed go in, 'we don't put the rest in until the project is a confirmed go.'
quarterly_data.figure: Record total backlog $53B; ~95% of generation work not yet in backlog; up to $300M booked-and-burned on a single technology site per quarter, outside backlog

quarterly_data.signal: Craft labour is NOT the binding constraint today - Duke Austin: 'We're nowhere near capacity.' More than 85,000 employees; roughly 15,500 people added over the past year, well over 7,000 of them organic with a significant portion in Q2; Quanta spends about $250 million a year on training. It takes about four years to make a craftsman and a journeyman, and he sees no oversupply of craft-skilled labour in the near future. Labour is fungible across segments - electricians and underground crews move between data-center work, industrial and gas compression work and T&D - which is where the acquisition synergies show up. Customers are securing craft as far out as their five- to seven-year capital plans, with 'decade-plus type arrangements out there'. Margin follows that utilisation: the electric segment can operate at 10% to 12% on the utility side, with 12% the utmost 'when you stack in large transmission and all aspects at once', and Duke sees room for further margin improvement in the second half.
quarterly_data.figure: 85,000+ employees, +15,500 over the year (>7,000 organic); ~$250M/yr training; 'nowhere near capacity'; electric segment margin range 10%-12% on the utility side

quarterly_data.signal: The stacking has not started. Duke Austin: the 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV projects and the generation work are 'just starting - a lot of it's in engineering'; they start hitting backlog in the later half of this year, crews go to the field around the second half of 2027, and the compounding effect then stacks out 'throughout what I would consider the decade' and 'well past 2030'. He compares it to 2012-2015, when a batch of big projects compounded, and says the base business is doing upper-single-digit to double-digit growth before any of that lands. The nearest concrete catalyst named on the call is the NiSource generation award: 'I do believe a significant amount of that will go into backlog in the third quarter.'
quarterly_data.figure: 765 kV / 345 kV / 500 kV plus generation work moves into backlog in the later half of 2026, into the field in the second half of 2027, stacking well past 2030; NiSource generation award expected to enter backlog in the third quarter

quarterly_data.signal: VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.
quarterly_data.figure: HICO high-voltage breaker JV plus owned transformer and utility-pole manufacturing; fabrication footprint ~seven million sq ft, +0.5 million sq ft from the recent acquisitions

quarterly_data.signal: Technology is now 15% to 20% of Quanta's business - 'a spectrum from chips to everything, not just data centers' - grown to that share over the last two years off the Cupertino Electric platform, and Duke Austin frames it as a second TAM 'every bit as big as our utility TAM'. Quanta sells direct to the hyperscalers and to the larger technology customers, and can self-perform 'call it 80% of what a data center build is, maybe 90%', taking balance-of-plant scope and full-scale data-center opportunities on more and more sites; it is also picking up work at semiconductor plants, at manufacturing and medical facilities, and at Tesla. The pitch is speed and certainty: 'Technology is trying to move as fast as possible. Utilities are working to protect the ratepayer, and Quanta sits in the middle of that nexus.' On state-level data-center moratoriums (New York): immaterial - 'nothing really gets built there' - and these are eight- to ten-year developments, not one-year builds, with multiyear projects extending well beyond 2030.
quarterly_data.figure: Technology = 15% to 20% of the business; Quanta can self-perform 80% to 90% of a data-center build

quarterly_data.signal: WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure (engine orders placed today carry a five- to six-year lead time; substation interconnection queue is the constraint)

quarterly_data.signal: REGULATORY UNLOCK FOR LARGE LOADS moving far faster than expected. FERC in June ordered EVERY RTO to justify (or revise) how its tariff provides just and reasonable interconnection of LARGE LOADS, and directed PJM to explain why co-located transmission services cannot be made available more quickly; FERC is also willing to study GENERATION AND LOAD TOGETHER AT A COMMON POINT OF INTERCONNECTION, which Constellation has advocated. PJM released proposals for the RELIABILITY BACKSTOP PROCUREMENT (RBP) and INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE (IRAS), set a target of 6.8 GW for the RBP, and is running a BILATERAL MATCHMAKING process to pair customers with new supply and shrink the centrally procured amount; the RBP auction is proposed for this fall with RESULTS BY YEAR-END. Co-location rule clarity is now expected in Q1-Q2 2027 (PJM response due ~November 2026, FERC order Q1-Q2 2027) versus PJM's earlier 2029 target. Separately Constellation is urging the EPA to exclude FERC-tariff-directed curtailments from the 50-HOUR ANNUAL LIMIT on data-center BACKUP GENERATORS, which management says may be the most effective way to cover the few peak hours
quarterly_data.figure: PJM RBP target 6.8 GW, auction this fall; co-location clarity Q1-Q2 2027 (was 2029)

quarterly_data.signal: THE STRANDED-CAPACITY THESIS, restated as the core commercial argument: the grid has unused generation and wires capacity in OVER 99% OF THE HOURS of the year - 'we have a peak capacity concern, not an energy concern' - so the fastest and cheapest path to powering AI is harvesting that latent capacity and managing the handful of peak hours with batteries, demand response, peaking resources and customer backup generation. Management argues existing and new supply are not bifurcated: even a customer that self-manages peaks via Connect and Manage 'will still need to buy energy for all of the other hours', which is where the existing fixed-price, carbon-free nuclear fleet becomes the multi-decade product customers want. Customer sophistication about the grid is now 'as good as the energy companies themselves' - not true two years ago. Management expects the data economy to invest 'upwards of $1 trillion in infrastructure ANNUALLY' and expects PJM deal flow to 'kick off with a bit of a bang' once rules are final

Delayed a few months by construction, automation-equipment issues and a utility-interconnection delay (the plant has been running on generators, preventing parallel commissioning work); limited production started in Q3, grid connection expected within weeks, FULL production in fiscal Q1 2027. Management put a hedge and a contingency in the plan and blew through both. Organizational response: Roman Loosen (Chief Enterprise Operations Officer, 20+ years at Siemens) takes over supply chain and manufacturing and Peter Williams moves to product, both reporting to the CEO; framed as an EXECUTION/process-scaling fix, not a change of suppliers. Once Houston is fully ramped, Fluence expects domestic-content capacity sufficient for its entire current backlog.

quarterly_data.signal: Management listed four new and developing uses of battery storage by large energy users such as data centers and C&I facilities. (1) Speed to power: storage speeds grid interconnection by matching power demand to grid capability and avoids the delays and expense of grid upgrades. (2) Quality of power: injecting reactive power to resolve voltage disturbances, managing demand (including disconnecting from the grid when needed) and smooth ramp-rate control. (3) Backup power: replacing higher-cost, carbon-intensive thermal gensets. (4) Support of on-site, bring-your-own generation behind the meter. Quality of power needs a response time below ten milliseconds; Fluence has a road map to deliver it, and this is where it competes with other technologies. Current data-center demand comes more from speed-to-power and bring-your-own-generation applications than from quality of power. Management cited product density, safety, reliability and cybersecurity as advantages, and noted that Fluence does not compete with its data-center customers.

On battery cells, Fluence is working with ASC (named AESC in the analyst's question) to resolve the prohibited foreign entity (PFE) status of ASC's Tennessee facility. Fluence made ASC an ownership proposal, but ASC gave assurances that it will meet the law's conditions another way, without Fluence joining the ownership structure; Fluence's priority is competitively priced, PFE-compliant cells. Management sees no real change in the competitive environment, only a significant diversification of battery-cell suppliers. quarterly_data.signal: Data center hub strategy: over 30 hubs with a year-end goal of roughly 40, feeding a base case of 15 GW of new generation for large load by 2035 (upside 30 GW or more), approximately 50% from gas-fired generation. Four origination channels, each with a named example: hyperscalers directly (collaboration with Google to recommission Duane Arnold), investor-owned utilities (a joint development agreement signed with Xcel earlier this week to jointly plan and deploy generation, storage and transmission for data center demand across Xcel's eight-state service territory), co-ops/municipalities (plan with Basin Electric to develop a 1.5 GW combined cycle plant in North Dakota), and the federal government. quarterly_data.signal: Battery storage (point in time): CEO said storage now represents almost one-third of the 30-gigawatt backlog, with nearly five gigawatts originated over the past twelve months, and that "battery storage is the only new capacity resource available at scale." Energy Resources placed over two gigawatts of battery storage into service in 2025, increasing its annual battery storage build from 2024 by roughly 220%. The stand-alone and co-located battery storage pipeline totals 95 gigawatts; co-locating storage at sites that already have grid connections can effectively double capacity at a site, expanding each site could potentially double total backlog, and long-duration opportunities are at an early stage. A domestic battery supply is secured through 2029.

quarterly_data.signal: Data center hub strategy (point in time): 20 potential hubs under discussion with the market, expected to rise to 40 by year-end, under the '15 by 35' origination channel whose goal is for Energy Resources to place in service 15 gigawatts of new generation for data center hubs by 2035; the CEO said he would be disappointed not to double the goal and deliver at least 30 gigawatts through the channel by 2035. The 15 gigawatts is roughly six gigawatts of gas-fired generation (the CEO clarified: by 2032) with renewables and storage for the balance. Energy Resources is positioning for bring your own generation (BYOG), where hyperscalers bring and pay for their own power generation infrastructure, using its renewables and storage portfolio as a speed-to-market 'hook' for a data center's initial phase before adding capacity through new gas-fired generation or SMRs. The CEO said larger deals will be announced as they happen rather than held for quarterly calls.

quarterly_data.signal: Nuclear: the Duane Arnold recommissioning in Iowa continues, made possible by the twenty-five-year power purchase agreement with Google announced last year. NextEra has six gigawatts of SMR co-location opportunities at its nuclear sites and is working to develop new greenfield sites; it narrowed the 96 or so SMR OEMs to about 12 for deep dives, has a development team focused 100% on SMRs, historically prefers competition among suppliers over locking in one counterparty, and requires risk sharing that caps its financial exposure (a four-party structure with the OEM, the hyperscaler and the government). CFO: SMRs are not in the base plan and would be upside. Point Beach (Wisconsin) received a subsequent license renewal for another twenty years and signed a PPA extension for 14% of the plant's capacity, contributing $0.03 of annual adjusted EPS (CEO: extrapolated to the rest of the plant, $0.21); Seabrook (New Hampshire) is seeing similar interest, with 1.7 gigawatts of capacity offered to the market between the two plants. Renewables recontracting opportunities total up to six gigawatts through 2032.

quarterly_data.signal: Transmission and gas infrastructure: NextEra Energy Transmission has $8 billion of total regulated and secured capital and has secured roughly $5 billion in new projects since 2023, including PJM's December recommendation that NextEra Energy Transmission and Exelon be selected to develop a new $1.7 billion high-voltage transmission line expected to enhance the flow of more than seven gigawatts of power across the region (PJM decision expected the month after the call; asked by an analyst about pushback in Pennsylvania, the CFO said confidence "continues to be high" and that PJM continues to support the project). Energy Resources holds ownership interests in more than 1,000 miles of FERC-regulated pipelines and acquired a portion of ConEd's interest in Mountain Valley Pipeline in January; on January 9 it closed the acquisition of natural gas supplier Symmetry Energy Solutions, which operates in 34 states. The combined electric and gas transmission business is expected to reach $20 billion of regulated and invested capital by 2032, a 20% CAGR off a 2025 base. Management put the 2026 reduction in gas infrastructure adjusted EBITDA at "$50 million or so".

Year-to-date operating earnings $3.01 per share versus $2.98. quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED LOAD ADDITIONS REACH 69 GIGAWATTS through 2030, up six gigawatts from the 63 GW disclosed last quarter — 'AEP contracted an additional six gigawatts of load, primarily driven by fully executed LOAs in Texas.' All of it is supported by fully executed ESAs and LOAs that require customers to secure land, complete interconnection studies, provide detailed load forecasts and fund the associated infrastructure investments. Geographic split: Texas 45 GW, Ohio 12 GW, and Oklahoma, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana and Virginia combined 12 GW. Management stresses counterparty quality — 'the vast majority of these projects are being advanced by well-capitalized hyperscalers and large industrial customers with significant financial resources.' Executed LOAs and ESAs have increased every quarter for the last six to seven quarters.

quarterly_data.signal: AEP TEXAS SUBMITTED 45 GIGAWATTS OF PROJECTS INTO ERCOT'S BATCH ZERO process, forecast between now and 2032, with ERCOT expected to determine eligibility on August 7. The credit support is already in hand: 'just over the past month, we have collected nearly $2 billion in cash or collateral for load commitments in ERCOT, which represents all the required credit support for the full 45 gigawatts included in AEP Texas's Batch Zero filing.' Of the 205 gigawatts ERCOT published as eligible for Batch Zero, AEP is 'roughly, call it, a quarter of that', and the CFO treats its 45 GW as firm — a worst case only slips projects from Batch Zero to Batch One. Critical for the equipment chain: the $78 billion capital plan assumed only about 13 gigawatts of interconnection in Texas and 'does not anticipate this magnitude of load growth', and there is 'almost 100 gigawatts in Texas behind that 45 gigawatts', with 195 gigawatts of parties actively trying to interconnect to the queue.
quarterly_data.figure: 45 GW submitted to ERCOT Batch Zero (out of 205 GW eligible); nearly $2 billion of cash/collateral posted; $78B plan assumed only about 13 GW of Texas interconnection; almost 100 GW more queued behind it; 195 GW in the interconnection queue

quarterly_data.signal: FIVE-YEAR CAPITAL PLAN OF $78 BILLION for 2026 through 2030, expected to result in nearly 11% rate base CAGR — 'AEP's five-year capital plan stood at just $38 billion only four years ago.' Beyond the base plan the company has 'line of sight to over $10 billion of incremental investments that are not included in the $78 billion, consisting of the fuel cells for the Wyoming project, the Piketon transmission opportunity, and incremental power generation.' A new 2027 to 2031 plan will be introduced on the third-quarter earnings call, with the secured generation investments expected to be an important driver of the long-term growth outlook. Financing for the base plan is de-risked: a $3 billion marketed equity transaction settled under forward contracts by May 2028 addresses all anticipated marketed equity needs, with a targeted FFO to debt ratio of 14% to 15%.
quarterly_data.figure: $78B five-year capital plan 2026-2030 (nearly 11% rate base CAGR), up from $38B four years ago; over $10B of identified incremental investment outside the plan

quarterly_data.signal: TURBINE SUPPLY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AND AEP IS PRE-BUYING IT: an additional three gigawatts of gas-fired turbines secured during the quarter takes total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 gigawatts for deployment through 2031, and AEP is 'leveraging our sizable market position and strategic manufacturer relationships to secure up to 10 gigawatts of incremental turbine capacity through 2035' — an option it is not committed to. CEO Bill Fehrman named the suppliers: 'using our size and scale and our relationships with namely GE Vernova and Mitsubishi to get this equipment locked up... we know that generation is going to be a driving force, and because of that, it's a scarce resource and will become increasingly more valuable.' Roughly half of the 13 GW already sits in the $78 billion plan; the other half rolls into the 2027-2031 plan. The 10 GW option is timed to replace aging coal and gas plants as they retire.
quarterly_data.figure: Three gigawatts of turbines added in the quarter, taking total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 GW through 2031; option on up to 10 GW more through 2035; about half of the 13 GW already inside the $78B plan

quarterly_data.signal: TWO PROJECTS BEYOND THE BASE PLAN ARE MOVING TO DEFINITIVE AGREEMENTS AHEAD OF THE THIRD-QUARTER CAPITAL-PLAN REFRESH. Piketon (Ohio) transmission: AEP is 'working towards definitive agreements with the prospective offtaker, SP Energy', anticipates executed documents in the third quarter and would then roll the project into the 2027-2031 five-year plan; the company frames it as showcasing 'our industry-leading expertise in developing and operating 765 kV transmission infrastructure.' Wyoming fuel cells: at the contractual June 30 deadline AEP amended the agreement with the unnamed hyperscaler offtaker, modifying key protection terms so AEP is 'adequately compensated for their requested timing accommodations' while keeping the original December 2026 milestone intact, after which the hyperscaler may deploy the fuel cells at an alternate location if the Cheyenne, Wyoming site does not advance. Timing is gating: the fuel cells 'need to be installed and ready to go by the end of 2028 to qualify for the investment tax credit.'
quarterly_data.figure: Piketon definitive agreements targeted for the third quarter with offtaker SP Energy; Wyoming fuel-cell December 2026 milestone intact, units must be installed by the end of 2028 to qualify for the investment tax credit

quarterly_data.signal: LARGE-LOAD TARIFF FRAMEWORK NOW COVERS FIVE JURISDICTIONS — Virginia approved AEP's proposed large load tariff in June, 'bringing the total number of approved tariffs across the portfolio to five', with three additional filings pending. The tariffs 'require customers to make long-term commitments and support the investments necessary to serve their demand' and provide protections against project delays and changing development timelines. Because new large load signs take-or-pay electric service agreements, AEP projects fixed cost offsets for residential customers of up to $16 billion at its vertically integrated utilities — already flowing through as base rate reductions (an Ohio order received; Indiana Michigan Power to file a base rate decrease later this summer).
quarterly_data.figure: Five large-load tariffs approved and three more filings pending; up to $16 billion of projected fixed-cost offsets for residential customers

quarterly_data.signal: GENERATION ADDITIONS TO SERVE THE LOAD: Public Service Company of Oklahoma received a separate order in May approving its request to procure 1.3 gigawatts of generation resources; AEP has announced one West Virginia project of about 1.2 gigawatts with 'a number of other projects that are heading down the pathway' toward the governor's 50 by 50 target; and it is evaluating a GenCo structure alongside an early-stage nuclear strategy 'driven by demand from potential customers who value alternative forms of long-term baseload generation to support their rapidly growing demand', on fee-based arrangements with robust capital protection measures. AEP also buys existing generation into rate base for its vertically integrated utilities (projects purchased for Indiana Michigan Power) and offers behind-the-meter bridging power so customers get immediate capacity while transmission and generation are built.
