quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED AI/DATA-CENTER LOAD CROSSES 17 GW. Four large-load projects were signed in the quarter alone: three projects in Alabama where Alabama Power added approximately 3 GW, plus a Georgia Power 3.2 GW, 25-year electric service contract with OpenAI at its newly announced site near Savannah, Georgia. Combined, those four projects represent 6 GW of newly contracted customer load, and together with agreements previously signed they bring total contracted large load agreements across Southern's electric subsidiaries to over 17 GW by the mid-2030s. CEO Christopher Womack framed the vertically integrated, state-regulated model (one-stop shop across generation, transmission and distribution) as the differentiator winning hyperscaler and data-center developer business in the Southeast.
quarterly_data.figure: 6 GW newly contracted in Q2 (Alabama ~3 GW + Georgia Power/OpenAI 3.2 GW); total contracted large load over 17 GW by mid-2030s

quarterly_data.signal: PROSPECTIVE LARGE-LOAD PIPELINE STILL ABOVE 75 GW, WITH 8 GW IN LATE-STAGE NEGOTIATION. Womack: new projects continue to be added to the prospective pipeline of large industrial and data-center projects, 'which remains well above 75 GW.' Beyond the 17 GW already contracted there are an additional 8 GW of projects in late stages, including 3 GW projected to be finalized in the near term; CFO David Poroch said those contracts are likely to go into 2028 and beyond, with a couple of them initiating their ramp-up in 2028 and running into the next decade. Womack also noted momentum migrating west, with 100 MW projects already succeeding in Mississippi and increasing activity there and in Alabama.
quarterly_data.figure: Prospective pipeline well above 75 GW; 8 GW late-stage of which 3 GW near-term; 100 MW projects in Mississippi

quarterly_data.signal: DATA-CENTER LOAD ACTUALLY ON THE SYSTEM IS COMPOUNDING FAST. System-wide data-center load now exceeds 1.2 GW, an increase of more than 500 megawatts over the prior year, and Poroch noted the company 'crossed over the 1,000 MW line this particular quarter.' Data-center usage was 55% higher than Q2 2025 and is up 49% year to date, primarily due to accelerating load ramps from large-load customers. That pulled weather-normal commercial sales up 7.4% in Q2 (+6% year to date) and total weather-normal retail electricity sales up 2.3% in the first half - the highest retail sales growth through June in nearly two decades. Q2 adjusted EPS was $1.13, up $0.21 versus Q2 2025 and $0.13 above the company's own estimate; first-half adjusted EPS was $2.46.
quarterly_data.figure: Data-center load >1.2 GW (+500 MW YoY); data-center usage +55% YoY in Q2, +49% YTD; commercial sales +7.4% Q2; Q2 adjusted EPS $1.13

quarterly_data.signal: GUIDANCE RAISED TO THE TOP OF THE RANGE ON LOAD GROWTH. Management now projects full-year 2026 adjusted earnings to be near or at the top of the $4.50-$4.60 adjusted EPS guidance range, with a Q3 adjusted EPS estimate of $1.50 per share, and reiterated the goal of being toward the top half of the long-term earnings trajectory. Drivers named were increased usage and customer growth, higher AFUDC from ongoing construction projects, higher earnings from equity-method investments, and contributions from Southern Company Gas and PowerSecure, where distributed, backup and bridge power solutions markets for data centers continue to expand.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance $4.50-$4.60, now expected near or at the top; Q3 estimate $1.50

quarterly_data.signal: GENERATION BUILDOUT FOR AI LOAD - 10 GW APPROVED AND GEORGIA ALREADY OVERSUBSCRIBED. Over the past several years Southern has secured regulatory approvals for 10 GW of new company-owned generation resources, including thermal, battery and solar, as well as hundreds of miles of new transmission lines. The first two of several battery sites are in service, and work on three combustion turbines at Plant Yates is advancing toward completion in the coming quarters. Poroch said the company is 'about 1 GW or 2 away from... selling out the capacity that we had approved in Georgia last year', and Womack added that 'the OpenAI contract in Georgia pushes us beyond our recently approved capacity by right around 1 GW' - i.e. the signed AI load has already outrun approved supply.
quarterly_data.figure: 10 GW of new company-owned generation approved (thermal/battery/solar) + hundreds of miles of transmission; Georgia capacity ~1 GW oversubscribed after the OpenAI contract

quarterly_data.signal: OPEN RFPs AT ALABAMA POWER AND GEORGIA POWER ARE INCREMENTAL CAPITAL NOT YET IN THE PLAN. Ongoing RFPs at both utilities are procuring additional generation for the early 2030s. Poroch was explicit that 'there is not placeholders in our capital plan... the RFPs that are open in Alabama, the RFPs that are open in Georgia, none of that is contemplated in our capital forecast at the moment,' and gave a sizing rule of thumb of 'about $2 billion or so, a little bit above maybe related to 1 GW of new generating capacity.' Timeline: selections known by year end 2026, a certification process running through much of 2027 with clarity in the latter part of 2027, spend feathering in around 2028, and the generation coming online in the 2030-2031 timeline. Alabama runs a near-parallel schedule.
quarterly_data.figure: Capital rule of thumb ~$2B per 1 GW of new generating capacity; RFP selections by year-end 2026, certification through 2027, generation online 2030-2031

quarterly_data.signal: HOW THE AI-LOAD CONTRACTS ARE CREDIT-PROTECTED - ABOUT $21 BILLION OF COLLATERAL BEHIND 17 GW. The large-load contracting framework has four pillars: long-term contracts (the OpenAI contract is 25 years), minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, default/termination provisions, and default payments tied to collateral. Poroch said forms of collateral include parent guarantees, lines of credit and surety bonds depending on counterparty credit quality, with the aim of a collateral portfolio equivalent to about A- or better. He initially cited '$20.8 billion of collateral... in the aggregate on full ramp' and then clarified that this refers to the entire portfolio: 'the whole portfolio of the 17 GW, we got about $21 billion of collateral.' Minimum bills effectively decouple revenue from actual customer ramp rates, which Womack said often differ from what was predicted at project approval.
quarterly_data.figure: About $21 billion of collateral in aggregate at full ramp across the 17 GW contracted portfolio; minimum bills cover 100% of incremental cost to serve

quarterly_data.signal: FIRST FLEXIBLE-DEMAND DATA CENTER: 1 GW OF DEMAND RESPONSE AT THE OPENAI SITE. The Savannah site features 1 GW of flexible demand response, and Womack confirmed this is the first time Southern has done that for a data center. Poroch said demand-response flexibility 'does enter into all those conversations' and is possible because the three electric jurisdictions are not limited to a tariff and can negotiate bilateral contracts that price hyperscaler flexibility. Womack said technical requirements - how a hyperscaler's operations affect the system and the grid, and whether it can be more than 'just a taker' - are raised very early in every hyperscaler conversation, and that peak shaving from this resource benefits the whole system.
quarterly_data.figure: 1 GW of flexible demand response at the OpenAI Savannah site - Southern's first for a data center

quarterly_data.signal: NEW NUCLEAR: HYPERSCALERS BEING ASKED TO SHARE AP1000 COST-OVERRUN RISK. Womack said the country needs more nuclear units in operation particularly in the mid-2030s, credited the administration for regulatory actions and for convening groups around long-lead-time items, but stated plainly that 'Southern Company is not going to be next' on a new nuclear build. Asked whether hyperscalers are willing to absorb cost overruns above budgeted amounts for AP1000s, he said he did not want to get ahead of a firm conclusion but 'yes, we are having conversations with them in terms of what role they can play.'

quarterly_data.signal: SOUTHERN POWER TOLLING AGREEMENTS ROLLING OFF ARE BEING RE-AIMED AT HYPERSCALERS. As existing tolling agreements expire, Womack said the team is in the midst of recontracting conversations with a host of counterparties, screened for creditworthiness, and sees upside in pricing versus where the contracts were originally struck - contributing to the durability and length of the long-term plan. Poroch added that conversations with both current and new Southern Power counterparties are 'proving to be very fruitful', covering repricing of expiring contracts into the next decade plus the previously announced uprate/brownfield opportunities, with an update expected later in the year; the business will not 'build something and see who shows up.'

quarterly_data.signal: ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT ANNOUNCEMENTS IN THE TERRITORY RAN AT THE SECOND-HIGHEST LEVEL EVER. Womack said there are no state-level moratoriums on data centers in the territory (though some counties have them) and that hyperscalers need to do a better job explaining the benefits, pointing to the OpenAI announcement as the template for community and rate-stability messaging.

Poroch: Georgia Power initiated the regulatory process for an all-source RFP to procure 2-6 GW of new dispatchable generation for in-service in 2032 and 2033; company-owned resources selected in the Alabama Power and Georgia Power RFPs would be substantial incremental investment above the base capital plan. Poroch: Southern Power is moving forward with 400 MW of additional capacity through natural gas turbine upgrades at multiple existing facilities in Alabama and Georgia, with commercial operation projected between 2029 and 2031, adding approximately $700 million to the capital plan; an additional 300 MW of natural gas uprates is under evaluation (covering the whole fleet; timing probably over the course of the next year or so). Contracting for the 400 MW is in fairly late-stage conversations; Womack said Southern Power has said numbers 'up in the mid-90s in terms of what's contracted' and that recontracting talks and conversations with potential hyperscalers are both underway. 'we don't take merchant risk.'

Poroch: an incremental $500 million of equity was sourced through the ATM program; including the $700 million of Southern Power capex, the remaining need for equity or equity equivalents is approximately $1.8 billion through 2030, on a path to 17% FFO to debt by 2029; incremental capital is expected to be funded about 40% with equity.

Poroch: robust interest from large load customers, including hyperscalers, has materialized into 26 signed contracts representing 10 gigawatts of fully contracted electric service agreements, 2 gigawatts higher than last quarter and 4 gigawatts higher than a year ago. Nearly all of the 26 projects are under construction, with load ramps totaling 8 gigawatts by the end of the 5-year planning horizon and ultimately 10 gigawatts beyond 2030. The company is in late-stage discussions for another 10 gigawatts, 3 gigawatts of which are 'working through final reviews and are highly likely to progress to an executed contract in the near term'; Poroch confirmed the 2030 plan includes the 10 gigawatts signed plus these 3 gigawatts and nothing beyond. The total large load pipeline has increased to over 75 gigawatts as momentum grows in Alabama and Mississippi. Poroch: retail electric sales across the three electric operating companies are projected to grow at least 3% in 2026, and annual electricity sales growth is projected to average 10% from 2026 through 2030, an increase of 2 percentage points from the prior long-term projection; Georgia Power's total retail electric sales growth is projected at approximately 13% over the same period. Poroch: 2026 adjusted EPS guidance is $4.50 to $4.60 per share (7% growth from the 2025 guidance range), with a first-quarter adjusted EPS estimate of $1.20. The company expects to grow adjusted EPS 8% to 9% from 2026 through 2028 and set initial ranges of $4.85 to $4.95 for 2027 (approximately 8% growth) and $5.25 and $5.45 for 2028 (approximately 9% growth), with approximately 7% to 8% growth longer term from the 2028 range - an average of 8% from the 2026 guidance midpoint to 2030. Poroch: the base capital investment forecast is $81 billion over the next 5 years, 95% of it at the state-regulated utilities, an $18 billion or approximately 30% increase from a year ago, driven mainly by new generation facilities (most announced or approved in 2025) and the approved Georgia IRP (uprates at existing natural gas and nuclear facilities, hydroelectric dam modernization). Roughly $42 billion through 2030 goes to serving projected growth through new generation, enhancements to existing generation and expansions of transmission and interstate pipeline systems, supporting state-regulated rate base growth of approximately 9%. The plan carries no capital placeholders; Alabama Power and Georgia Power RFPs for generation needed in the early to mid-2030s 'could represent several gigawatts of additional new generation', and Poroch gave a rough rule of thumb of $2 billion for a gig of incremental generation. Poroch noted Georgia Power 'just closed in December on 10 gigawatts' and said incremental capital above the plan would be financed with approximately 40% equity or equity equivalents.
quarterly_data.figure: base capital investment forecast $81 billion over the next 5 years, 95% at state-regulated utilities; $18 billion or approximately 30% increase; roughly $42 billion to serve projected growth; rate base growth of approximately 9%; $2 billion for a gig of incremental generation

quarterly_data.signal: LARGE-LOAD CONTRACT TERMS: 15-YEAR MINIMUMS, TAKE-OR-PAY-STYLE MINIMUM BILLS, COLLATERAL. Poroch: all three electric jurisdictions allow bilaterally negotiated large-load contracts rather than a standard tariff. Data-center contracts carry minimum terms of at least 15 years, fixed or minimum bill provisions 'similar to take-or-pay structures' designed to cover at least 100% of the annual incremental cost to serve (generation and transmission investment, incremental O&M and cost of capital), and termination payments backed by significant collateral requirements. As part of its December certification process for new generation, Georgia Power quantified at least approximately $1.7 billion of benefits lowering the cost to serve existing customers from 2029 through 2031, 'directly attributable to the value created by our approach to contracting'. Load taken beyond the minimum is priced at roughly the marginal cost and is upside to the plan.
quarterly_data.figure: minimum terms of at least 15 years; minimum bills to cover at least 100% of the annual incremental cost to serve; at least approximately $1.7 billion of benefits from 2029 through 2031

quarterly_data.signal: SOUTHERN POWER: GAS FLEET REPRICING AND UPRATES AS UPSIDE OUTSIDE THE PLAN. Womack: Southern Power has over 13 gigawatts of capacity across 55 generating facilities in 15 states, including over 7 gigawatts of natural gas generation in the Southeast, substantially all under long-term contracts. As gas-fleet contracts come up for renewal from the early 2030s, 'The market demand for capacity has increased pricing roughly 2 to 3x higher than where many of these assets are currently contracted', and by 2030 approximately 1,000 megawatts can be remarketed; Poroch cited market examples of 'around $20, maybe $25 a kilowatt month.' The company is in late-stage discussions on uprates of up to an additional 700 megawatts (as soon as '29 per Womack, not included in the plan) and is evaluating 6 brownfield sites in the Southeast for potential new gas development, always under long-term contracts with creditworthy counterparties. Asked whether the uprate capacity would be contracted with co-ops and other power companies rather than sold directly to data centers, Poroch said 'that's a very safe bet.'

Roadmap: Vertiv's technology must land well ahead of the most advanced silicon, so with NVIDIA or other silicon technology providers it looks out two, three years or beyond, and it architects technology with many customers one to three years out. On content per megawatt, the CEO says the analyst's dollar-per-megawatt framework can be used for now, and technology complexity is, if anything, good for TAM per megawatt.

Because plants were already being staffed and prepared for significantly higher volume, the part shortages caused temporary downtime and lower-than-planned capacity utilisation across the expansion sites: excess labour plus unfavourable overhead absorption on the lower volumes had a 450-550 basis point impact on Data Center margin in the quarter, on top of a 150 basis point year-over-year warranty variance from a large prior-year settlement. Modine repositioned available parts to its highest-producing, most efficient lines and idled others, and rationed supply so that its largest key accounts got priority over smaller customers. By the third month of the quarter (June) Data Center margin was 'right back where we'd expect it to be,' and management said it has now secured the supply chain needed to meet demand for the rest of the year.

quarterly_data.signal: Kumamoto earthquake impact limited: Nishiki back-end factory has resumed full production; Kawashiri front-end factory (about 13% of company-wide sales) expected to resume production on August 5 with about three weeks to full operation - wafer testing already resumed, pure-water and facility repairs under way. Die bank and inventory had been secured beforehand; shake was smaller than the 2016 quake and countermeasures (anti-seismic equipment mounting, BCP inventory) sped recovery. J-OSAT partner in Kyushu also impacted but outlook limited; customer supply chains being monitored. Separately, the Takasaki 6-inch front-end factory will be gradually closed (6-inch equipment maintenance/parts no longer supportable industry-wide), production migrating to 8-inch plus; employment maintained and the site shifts toward R&D.
quarterly_data.figure: Kawashiri plant (13% of sales) restart August 5, ~3 weeks to full operation; Takasaki 6-inch plant to close gradually

TI has invested in technology for the higher-power rails (VCore, where much of the current going into an accelerator or CPU comes from), which TI is building in Sherman, Texas, where its BCD process 'is serving us very well': 'That product is sampling, and we expect our opportunity in data center to further expand in the coming years.' TI plans to play across the different data-center sockets as long as CapEx continues into this market.

quarterly_data.signal: Pricing and supply posture: asked whether TI is raising prices in Q1 2026 (analysts cited peers discussing early-2026 increases), the CEO said 'the answer is no. It's not pricing related' — the like-for-like price effect in 2025 finished low single digits down as expected ('think about two or 3% down'), and that is also TI's assumption for 2026, though TI would respond if pricing conditions change; Q1 pricing usually goes down a little because of yearly negotiations, with 'Definitely no step function planned in Q1'. Lead times are unchanged, 'on average, below thirteen weeks', 'probably the lowest in the industry'. Inventory ended Q4 at $4.8 billion (down $25 million QoQ; 222 days), which management calls an asset for real-time demand, and TI is 'well-positioned with capacity'. The CEO noted 'we all know about the memory shortages', and management said customers that finally complete their bill of materials have come in at the last minute wanting product shipped right away.

quarterly_data.signal: Manufacturing (CEO): the Sherman fab 'ramped ahead of schedule, high yield', and with its new equipment the factory is 'more capable than we originally hoped', so a high level of throughput is planned; Sherman one's clean room already has some production lines running, and TI has additional shell space ('Shell instrument two' as transcribed) it can build into if demand is very strong. The 'Lehigh' fab (as transcribed) is on schedule, insourcing wafers from foundries — mainly embedded processing, a tailwind that continues in 2026: TI completed its 65-nanometer transition in 2025, yielding at the same level as in the foundries, and is now moving its 45-nanometer technology, mainly for its automotive radar business. quarterly_data.signal: Management is decidedly more optimistic on H2 than at the Q1 call: the wafer-allocation doubts voiced in Q1 have eased because of the deep TSMC relationship ('we have more chance to get upside capacity'), and by late Q1/early Q2 the company found TSMC support and customers' capacity commitments much firmer. Cloud-related shipments (cloud compute, cloud training, cloud connectivity) were close to 80% of Q2 shipments with the remaining ~20% consumer/crypto/memory-related; the H2 mix should be similar, with crypto fading toward nothing and automotive ramping in its place. Versus last year, China's share of revenue declines (absolute volume still up), while the US share and Taiwan share both increase. Full-year gross margin: still confident, but dependent on customers' production ramp success and whether NRE tape-outs land this year or slip to next year.

quarterly_data.signal: Pre-payments rose notably in Q2 because GUC pre-buys materials for large CSP turnkey programs - besides CoWoS it must secure HBM stacks and substrate ahead of the build so everything (substrate, HBM, the SoC from TSMC) arrives together for packaging. GUC sells the customer the finished CoWoS package with HBM inside; if HBM prices rise the chip price rises with it, so the cost risk sits with the customer, not GUC. Management cited HBM pricing going from about 240 at the start of the year to 700 and up to 900 (as spoken; unit not stated), fully passed through. Whether HBM procurement flows through GUC's own P&L or is booked as a service fee is still being worked out case by case at this early stage.
quarterly_data.figure: HBM price cited from ~240 early in the year to 700-900 (as spoken), passed through to customers

quarterly_data.signal: North America CPU customer: GUC has won the next-generation project; the next chip is expected to reach volume production around the end of this year / early next year, while the current project has been shipping for almost two years. Next year's wafer capacity allocation is being opened up by TSMC over the coming 1-2 months and management is 'very optimistic', though the outcome depends on TSMC capacity and the customer's own forecast. Management is confident the customer will keep outsourcing back-end physical design even as it builds in-house capability, because one product line spans too many SKUs to take fully in-house. Automotive: the China automotive customer (combined cockpit+ADAS single chip, taped out around October-November last year) should start contributing revenue next year; for the North America automotive customer GUC did the current-generation tape-out and is in talks for the next generation, with the volume timing dependent on that customer's robotics plans.

The R&D roadmap already includes CPO, IVR (integrated voltage regulator), next-generation UCIe die-to-die, and N2-on-N2 advanced-process development; opex should grow only modestly versus a clearly larger revenue increase next year.

quarterly_data.signal: 2026 logic and industry outlook: management expects Entegris to benefit from node transitions in both logic and memory. Rising demand for two-nanometer devices should meaningfully lift wafer output through 2026, and that node carries both higher content per wafer and strong share for Entegris. Advanced logic fab utilization is already near 100%, and customers are investing aggressively in more capacity. At the most advanced logic node, Entegris has secured strong POR (position of record) positions in CMP consumables, advanced deposition and implant materials, liquid purification and filtration, and wafer handling. The team is now focused on winning incremental share and PORs at subsequent advanced nodes. Separately, the CEO said it takes time to grow two-nanometer and to transition to new nodes such as 1.4 nanometer. Management expects 'middish single-digit' industry MSI (wafer starts) growth in 2026 and strong WFE growth. Fab construction CapEx should grow modestly after last year's high single-digit decline, weighted to the second half, with a bigger acceleration in 2027 as work starts on new fabs. Management flagged ongoing memory shortages as a possible second-half 2026 risk for mainstream end markets; guidance assumes no impact.
quarterly_data.figure: middish single-digit industry MSI growth expected in 2026; advanced logic utilization near 100%

quarterly_data.signal: NAND: the move from roughly 250 layers to approximately 300 layers is under way. Management expects more than 20% NAND bit growth in 2026, driven mainly by higher-layer, higher-capacity NAND rather than a big increase in wafer starts. Entegris expects a double-digit increase in its NAND content per wafer as customers move to higher layer counts and adopt new materials such as moly and selective etch. It has won strong POR positions in NAND deposition materials, CMP and selective etch. NAND utilization is around 85%, and layer-count increases are absorbing most of the remaining 15% of capacity, with fewer new wafer starts. If demand stays strong, flash makers will likely need to add significant fab capacity, setting up higher NAND MSI growth in 2027. The CEO said Entegris gains from both layer growth and wafer growth, with slightly more from a full wafer start.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 20% NAND bit growth expected in 2026; double-digit increase in NAND content per wafer; NAND utilization around 85%

quarterly_data.signal: DRAM, HBM and advanced packaging: DRAM capacity was nearly fully utilized at the end of 2025, and management expects it to stay that way through 2026. More DRAM is shifting from standalone DDR5 into HBM, which adds some content per wafer, though less than a new wafer start would. Management expects tight supply in HBM, DDR5 and advanced packaging to require additional fab capacity heading into 2027. Entegris is gaining traction in DRAM and HBM, particularly with CMP consumables and advanced packaging solutions. The CEO said advanced packaging revenue grew nicely in 2025, to 'roughly a $100 million plus minus', and should keep growing in 2026. Several product lines for advanced packaging are sampling now and more will sample later in the year, so the larger benefit is expected in 2027 and beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: advanced packaging revenue roughly $100 million (2025), expected to keep growing in 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and capex: the multiyear manufacturing capex cycle that began in 2022 is complete. Capex was $299 million in 2025 (approximately 9% of sales) and is expected to fall to $250 million in 2026, returning longer term to approximately 7% to 8% of sales. Management said the new capacity plus the existing base can deliver significantly more than $1 billion in incremental revenue with limited further investment. The Taiwan facility is still ramping, and the Colorado facility should substantially complete key customer product qualifications in 2026. Entegris exited its Chester, Pennsylvania facility in Q4 and expects to rationalize at least one additional facility in 2026. Free cash flow was $404 million in 2025, a 12.7% margin (up nearly 300 basis points year over year). Net leverage ended 2025 at 3.8 times, against a target of below 3.5 times by the end of 2026, and Entegris paid down $300 million of its term loan during 2025.

quarterly_data.signal: Mechanism behind the better-than-expected July quarter, which the Q3 call did not spell out. April-quarter push-outs came from customers being unable to capture memory and from Asian fabs at unusually high utilization telling chip designs 'You have to delay your design because we don't have the capacity for it'. Through the July quarter those designs started to be released because the same fabs 'added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range', and in some cases told a customer with a 40 nanometer design 'if you move that chip design to 28 nanometers or 22 nanometers, I will then manufacture it for you' - i.e. the capacity shortage is actively forcing node migration, which is the ASP-positive trend Photronics benefits from. On the display side Korea is strong on high-end consumer electronics launching this fall while China has pulled back because low-end consumer electronics cannot capture memory; Moreau relayed that the memory companies are talking about 'another 2, 3, 4 years before supply and demand comes into equilibrium'.

The balance sheet has $673 million of cash, but $504 million of it sits in the two 50/50 semiconductor joint ventures (Taiwan, entered 2013-2014; China, 2018-2019; ownership 50.01%) and can only be spent at those facilities - dividending $100 million out returns roughly $40 million after the partner split and a 20% tax, 'not a really productive use of cash'. Only about $165 million of cash sits outside the joint ventures, so 'if we need cash, we would either issue debt or a line of credit... Not likely to use equity'. CEO John Lee framed the content opportunity by layer count: smartphone PCBs are around 10 to 12 layers and go up a couple of layers every cycle, AI also needs multilayer boards of 30 to 40 layers plus package-substrate layers, and for AI 'we're talking about doubling the number of layers'; AI's share of chemistry revenue rose sequentially quarter after quarter in 2025 and is expected to keep taking a larger share, with AI chemistry more than making up for any slight decrease in PCs and smartphones because AI supply-chain customers are running at capacity and continue to add tools. contracts.signal: PTI and Broadcom will form a joint venture in Singapore - a major milestone making PTI a strategic and preferred partner of Broadcom. edges.relationship: Joint X-ray process-control solutions (Onto AI Diffract software + Rigaku X-ray metrology)

contracts.signal: Expanded collaboration to deliver new process-control solutions combining Onto software with Rigaku X-ray metrology for 3D and exotic materials; positive customer response, incremental opportunity into 2027-2028

contracts.source: Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
contracts.signal: Plisinski confirmed the Rigaku transaction has closed ('First it's closed, so that's done deal') and declined to discuss further steps. He said the partnership is strategic not because OCD is running out of steam - Onto believes it can keep pushing OCD for the foreseeable future - but because as the world moves to more 3D transistors and 3D stacking of die or wafers there are elements between layers that optical cannot solve, where X-ray can see through. Onto has already started with two different customers, went up against the leading player in X-ray and beat them at both customers, on the strength of Onto's AI Diffract modelling engine combined with Rigaku's sensor/X-ray capability. The next step is hybrid metrology - the speed of optical combined with the precision of slower X-ray - made simpler because AI Diffract already aggregates and models the data streams together.
